docs.text:
A–E a rating per application, with the why behind it

Wave 1 the components that can run in Linux containers now, even when the rest stays on Windows

B → A one LLM order makes the code changes, verified in the sandbox

1 VM web UI, scanner, SQL Server, k3s sandbox, registry, Grafana

docs.title: Which of your applications can run in containers?
docs.text:
Containerizer scans your whole application portfolio, rates every application from A (container-ready: a modern stack that moves to containers without code changes) to E (not feasible: stays on Windows), explains each obstacle with a fix and references, plans the move in waves (what can run in Linux containers now, what after code changes, what stays on Windows), and generates hardened Dockerfiles and Kubernetes manifests for everything that can move. Then it proves them by building, running and deploying them in its own sandbox cluster.

Get started How it works GitHub

docs.title: Why Containerizer?
docs.text:
• Rules first, AI last

    A data-driven rule set classifies every component, so results are repeatable, explainable and free. An LLM is asked only about what the rules are unsure of, and its answers are validated first.

    How it works

  • Learns by doing

    When unsure, it builds and runs the container, matches failures, patches the plan and retries. Fixes that work become rule proposals that a person approves, so the next run needs no retries.

    Rule review

  • Secure by default

    Chiseled images, non-root, read-only root filesystem, no capabilities, seccomp, Pod Security restricted, and a gate that scans with Trivy and Grype. Every exception is recorded with its reason.

    Security gate

  • Your whole organization

    Schedule scans of Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitLab organizations. New repositories are found automatically, and the A-rated ones are pushed and committed for Flux.

    Organization scans

  • Proven in a sandbox

    A built-in k3s cluster deploys what was generated and reports "deployed and healthy" or exactly why not, even with a restored copy of the application's development database.

    The sandbox cluster

  • A migration plan, not just a verdict

    Every blocker maps to a Linux replacement: System.Drawing to SkiaSharp, WCF to CoreWCF, Windows Service to a worker service, with packages, steps and checks.

    Migration assistant

  • Refactoring patches, verified

    For a B-rated application the LLM makes the targeted code changes, one file at a time. The patch is applied to the assessed commit, checked with the rules, built and run before you download it.

    Refactoring patches

  • Build pipelines for your CI

    GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD or Azure Pipelines, for where the code lives: build every component, SBOM and scan it on pull requests, push and sign from the default branch, as a patch to git am.

    Build pipelines

  • Runs in your network

    One immutable appliance with signed upgrades and roll back, only SSH and HTTPS in, and outgoing traffic blocked except for hosts an admin allows. Use Claude, your own self-hosted LLM, or the appliance's built-in CPU LLM when you have no GPU.

    Appliance · The LLM

  • Built for management and audit

    Single sign-on, admins, product owners and operators, an audit log of every change, an access log, and trends over time.

    Sign-in and roles

docs.title: Every application, explained
docs.text:
Open an application to see its components, the rating, the main obstacles, and for each finding what to change, why, and where to read more. Everything links back to the rule that decided it.

How it works

docs.title: Start with what is ready
docs.text:
An application rated for the parts that must stay on Windows often has components that can run in Linux containers today. Its migration plan splits it into waves: what runs now (and is in the sandbox already), what follows after code changes, what stays on Windows, and the calls between the parts.

Migration plan

docs.title: From blocker to a concrete plan
docs.text:
The migration assistant turns each blocking finding into a Linux-compatible replacement with packages to add and remove, steps and checks. What can't move is marked "keep on Windows" instead of being forced.

Migration assistant

docs.title: Make it A
docs.text:
One order has the LLM fix everything that keeps a B application from A, verifies and repairs the patch, assesses it again and deploys the patched copy to the sandbox in place of the application's scan output. Every order shows its tokens and time, and needs an administrator's approval until you trust it.

Refactoring patches

docs.title: See what every app needs from the network
docs.text:
Each application's page draws what it connects to, from its configuration, its NetworkPolicy, what the sandbox blocked and the other applications it calls. An LLM proposes the egress rules the configuration explains and flags the suspicious ones; a person approves, and connectivity.yaml next to the manifests gives the firewall team the FQDNs.

Egress and network connectivity

docs.title: Connect the applications that call each other
docs.text:
Components in different repositories and products are linked when one's configuration names the other's service, the sandbox sees the call, or the LLM matches an internal name. A person confirms the link; both NetworkPolicies allow it, and both connectivity.yaml files document it.

Links between applications

docs.title: Watch the portfolio move
docs.text:
Trends show how ratings change over time per business unit and product, so you can see the effect of each fix and each newly learned rule.

Install the appliance

docs.title: Tag it, filter by it
docs.text:
Administrators and operators tag applications (customer-facing, PCI, migration wave 1, ...), and everyone filters the front page by a tag: the tiles and bars then count only those applications.

Application tags

docs.title: Scans that run themselves
docs.text:
Define organization scans on the admin pages, by day and time or on demand. Discover first lists the projects, repositories and latest commits without cloning anything, so deprecated ones can be disabled before the full scan. Every repository shows its last result, and skipped ones are listed with the reason, such as "no source code".

Organization scans

docs.title: Who owns which repository?
docs.text:
Every scan reads who committed where in the last six months. Give the developers their business units, and the repositories and products nobody mapped get a suggested business unit, weighed by commits. To start with, each Azure DevOps project (GitLab subgroup) becomes a product, with its applications mapped to it.

Developers and ownership

docs.title: A slow LLM never holds up a scan
docs.text:
With a CPU-only or busy LLM, scans can leave the LLM reviews to a queue: uncertain components first, then a second opinion on blockers. Reorder it, limit it to quiet hours or an idle machine, and see how many tokens and hours are left, estimated from the speed it has measured on your LLM.

The LLM queue

docs.title: From finding to a verified patch
docs.text:
For applications that need targeted code changes, an operator presses Make it A. The LLM makes the changes, then Containerizer applies them to the assessed commit, runs the rules again and builds and runs the container. You get a coloured diff, the result per finding and a .patch to apply with git am.

Refactoring patches

docs.title: A person approves what the AI learns
docs.text:
Fixes the learning loop discovers arrive as rule proposals with their evidence. Approve, edit or reject them; approved rules make the next run faster and AI-free.

Rule review

docs.title: From B to A, running in the sandbox
docs.text:
The front page lists the applications a verified Make it A patch makes A, and whether that patched copy runs in the sandbox right now.

Make it A

docs.title: Try what already runs
docs.text:
The parts of an application that are ready run in the sandbox before the rest is changed. The front page lists every application that runs there, whole or in part ("12 of 16 components"), with a link to open it, and the application's page says the same at the top.

Migration plan

docs.title: Operations you can see
docs.text:
The scan worker exports Prometheus metrics about scans, the process and the VM, with a Grafana dashboard included in the appliance.

Metrics and Grafana

docs.title: Try it
docs.text:
Download the appliance from the latest release, boot it, and point it at your source control.

Install the appliance How it works Releases

docs.title: API
docs.text:
Scripts and other tools can read the results and maintain the business units, products and application mapping through a JSON API under /api/v1. Callers authenticate with an API key, or with an OAuth access token from the same identity provider as the sign-in. Cookies are never used.

The API is on whenever the admin pages are (with sign-in, or in development mode).

docs.title: API keys
docs.text:
Administrators make keys on Admin → API, which also shows how to call the API from this server with curl and Python. A key (czk_…) has a name, a role and an optional expiry:

Role May Read only GET everything the API offers Full also add, change and remove business units and products, and map applications

The key is shown once, when it is made: only its SHA-256 is stored. The page lists every key with its status, who made it and when, when it expires and when it was last used, and revokes keys. Making and revoking keys, and every change made with a key (as api-key:<prefix>), are in the change history.

curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $CZ_API_KEY" https://containerizer.example.com/api/v1/applications

docs.title: Access tokens (OpenID Connect)
docs.text:
To let automation use access tokens from your identity provider instead, add two settings to /etc/containerizer/web.env next to the sign-in ones and restart the web UI:

Variable Meaning CONTAINERIZER_API_AUDIENCE The audience access tokens must be issued for, e.g. api://containerizer (Entra ID: the Application ID URI of the app registration). CONTAINERIZER_API_CLIENTS Automation that may change everything, comma separated: client:<client id> (the token's azp, appid or client_id), or role:, group:, email:, domain:, sub: rules. Optional when the roles are enough.

With Entra ID: set accessTokenAcceptedVersion to 2 in the API app's manifest so its access tokens carry the same v2.0 issuer as the sign-in, define an app role (e.g. Containerizer.Write, allowed member type Applications), grant it to the client app, and set CONTAINERIZER_API_CLIENTS=role:Containerizer.Write.

docs.title: Authentication and authorization
docs.text:
Callers send Authorization: Bearer <API key or access token>. For access tokens: the client-credentials flow for automation, or a user's token. Signature, issuer, audience and expiry are checked; an ID token is refused (its audience is the web app). Cookies are ignored, so there is no CSRF surface.

The roles apply to tokens too: admins and API clients can change everything, product owners only their own products and applications (403 forbidden outside them), operators only read. A token that matches none of these (viewers included) gets 403 insufficient_scope. Changes appear in the change history with Via API and the user's e-mail, or client:<client id> for an application.

docs.title: Endpoints
docs.text:
Bodies are JSON (Content-Type: application/json, up to 64 KiB); unknown fields are refused.

Method and path Does GET /api/v1/business-units · POST list (?name=) · create {"name", "owner", "description"} GET · PATCH · PUT · DELETE /api/v1/business-units/{id} read · change some fields · replace · delete (409 while products are in it) GET /api/v1/products · POST list (?name=, ?businessUnitId=) · create {"name", "businessUnitId", "infoUrl", "owner", "description"} GET · PATCH · PUT · DELETE /api/v1/products/{id} as above (409 while applications are mapped to it) GET /api/v1/applications list with the latest rating and the tags (?unmapped=true, ?productId=, ?name=, ?tag=, ?retired=true) GET · PATCH /api/v1/applications/{id} read · set productId, displayName, owner, description, retired (applications themselves come from scans) GET /api/v1/audit the change history (?table=Application, ?rowId=, ?limit= up to 1000)

businessUnitId and productId filters take an id or none (not assigned). Errors are {"error": "...", "message": "..."} with 400 (invalid field), 401 (no or bad token), 403 (not allowed), 404, 405, 409 (name taken, referenced row missing or still in use), 413 or 415.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
# Entra ID client credentials (a second app registration as the client, granted the API's app role)
TOKEN=$(curl -s https://login.microsoftonline.com/$TENANT/oauth2/v2.0/token \
  -d grant_type=client_credentials -d client_id=$CLIENT_ID -d client_secret=$CLIENT_SECRET \
  -d scope=api://containerizer/.default | jq -r .access_token)
API=https://containerizer.example.com/api/v1

# map every unmapped application from one repository to the Billing product
PRODUCT=$(curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$API/products?name=Billing" | jq '.items[0].id')
curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" "$API/applications?unmapped=true" \
  | jq -r '.items[] | select(.repositoryUrl == "https://dev.azure.com/contoso/Billing/_git/billing") | .id' \
  | while read id; do
      curl -s -X PATCH -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
        -d "{\"productId\": $PRODUCT}" "$API/applications/$id"
    done

docs.title: Running the appliance
docs.text: The appliance is an immutable OS image built with the Elemental toolkit (as in Firewall4AI), installed from an ISO or started from a disk image, and upgraded from the admin pages. To install it, see Getting started.

docs.title: What it runs
docs.text:
Part How Reached at Web UI and API (results, admin pages, System, Firewall and Sandbox HTTPS pages) systemd service, user cz-web, no privileges https://<appliance>/ Scan worker (organization scans) systemd service, user containerizer; Docker only through the Docker socket guard - LLM queue runner (queued LLM reviews, refactoring patches) systemd service containerizer-llm-queue, user containerizer, Docker through the guard (to build and run refactoring patches), reads the scan worker's clones, writes only its answer cache and /var/lib/containerizer/refactor Admin → LLM queue, Admin → Refactoring Egress observer: what the sandbox blocks (its NetworkPolicies, the firewall, the DNS filter) systemd service containerizer-egress-observer, user containerizer with CAP_NET_ADMIN (the NFLOG drop log) and CAP_SYSLOG (the kernel log, for the firewall's drops) only, its own read-only Kubernetes account Admin → Egress, the results pages' Network connectivity SQL Server 2025 (results database), or your own SQL Server (external database) container, non-root, data on the persistent partition 127.0.0.1:1433 only Sandbox cluster: k3s (single node) with Flux and Traefik systemd service kubectl and helm on the appliance; apps at https://<component>-<app>.<domain>/ with Sandbox HTTPS Lab services for the sandboxed apps: SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, Redis, RabbitMQ, Kafka, S3, Azure Blob storage, SFTP, a catch-all mailbox for the mail the apps send (each optional) k3s, namespace containerizer-lab, data on the persistent partition Admin → Lab services; inside the cluster only Local container registry container 127.0.0.1:5000 only (Docker and k3s) Prometheus and Grafana, with the scan worker's, k3s' and Flux's metrics, alerts and dashboards (metrics) containers https://<appliance>/grafana/ HTTPS (Caddy), SSH systemd services ports 443 and 22: the only open ports Firewall and DNS filter: every outgoing connection is blocked unless an allow-list rule covers it nftables + dnsmasq Admin → Firewall Built-in LLM (optional, off by default): llama.cpp with Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B on the CPU container, non-root, read-only model 127.0.0.1:8090 (and up, one port per server) only; Admin → Source control & LLM kubemg (optional, off by default): audited console and kubectl access to the sandbox cluster containers (kubemg and its PostgreSQL), non-root, read-only; its agent in the sandbox cluster https://kubemg.<appliance>/ (its own name on 443) 
                 443 (HTTPS)                                  22 (SSH, root)    
                     │                                              │
 ┌───────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Caddy ──► web UI + API ──(status, requests)──► system agent (root): upgrade, roll back, firewall    │
 │   │        │                                                                                       │
 │   │        └──► SQL Server ◄── scan worker ──► Docker (builds, scans) ──push──► registry :5000      │
 │   └──► Grafana ──► Prometheus ──scrape──┘                                           │ pull         │
 │                                                         k3s + Flux ◄── output repo ─┘              │
 │ nftables: in 22/443 only · out: only to addresses of allowed names (dnsmasq fills the sets)        │
 └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
   OS: read-only btrfs snapshot (A/B with fallback)      data: COS_PERSISTENT partition (rest of the disk)

The OS is a read-only snapshot of the container image ghcr.io/olljanat-ai/containerizer-appliance. Everything that has to survive a restart or an upgrade is on the persistent partition: the database, /etc/containerizer (configuration and generated secrets), Docker and k3s data, the registry, clones, learned rules, logs. An upgrade writes the new version as a new snapshot next to the running one; if it does not start properly, the appliance goes back to the previous snapshot by itself.

docs.title: Root password and SSH
docs.text:
root is the only administrator account on the OS. It signs in on the console or over SSH with its password, or over SSH with a key in /root/.ssh/authorized_keys. The password is containerizer and (except in 0.3.4, where you change it yourself with passwd) expired on a new appliance, so the first sign-in, on the console or over SSH, asks for a new one (until then PAM may refuse an SSH key as well). /etc is rebuilt at every boot, so the appliance keeps root's password entry in /etc/containerizer/secrets/root-shadow (persistent partition) and puts it back at every start; changes with passwd are saved there by themselves (containerizer-root-password.path).

  • Keys only: after adding your key, passwd -l root locks the password: password sign-in stops working on SSH and the console, keys keep working. passwd -u root unlocks it.
  • Forgotten password: start the recovery system from the GRUB menu (it always starts with the default password, expired), mount the persistent partition (label COS_PERSISTENT) and delete root-shadow from the secrets folder of /etc/containerizer there; the next start of the appliance goes back to the default password.
  • The recovery system does not keep a changed password: each start asks for a new one again.

docs.title: Unattended installs
docs.text:
Pass an Elemental cloud-config with the key, e.g. elemental install --cloud-init my.yaml /dev/sda from the ISO, or put the file into the OEM partition:

stages:
  fs:
    - name: "SSH key of the administrator"
      authorized_keys:
        root:
          - "ssh-ed25519 AAAA... you@example.com"

The root password is the default (containerizer) and expired on unattended installs too.

docs.title: Configuration files
docs.text:
The first boot creates /etc/containerizer/ (mode 700) with:

File What to set appliance.env CZ_HOSTNAME (the DNS name users open, usually the FQDN: the name in the HTTPS certificate and the sign-in redirect; it does not rename the machine), CZ_ACME_EMAIL (Let's Encrypt instead of the appliance's own CA; your own certificate: HTTPS certificate), CZ_DNS_SERVERS, CZ_MSSQL_EDITION, CZ_MSSQL_MEMORY, CZ_SQL_* (external database), CZ_LLM_HEAVY (LLM-heavy mode, off by default) web.env Sign-in for the web UI: CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_*, CONTAINERIZER_ADMINS, roles, viewers, API (sign-in and roles). CONTAINERIZER_ROLE_SOURCE=ui gives the operator, product owner and viewer roles on Admin → Users and roles instead of in this file (roles on the admin pages) worker.env Push credentials for an external image registry, and extra registry hosts the worker may push to. Scans that push to the appliance's own registry need none; source control tokens are registered on the admin pages (source-control.md) sandbox.env The output repository the sandbox cluster deploys from (the sandbox cluster) grafana.env Optional Grafana settings, e.g. sign-in with your identity provider egress.json The egress allow-list: change it on the Firewall page, not here secrets/ Generated passwords (SQL Server logins, Grafana admin), the root password (root-shadow), sql-owner for an external database and the key pair that seals source control tokens (credential-key for the worker only, credential-key.pub for the web UI): root-only, never shown in the web UI. Keep credential-key when restoring a backup: the registered tokens open only with it network/ Optional systemd-networkd .network files for static addresses (default: every NIC in one bond, DHCP on it: Network)

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
As olljanat/nomad-qemu-node does with netplan: every wired interface (e*) joins one bond, bond0, in active-backup mode; the bond is the only port of a bridge, br0, and the appliance takes its address on br0 by DHCP (IPv4, and IPv6 router advertisements). The interfaces and the bond have no address of their own. On a physical server, cable every NIC you want to use: when the active one loses its link (a cable, a NIC or a switch port), another takes over within a fraction of a second, on the same address. Connect them to the same network (VLAN); no switch configuration is needed (no LACP). On a VM with one NIC the bond is just that NIC. The bridge has STP off and no forward delay (one port), and VLAN filtering on with VLAN 1 untagged.

  • Management controllers: the USB network interface a server's management controller gives the OS (Dell iDRAC, HPE iLO, Lenovo XCC: drivers cdc_ether, rndis_host, cdc_ncm, cdc_eem) never joins the bond. It is always up and leads to the controller only; in the bond, active-backup could choose it, and nothing reached the network (0.13.0).
  • MAC address: the bond and the bridge use the MAC of the first interface, so a hypervisor that allows only the MAC it assigned (Hyper-V, vSphere port groups that reject forged transmits) still passes the traffic. Every interface of the bond shows that MAC (its own is in cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0, "Permanent HW addr").
  • DHCP reservation: the DHCP client ID is that MAC address, so the appliance keeps one address from the first boot of the installer on, through installing, reinstalling and upgrading. Reserve the address by that MAC address (networkctl status br0 shows it and the lease), or set a static address. The host name is neither sent nor taken from DHCP (it is the sandbox cluster's node name). The console's sign-in banner shows the address of br0 and the network commands.

  • Static address: on the console (or over SSH), as root, with the appliance's cz command:

    cz network static 192.0.2.10/24 192.0.2.1 192.0.2.53     # address/prefix, gateway, 1 to 3 DNS servers
cz network show                                          # the address, gateway and DNS servers in use
cz network dhcp                                          # back to DHCP

It is checked first (the gateway in the address's network, at least one DNS server, IPv4 or IPv6) and applied at once, without a restart: an SSH session over the old address ends, so change it on the console (a server's remote console works) or from where you can reach the new one. The DNS filter is rebuilt with the DNS servers given (unless CZ_DNS_SERVERS in appliance.env names others), and the HTTPS certificate from the appliance's own CA gets the new address. The setting is the file /etc/containerizer/network/10-static.network (systemd-networkd, for br0), kept over restarts and upgrades; a static file of 0.13.x (for bond0) is moved to br0 at the first start of 0.14.0. Any .network file in that folder that sorts before 20-uplink.network works the same way: one that matches some NICs by name with Bond=bond0 (Name=eno1 eno2) and one with [Link] Unmanaged=yes for the others (Name=e*) limit the bond to those NICs. - Switches: the appliance sends and receives LLDP on every port, so the switch shows which port it is on, and networkctl lldp shows the switch and port of each NIC. - cat /proc/net/bonding/bond0 shows the active interface and each port's link. - cz runs the appliance's administration commands (the system agent, as root): cz network ..., cz upgrade vX.Y.Z, cz rollback <snapshot>, cz app-patch remove, cz firewall show; cz alone lists them.

docs.title: HTTPS certificate
docs.text:
The web UI and Grafana are served over HTTPS for CZ_HOSTNAME (appliance.env) with one of three certificates, the first that applies:

  1. Your own, for example from your company's CA: put the certificate in /etc/containerizer/tls/cert.pem, followed by its intermediate CA certificates (PEM, server certificate first; the root is not needed), and its private key, unencrypted, in /etc/containerizer/tls/key.pem (chmod 600). It must name CZ_HOSTNAME (subject alternative name). Then systemctl reboot. Renew it the same way: replace both files and restart. It wins over CZ_ACME_EMAIL.
  2. Let's Encrypt, with CZ_ACME_EMAIL set: the name must resolve to the appliance from the internet (TLS-ALPN challenge on 443), and acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org must be allowed on the Firewall page.
  3. The appliance's own CA (default): browsers warn until you trust its root, /var/lib/caddy/.local/share/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt.

Only the internal CA's certificate also covers the appliance's IP addresses. If the web UI does not answer after a change, journalctl -b -u caddy -u containerizer-firstboot says why (for example a key that does not match the certificate).

docs.title: External database
docs.text:
By default the results database runs on the appliance, and you back it up (Backup). To keep it on a SQL Server you already run and back up (SQL Server 2019 or later, or Azure SQL Managed Instance), point the appliance at it in appliance.env. SQL Server then does not run on the appliance, and the database is backed up with your server; the appliance's files still need their backup (Backup).

  1. On your server, create the database and a login that owns it (db_owner). With CZ_SQL_LOGINS=create (the default) the login also needs ALTER ANY LOGIN (e.g. securityadmin): it creates the logins cz_scanner, cz_web and cz_admin with generated passwords. If your DBA creates logins instead, create those three yourself and set CZ_SQL_LOGINS=existing.

  2. In /etc/containerizer/appliance.env:

    CZ_SQL_SERVER=sql01.example.com,1433
CZ_SQL_DATABASE=Containerizer
CZ_SQL_USER=containerizer_owner
CZ_SQL_LOGINS=create
# optional: more connection string options, in quotes
CZ_SQL_OPTIONS="Schema=containerizer"
# optional: the CA of the server's certificate when the system CAs do not cover it
CZ_SQL_CA=/etc/containerizer/sql-ca.pem

  3. Put the passwords in place (root only):

    install -m 0400 /dev/stdin /etc/containerizer/secrets/sql-owner      # the password of CZ_SQL_USER, then Ctrl-D
# only with CZ_SQL_LOGINS=existing: the three logins' passwords, the same way, into
# secrets/cz-scanner, secrets/cz-web and secrets/cz-admin

  4. Reboot.

At every start containerizer-db-init creates or upgrades the schema on that server as CZ_SQL_USER (the same as on the appliance's own SQL Server), so an upgrade of the appliance upgrades the database. The connection is encrypted and the server certificate is checked (the system CAs, or CZ_SQL_CA); TrustServerCertificate=yes in CZ_SQL_OPTIONS turns the check off, for test servers only. The firewall allows the server and port by itself (Firewall page → Always allowed); a DNS name must resolve through the appliance's DNS servers (CZ_DNS_SERVERS). Named instances (host\instance) are not supported: give the port. The login names are fixed, so one SQL Server instance serves one appliance with CZ_SQL_LOGINS=create.

Every connection names its part of Containerizer as the application name (program_name in sys.dm_exec_sessions, Activity Monitor, audits): containerizer-web, containerizer-worker, containerizer-llm-queue, containerizer-db (schema upgrades), containerizer-sysagent, containerizer-labagent, or containerizer-<command> for the command line. Application Name= in CZ_SQL_OPTIONS (or CONTAINERIZER_SQL_APP_NAME) sets one name for all of them, for example to tell several appliances apart on one server.

To move the data of an appliance that already ran scans: back up its database (Backup), restore the .bak on your server, then set it up as above: the restored database users cz_scanner, cz_web and cz_admin are mapped to the logins of that server by themselves. The appliance no longer uses /var/lib/containerizer/mssql; keep it until a scan has written to the external database, then delete it. To go back to the appliance's own SQL Server, empty CZ_SQL_SERVER and reboot (it starts with what that folder holds).

If the settings are not valid, the web UI and the scan worker do not start: journalctl -b -u containerizer-firstboot -u containerizer-db-init says why.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
Inbound: only TCP 22 (SSH) and 443 (HTTPS), and ping (ICMP and ICMPv6 echo requests, at most 20 a second). The k3s API, SQL Server, the registry, Prometheus and Grafana listen on the loopback interface or are not reachable from outside; NodePorts of the sandbox cluster are blocked too (use ssh -L to reach anything else).

Outbound: blocked, except to the names and networks on the allow-list. This holds for the appliance itself, the scan worker, every container Docker builds or runs, and every pod in the sandbox cluster.

How it works: the host, Docker and k3s resolve names only through the appliance's DNS filter (dnsmasq on 169.254.53.53). It answers only names an allow-list rule covers (anything else gets REFUSED), and puts the addresses of the answer into nftables sets of that rule's ports. The firewall lets connections out only to addresses in those sets (and to the networks of network rules), on the rule's ports. A connection to an address nobody resolved through the filter, an address of a name that is not allowed, or another port is dropped and logged.

Admin → Firewall (administrators only):

  • Allow a name (it covers its subdomains: nuget.org also allows api.nuget.org) or a network (10.20.0.0/16), with ports (443, 80,443, udp/123) and a note.
  • Refused names, last 24 hours: what something on the appliance tried to resolve and was refused, with an Allow button. Run a scan, then allow what it needs.
  • Blocked connections: addresses and ports the firewall dropped.
  • Log only mode lets everything out but still lists what would have been refused, to build the list. Turn blocking back on when you are done.
  • Always allowed: what the appliance needs itself (GHCR and Sigstore for upgrades and their signatures, Docker Hub and the Microsoft registry for its own service images). Part of the OS image. While the built-in LLM's model downloads, huggingface.co and hf.co are listed here too.
  • Change history: who changed what, kept on the persistent partition.

The web UI does not change the firewall itself: it asks the system agent (root), which checks the rules again, loads the new ruleset in one transaction (checked with nft -c first, and the previous ruleset is kept if the new one does not load) and restarts the DNS filter. On the console: cz firewall show.

docs.title: Local registry and the sandbox cluster
docs.text:
The registry at localhost:5000 is for images of the sandbox: in an organization scan, set the registry to localhost:5000/<path> and turn pushing on; the scan worker pushes there without credentials, and k3s pulls from it (/etc/rancher/k3s/registries.yaml) without pull secrets. It is not reachable from outside the appliance. Deleted tags free their space after a garbage collection: docker exec cz-registry registry garbage-collect --delete-untagged /etc/distribution/config.yml (stop the worker first).

k3s also runs External Secrets Operator, and the generated configurations get every secret through it (external-secrets.md). The values live in namespace containerizer-secrets, which runs no pods, and each namespace can read only its own keys.

To deploy what the scans generate, set sandbox.env (output repository URL, branch, read-only token). Every 2 minutes cz-sandbox puts the read-only token in the secret store for Flux's root sync and for every app namespace, and creates the root GitRepository + Kustomization of the output repository's clusters/sandbox/flux/. Until sandbox.env names the repository nothing is deployed, even when the scans and Make it A write to it with the write token of Admin → Source control: the two are set separately. What cz-sandbox last found is at the top of Grafana's Flux dashboard and in journalctl -u containerizer-sandbox (each change), and the alert ContainerizerSandboxNotConnected fires after 15 minutes without a connection. Each app reconciles as its own ServiceAccount with its own copy of the token (the sandbox cluster). Allow the Git server on the Firewall page. kubectl (as root on the appliance) shows the result, and helm is there for looking at and installing charts by hand (helm list -A); what Helm installs by hand is not in the output repository. Flux is the only GitOps tool. An application moved to an output repository of its own is deployed from that repository, with its token: the LLM queue runner writes it to /var/lib/containerizer/refactor/sandbox-git/<namespace> (0600, its own user) and cz-sandbox puts it in that namespace's key.

Flux polls the output repository every 5 minutes; after each push the scan worker and the LLM queue runner also call a Flux webhook (Receiver flux-system/containerizer-sandbox, which cz-sandbox keeps up to date) so the commit deploys at once. Its URL, the secret, is in /run/containerizer/flux-webhook (root:containerizer 0640) and reachable from the appliance only (polling and the webhook).

To reach the deployed apps over HTTPS, set up a wildcard domain and certificate on Admin → Sandbox HTTPS: Caddy answers for *.<domain> on the same port 443 and passes the requests to Traefik in k3s, and every web component gets https://<component>-<app>.<domain>/ (sandbox-https.md).

Components that sign users in get the sandbox identity provider, WSO2 Identity Server at https://containerizer-idp.<sandbox domain>/ (sandbox-idp.md). cz-sandbox creates its passwords and client secrets in the secret store once Flux has deployed it. containerizer idp users (as root) prints the test users and their passwords. Its images come from Docker Hub, which the default firewall rules allow.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Grafana (https://<appliance>/grafana/, Grafana ↗ on the admin pages) has four dashboards, in the containerizer folder (the dashboard list at the top of each links to the others):

Dashboard Shows Containerizer: organization scans (the home page) Scans, the scan worker, LLM usage, the LLM queue and the built-in LLM (scheduled-scans.md) Containerizer: LLM token usage The tokens the LLMs reported in their answers, for the long run, by business unit, product, application and component, by feature and model, with their cost: from the results database, not Prometheus (LLM token usage) Containerizer: k3s sandbox cluster Whether the API server and kubelet answer, pods running and not running, containers waiting (CrashLoopBackOff, ImagePullBackOff, ...), restarts, deployments short of replicas, CPU, memory and network by namespace and the top pods, volume usage, and the API server's requests and latency Containerizer: Flux First, whether the sandbox is connected to the output repository at all: what cz-sandbox last found (connected, or why not: sandbox.env without a repository URL, no token, the secret store or Flux not ready) and when, and the root sync's GitRepository and Kustomization (flux-system/containerizer-sandbox: missing, not ready with the reason, or ready at a revision); the applications' containers that do not start (ImagePullBackOff, CrashLoopBackOff, ...) and restart. Then every Flux object (Kustomizations, Git, OCI and Helm sources, Helm releases, image automation) with its Ready state, reason, revision and suspend flag; the ones not ready first; the controllers' reconciliations, errors, reconcile time, work queues, CPU and memory

docs.title: LLM token usage
docs.text:
Every call an LLM answers is recorded in the results database, in the table LlmUsage: the input and output tokens the LLM reported in its answer (never an estimate; a cached answer and a failed call cost nothing and are not recorded), the time, the backend and model, the cost (Claude's list prices, or CONTAINERIZER_LLM_PRICE_INPUT / _OUTPUT for a self-hosted LLM), the feature (assessment: the component reviews of scans; refactor-queued: Make it A and other refactoring orders; sandbox-tester, build-diagnosis, platform-migration, egress and link reviews ...), the application, the component, and the LLM queue job or the scan it was for. The scan worker and the LLM queue runner write it as the answers come. Unlike Prometheus, which keeps 90 days, it is kept for the long run.

The view vLlmUsage adds the application's name, product and business unit (as they are mapped now, on Admin → Applications), and vLlmUsageDaily sums it by day. The Containerizer: LLM token usage dashboard reads them through its own data source, Containerizer results: the login cz_grafana, whose role (usage) can read those two views and nothing else. Filter by business unit, product and application at the top; the tables at the bottom sum it per application and per component. The system agent sets the login, the data source and the dashboard up (within 5 minutes of the start or of an app update, and again if Grafana loses them), with the results database's owner and Grafana's admin account: if you changed that account's password in Grafana, they stay as they were (journalctl -u containerizer-sysagent-status says so). With an external results database whose logins your DBA makes (CZ_SQL_LOGINS=existing), make cz_grafana too (its password is in /etc/containerizer/secrets/cz-grafana): until then the dashboard stays empty. Report on it with any SQL client that can read the views (the reader and admin roles can too).

Prometheus keeps 90 days. What it reads from the sandbox cluster:

  • kube-state-metrics (namespace cz-monitoring, from /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/containerizer-monitoring.yaml): the state of the cluster's objects and, through its custom resource configuration, of Flux's objects (gotk_resource_info).
  • Flux's controllers (namespace flux-system, their http-prom port) and kube-state-metrics, found through the API server.
  • The API server and the kubelet (127.0.0.1:6443, 127.0.0.1:10250; CPU and memory per pod from cAdvisor), only the metrics the dashboards use.

It reads them as the read-only ServiceAccount cz-monitoring/cz-prometheus (pods, nodes, endpoints and services listed; node and API server metrics), whose token containerizer-prometheus-k8s.service copies to /run/containerizer/prometheus-k8s with the cluster's CA when k3s is up; the TLS certificates are verified. Until then, and while k3s is down, those targets are down (up{job=~"k3s-apiserver|kubelet.*|flux|kube-state-metrics"}).

docs.title: Upgrade, roll back and restart
docs.text:
Admin → System (administrators only) shows the running version, the snapshots on the disk and the last upgrade or roll back with its outcome, and checks GHCR for newer releases.

  • Planned restart: a restart, an upgrade and a roll back are planned the same way: now or at a time (UTC, within 30 days), and how long to wait for running scans and LLM jobs (not at all, at most 30 minutes to 8 hours, or until they are done; 2 hours by default). From the planned time on, the scan worker starts no new scan run and the LLM queue runner no new job (its page says why); queued runs and jobs keep their place. The appliance restarts, or upgrades or rolls back and then restarts, as soon as nothing runs any more, or when the wait is over: a scan cut off then is marked failed and the next run processes every repository again, an LLM job cut off goes back to the queue. The page shows the plan, how much work it still waits for and when it restarts at the latest; Cancel the planned restart lets everything go on. One plan at a time; it survives an unplanned restart (containerizer-restart.timer checks it every minute, as root).
  • Upgrade: pick a newer release and confirm. The system agent checks with cosign that the image was signed by this repository's release workflow (keyless signature, GitHub's OIDC identity of .github/workflows/release.yml on a vX.Y.Z tag), then installs exactly the verified digest as a new snapshot and restarts. Only release tags of the appliance's own image repository are accepted, whatever the web UI sends.
  • App updates (patch releases): a newer patch release of the running series (for example 0.12.3 on an appliance of 0.12.0 to 0.12.2) is installed as an app update, not as a new OS: the list marks each release "app update, the OS does not restart" or "OS upgrade". A patch release changes only the application (the code and the rules; the release workflow refuses one that changes the OS image), so the system agent downloads just that, a few MB: the signed image ghcr.io/olljanat-ai/containerizer-app:vX.Y.Z, checked with cosign against the same release workflow identity and fetched by its verified digest. It is unpacked on the persistent partition (/var/lib/containerizer/app-patches/), its code must import with the OS's Python packages, and it is mounted read-only on /run/containerizer/app-patch, which Python reads before the OS image's own code. The new code then upgrades the results database's schema, as containerizer-db-init does at every start. Only the containerizer services (web UI, scan worker, LLM queue runner, egress observer) restart; when they do not come up within 2 minutes, the code that ran before is put back. Planning and waiting for the work in progress work as for an OS upgrade, except for the LLM queue: an app update does not wait for its jobs and does not cut them off. The runner is told to drain instead: it starts no new job, lets the LLM finish the answer it is working on, then puts its jobs back in the queue and restarts with the new code by itself; the jobs continue there with the answers they already had (from the answer cache), and only their work outside the LLM (builds, runs) is done again. The System page says so meanwhile. The plan's wait, counted from the planned time, still applies: a call not answered when it is over is cut off, as before. (The LLM runner imports all its code when it starts, so the new version's files under it do not mix with the code it runs.) A minor or major release is always an OS upgrade, and the app update is not used any more on its new OS (it was built for the previous series). Remove the app update on the System page goes back to the OS image's own code; a roll back to a snapshot removes it too. Appliances whose OS image predates app updates (0.11.x and older) take one OS upgrade first. A patch release's OS image is its series' vX.Y.0 image (the release workflow does not build the OS for a patch release), so an appliance of another series that upgrades to 0.12.3, say, runs 0.12.0 after the restart and then lists 0.12.3 as an app update.
  • Automatic fallback: after an upgrade the boot assessment checks that the firewall is loaded and the DNS filter, Docker and k3s run and the application starts. If that fails 5 times, the appliance restarts into the previous snapshot, and the System page shows the upgrade as failed.
  • Roll back: pick an earlier snapshot. It is installed as a new active snapshot (no download) and the appliance restarts. Data on the persistent partition is not rolled back: the database keeps its schema (newer versions only add to it, and older code reads it).
  • The GRUB menu at start-up also lists the snapshots, and a recovery system.

On the console: cz upgrade vX.Y.Z or cz rollback <snapshot> do it at once, without waiting for the work in progress; upgrade vX.Y.Z --full installs a patch release as a whole OS instead of an app update, and app-patch remove removes the app update. Should an app update break the agent itself, run the OS image's own code: PYTHONPATH=/usr/lib/containerizer/app /usr/lib/containerizer/venv/bin/python -m containerizer.sysagent app-patch remove. The appliance checks GHCR anonymously, so the containerizer-appliance and containerizer-app packages must be public.

docs.title: Built-in LLM
docs.text:
For sites without an LLM server of their own (a GPU server, or the Claude API), the appliance can run one itself, on its CPU. It is off by default and is turned on under Admin → Source control & LLM (administrators only). Scans with Ask the LLM use it when no LLM is set on that page; an LLM set there always wins. See the LLM for what it is asked.

Model Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B Instruct, ByteShape's IQ4_XS-4.20bpw GGUF build (16 GB, Apache 2.0), served as qwen3-coder-30b-a3b Server llama.cpp llama-server (image CZ_IMAGE_LLAMA_CPP in images.env, pinned by digest): one per NUMA node (see below), containerizer-local-llm@<n>.service, container cz-llm-<n>, on 127.0.0.1:8090+n Listens on 127.0.0.1:8090+n only. The LLM queue asks each server as an LLM of its own, one request at a time each, taken per LLM call (a server still loading its model takes none yet); scans that ask directly use the first server that is up. Prometheus reads each server's metrics Memory at least 40 GB on the machine. The model (15.6 GB) is locked in RAM, so builds cannot push it out; each answer slot adds about 2 GB Disk about 20 GB free on the persistent partition for the download (16 GB plus 4 GB to spare) Speed about 7 to 12 tokens per second on a 22-core server; reading a 5,000 to 15,000 token evidence pack takes 1.5 to 5 minutes, so an answer takes about 5 minutes. Calls may take up to an hour (CONTAINERIZER_LLM_TIMEOUT=3600 is set for it)

Turning it on. The system agent checks the memory and the free space again (the page shows both), then downloads the model once from Hugging Face, from a fixed commit of the repository, resuming a partial download, and checks its size and SHA-256 before it is used. huggingface.co and hf.co (which covers the download servers it redirects to) are on the allow-list only while the download runs, as system rules on the Firewall page; then they are removed again. If the download is refused anyway, the refused names are listed on Admin → Firewall. The page shows the progress; after the download the server loads the model, which takes a minute or two, and the state turns to Running. A failed download (network, checksum) is not retried by itself: Try again resumes it. A file that fails the checksum is deleted.

Sizing. The answer slots (requests answered together, for about the cost of one, since speed follows memory bandwidth) and the container's memory limit follow the machine's memory:

Memory Slots Context per slot Memory limit of cz-llm 40 to 47 GB 1 22,016 tokens 24 GB 48 to 63 GB 2 22,016 tokens 27 GB 64 GB or more 3 22,016 tokens 30 GB

Two CPU sockets (NUMA). On a CPU the speed follows memory bandwidth, and each socket has its own memory. When the machine has several NUMA nodes and the RAM for a copy of the model on each (16 GB for the appliance plus at least 23 GB per copy, and each node's own memory at least its server's limit), the appliance runs one server per node, pinned to that node's CPUs and memory (docker run --cpuset-cpus --cpuset-mems, as many threads as the node has CPUs). Each answers at full speed, so two sockets answer about twice as many jobs per hour. The LLM queue lists each server as an LLM of its own (built-in-0, built-in-1, ... on the LLM queue page) and sends one request per server at once (a higher Parallel requests setting is shared out between them); a job holds a server only while one of its LLM calls is answered, not while it builds or verifies. The LLM queue's Jobs at once (automatic: the servers' requests plus one) keeps the builds of refactoring orders from crowding the CPUs the built-in LLM needs. One server on both sockets instead would read half of its weights across the link between them. With one node, or not enough RAM, it is one server on the whole machine, as before. The page shows how it is sized and each server's state. The RAM is shared out between the servers before the slots are sized (the table above, per server): 128 GB with two nodes gives two servers of 3 slots.

In a Hyper-V VM the guest sees the host's sockets only when Dynamic Memory is off and the VM has more vCPUs and memory than one node (VM settings → Processor → NUMA: Use Hardware Topology; NUMA spanning allowed in the host's Hyper-V settings). Check on the appliance with lscpu | grep -i numa: NUMA node(s): 2. The servers are sized again every 5 minutes and when the built-in LLM is turned on.

It gets a quarter of the CPU's weight (--cpu-shares 256), so the scans' builds go first when both want the CPU. Use the queued LLM mode for organization scans where it is offered, and leave LLM-heavy mode off: it makes many calls, and on a CPU that turns a scan into hours or days.

Turning it off stops the server (or the download) at once; the model file stays, so turning it on again starts the server without a new download. Remove next to Turn on deletes the model file to free its 16 GB.

Files:

What Where On or off, the download's state and the change history /var/lib/containerizer/system/local-llm.json The model file (re-downloadable) /var/lib/containerizer/llm/ What the page and the scan worker read /run/containerizer/system/local-llm-status.json Each server's settings (slots, context, memory, NUMA node) /run/containerizer/local-llm-<n>.env

On the console: systemctl status 'containerizer-local-llm*', docker logs cz-llm-0, and curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8090/health (8091 for the second server). It is not part of the start-up check of an upgrade: a missing or slow model never makes the appliance go back to the previous snapshot. The Grafana dashboard has a Built-in LLM row: whether each server is up, requests in progress and waiting, the tokens per second it generates (each per server, label server), and the LLM queue's requests in progress on each LLM now (built-in-<n> for the built-in LLM's servers).

docs.title: kubemg
docs.text:
kubemg is an audited console and kubectl gateway for Kubernetes clusters: people sign in, browse the sandbox cluster's resources, read logs, open a shell, scale and restart, or take a short-lived kubeconfig for their own kubectl. The cluster's RBAC decides what each one may do, and every call is on the record (with recorded shell sessions). It is off by default. To turn it on, set this in /etc/containerizer/appliance.env and reboot:

CZ_KUBEMG=true
# its own name, on port 443 (it cannot run under a path such as /kubemg/). Empty: kubemg.<CZ_HOSTNAME>
CZ_KUBEMG_HOSTNAME=

Then:

  1. DNS: point the name (kubemg.containerizer.example.com) at the appliance.
  2. Certificate: it must cover that name. With your own certificate, add the name (or a wildcard) to it. Let's Encrypt (CZ_ACME_EMAIL) issues one for it by itself when the name is public. Caddy's own CA issues one too, and browsers warn until they trust that CA, as for the web UI.
  3. Sign in at https://kubemg.<appliance>/ as admin with the password in /etc/containerizer/secrets/kubemg-admin (root only; /usr/lib/containerizer/bin/cz-kubemg password prints it). The appliance generates it, so kubemg does not print one to its log as its sign-in page says, and journalctl -u containerizer-kubemg says where it is. kubemg's setup wizard asks you to change it, and offers SSO: OIDC (the identity provider the web UI uses works, with the redirect URI https://kubemg.<appliance>/api/v1/auth/sso/providers/<id>/callback), SAML or LDAP. Admin → Settings → SSO in kubemg sets it up, with group mappings to kubemg roles.

The sandbox cluster is registered at the first start, as sandbox in agent mode. Its agent runs in the namespace kubemg-system and connects out to https://kubemg.<appliance>/. Nothing listens for it, and the firewall allows it as it allows any HTTPS client (the agent resolves the name to the appliance by itself). The agent trusts the CA of the appliance's certificate: your own (/etc/containerizer/tls/ca.pem, else the chain in cert.pem), Caddy's own CA, or the public CAs for Let's Encrypt. The appliance registers the cluster with the generated admin password, so this works only before you change that password. If the agent is removed after that, register the cluster again in kubemg (Admin → Clusters → Add, agent mode) and apply its manifest with k3s kubectl apply -f.

Its log (docker logs cz-kubemg, also in journalctl -u containerizer-kubemg) has no level to set. Its audit trail is always in it, one JSON line per call, among them kubemg's own look for shell pods every 2 minutes (kubemg:shell-runner). A record not found line with its SQL at the start is a setting not made yet, not an error. Helm chart repositories: kubemg adds six public ones on its first start (argo, bitnami, grafana, ingress-nginx, jetstack, prometheus-community), and the appliance's outbound allow-list blocks them, so each hourly sync would log server misbehaving for them. The appliance deletes them while the generated admin password still works; after that, delete them in kubemg (Admin → Settings → Helm, Chart repositories). To use charts, add a repository the allow-list lets through (your mirror), or put the repositories' hosts on the allow-list.

Services containerizer-kubemg.service (kubemg, HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:8444 behind Caddy, with a certificate of a local CA that only Caddy trusts, in /var/lib/containerizer/kubemg/tls), containerizer-kubemg-db.service (PostgreSQL 16, 127.0.0.1:5434), containerizer-kubemg-sandbox.service (the registration) Data /var/lib/containerizer/kubemg (the database and the recorded sessions) Secrets /etc/containerizer/secrets/kubemg-*. kubemg-secret-key encrypts the credentials in kubemg's database: keep it with the database, which is unreadable without it Images pinned by digest in /usr/lib/containerizer/images.env (CZ_IMAGE_KUBEMG*); the agent and the browser shell are pulled by k3s from ghcr.io License kubemg's server is AGPL-3.0 and its agent Apache-2.0: the appliance runs the published images unmodified

Turning it off (CZ_KUBEMG=false, reboot) stops kubemg and keeps its data and secrets. The agent stays in the sandbox cluster, trying to reconnect, until you delete it: k3s kubectl delete namespace kubemg-system.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
The OS is rebuilt from the image; what has to be backed up is on the persistent partition. Scans rebuild the clones, images in the local registry and the sandbox apps, but not the rest:

What Where Why it matters Results database SQL Server, /var/lib/containerizer/mssql (back it up with BACKUP DATABASE, below) Results, history, mapping, scan settings, sealed tokens, rule review Configuration and secrets /etc/containerizer .env files, firewall allow-list, SQL Server and Grafana passwords, the root password, and secrets/credential-key: the tokens in the database open only with it Dev database uploads /var/lib/containerizer/devdb The uploaded backups. The database keeps only their name and SHA-256, so without the files the next scan of those apps has no backup to restore Appliance settings and their history /var/lib/containerizer/system Sandbox HTTPS certificate, key and settings, the lab service switches, and the change history of the firewall and Sandbox HTTPS (these two are files here, not in the database) Learned rules /var/lib/containerizer/learned Rules the learning loop added on this appliance. Rules approved in the rule review are in your rules repository HTTPS certificate authority /var/lib/caddy Without CZ_ACME_EMAIL, the appliance's own CA: a new one means every browser has to trust a new root Metrics (optional) /var/lib/containerizer/prometheus, /var/lib/containerizer/grafana 90 days of scan and LLM usage metrics, and changes made in Grafana OpenBao /var/lib/containerizer/openbao (with secrets/openbao-unseal.key, openbao-recovery-key, openbao-sync-token) The values administrators and operators entered for the sandbox apps, users, policies and sign-in settings (Secret values in OpenBao) kubemg (optional) /var/lib/containerizer/kubemg (with secrets/kubemg-secret-key) kubemg's users, SSO settings, audit trail and recorded sessions

The configuration without its secrets is also in the output repository. At every boot the appliance copies appliance.env, web.env, worker.env, sandbox.env, grafana.env, egress.json and network/*.network to .appliance/<CZ_HOSTNAME>/config/ of every output repository it has a write token for (Admin → Source control), in one commit and only when something changed. A setting whose value is a secret (its name has TOKEN, PASSWORD, SECRET, KEY, ...) keeps its name and says only whether it is set; passwords inside values (connection strings, user:password@ in URLs) are cut out, and secrets/ and tls/ are never copied. So the history of the settings is in Git, and a rebuilt appliance can be set up from it, with the secrets from your own backup. The files change only by hand and a reboot applies them, so the boot is when they are copied (cz-firstboot stages them in /run/containerizer/config-backup; the LLM queue runner commits them).

The built-in LLM's model file (/var/lib/containerizer/llm, 16 GB) can be downloaded again: leave it out of backups (the archive below does). Its on/off setting is in /var/lib/containerizer/system.

Lab service data and restored dev databases in the sandbox cluster (/var/lib/rancher) are test data: a new cluster starts them empty, or restores the uploaded backups again, and creates new credentials.

With an external database the results database is backed up with your SQL Server: skip its row and the BACKUP DATABASE step below. The files are still needed.

Back up the database (from the appliance):

docker exec cz-mssql /opt/mssql-tools18/bin/sqlcmd -C -S localhost -U sa -P "$(cat /etc/containerizer/secrets/mssql-sa)" \
  -Q "BACKUP DATABASE Containerizer TO DISK = N'/var/opt/mssql/backup/containerizer.bak' WITH COMPRESSION, INIT"
# the file is /var/lib/containerizer/mssql/backup/containerizer.bak

and the folders (the database backup above included):

tar -C / -czf /root/containerizer-backup.tgz etc/containerizer var/lib/containerizer/mssql/backup \
  var/lib/containerizer/devdb var/lib/containerizer/system var/lib/containerizer/learned var/lib/caddy

With kubemg on, dump its database too, and add the dump and its recordings (the secret key is in etc/containerizer already):

docker exec cz-kubemg-db pg_dump -p 5434 -U kubemg -Fc kubemg > /var/lib/containerizer/kubemg/kubemg.dump
tar -C / -czf /root/containerizer-kubemg.tgz var/lib/containerizer/kubemg/kubemg.dump var/lib/containerizer/kubemg/recordings

Copy the archive off the appliance (scp root@<appliance>:/root/containerizer-backup.tgz .): it holds every secret of the appliance, so keep it like one.

To restore on a new appliance, after its first start (with its own sa password, which you keep):

systemctl stop containerizer-web containerizer-worker
tar -C / -xzf /root/containerizer-backup.tgz \
  --exclude=etc/containerizer/secrets/mssql-sa --exclude=etc/containerizer/secrets/mssql.env
docker exec cz-mssql /opt/mssql-tools18/bin/sqlcmd -C -S localhost -U sa -P "$(cat /etc/containerizer/secrets/mssql-sa)" \
  -Q "RESTORE DATABASE Containerizer FROM DISK = N'/var/opt/mssql/backup/containerizer.bak' WITH REPLACE"
systemctl reboot

At the next start the schema is upgraded if the backup is older, and the logins of the web UI and the scan worker get the passwords of the backup and are linked to their users in the restored database again.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• OS: read-only, signed upgrades only, no package manager in use, kernel and network hardening sysctls, root's default password must be changed at the first sign-in (passwd -l root for SSH keys only), no service but SSH and HTTPS reachable, outbound allow-list for everything.
  • Web UI: no privileges (systemd sandbox: read-only system, no capabilities, system call filter); its database passwords come as systemd credentials. It cannot change the OS: upgrades, roll backs and the firewall go through the system agent, which checks every request again.
  • SQL Server: non-root, every capability dropped except binding its port, loopback only. An external database is reached encrypted, with the server certificate checked, and with the same three logins. Edition: Express by default (free, 10 GB per database); Developer is not licensed for production.
  • The scan worker and the LLM queue runner are not in the docker group (equivalent to root): they build and run the scanned repositories' images through the Docker socket guard, and those builds and runs reach nothing on the appliance (Builds of scanned code). Give them no credentials beyond the scans' tokens.
  • k3s: secrets encrypted at rest, delivered by External Secrets Operator from a namespace without pods, audit log (/var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/logs/audit.log), kernel defaults protected, API reachable only from the appliance and its pods. Each app's namespace runs under Pod Security "restricted".
  • The sandbox is isolated: its applications reach nothing outside the appliance but what an egress rule on the Firewall page allows (the firewall's forward chain drops the rest, and the DNS filter refuses every other name), whatever their NetworkPolicies say. Approving egress on the results pages or Admin → Egress only documents a destination for the real environment (connectivity.yaml); it changes no rule here.
  • Egress observer (egress): not root; the containerizer user with two capabilities: CAP_NET_ADMIN, to read kube-router's drop log (NFLOG group 100: the first 128 bytes of each dropped packet, addresses and ports, at most 10 packets a minute per policy), and CAP_SYSLOG, to read the firewall's cz-egress-drop lines from the kernel log (/dev/kmsg, the only device it sees; at most 30 a minute). Its Kubernetes account reads pods and the CoreDNS query log (names pods look up, and the ones the DNS filter refused), nothing else; the query log is on for that reason (coredns-custom). It changes no firewall rule.
  • Containers of the appliance's own services are pinned by digest in the OS image (/usr/lib/containerizer/images.env).

docs.title: Builds of scanned code
docs.text:
Verification, the security gate and refactoring patches build and run the scanned repositories' code on the appliance, and to the appliance that code is untrusted: npm install runs a package's scripts, dotnet restore and MSBuild run a repository's targets, Maven and Gradle run plugins. Containerizer does not change that code (it is the application's own); it keeps the platform safe from it instead:

A build step (RUN) or a verification run can reach Allowed names on the Firewall page (package feeds, registries), through the DNS filter yes, as everything else on the appliance The DNS filter (169.254.53.53:53) yes The feed proxies (169.254.53.53:3128 and 3129) yes: they add the tokens of package feeds to requests to those feeds, refuse the appliance's own addresses and its container networks, and pass everything else on under the same allow-list SQL Server (results database, 1433), the registry (5000), Grafana, Prometheus, the web UI, kubemg no: loopback only, and the firewall answers nothing but DNS on Docker's bridges The k3s API (6443), the kubelet (10250), pods and services of the sandbox cluster (lab services, the IdP, sandboxed apps) no: Docker's bridges never reach the k3s networks, nor the other way round The host's network namespace no: builds never use --network host (the scan worker forces CONTAINERIZER_BUILD_HOST_NETWORK=0, and Docker refuses the network.host and security.insecure build entitlements, /etc/docker/daemon.json) The same services through Docker itself (ADD http://127.0.0.1:9090/..., a remote build context: the daemon fetches those on the host's network) no: cz-docker-egress (run with each start of Docker) keeps the daemon's own connections off the appliance's addresses, except the registry and DNS, and off the k3s networks Other networks (your LAN, an external SQL Server) only what a network rule on the Firewall page allows

Docker socket guard. The scan worker and the LLM queue runner are not in the docker group: Docker's own socket is root on the host. They use DOCKER_HOST=unix:///run/containerizer/docker-guard.sock (containerizer-docker-guard.socket, group containerizer), served by containerizer-docker-guard.service (python -m containerizer.dockerguard, user cz-dockerguard, no network, read-only system). It forwards what builds, verification runs, the security gate and the image scanner need, and refuses:

  • privileged containers, the host's network, PID, IPC, UTS, user or cgroup namespace, devices, capabilities beyond Docker's default set, sysctls that are not namespaced, seccomp/AppArmor/SELinux opt-outs and no-new-privileges=false;
  • bind mounts from anywhere but /var/lib/containerizer/worker and /var/lib/containerizer/refactor (symbolic links resolved first), and the CA bundle (CONTAINERIZER_CA_BUNDLE) and the guard's own socket for the image scanner;
  • ports published on anything but loopback;
  • any call on a container it did not create (each one gets the label io.containerizer.owner=worker): no docker exec, inspect, logs, cp, commit or rm on SQL Server, the registry, Grafana or kubemg;
  • builds with the host network or a cgroup parent, plugins, swarm, network creation, volumes with driver options, docker container prune.

A refused call fails with containerizer docker guard: <reason> in the scan's log. Docker's daemon also runs every container with no-new-privileges by default.

What is left, by design: the guard itself is in the docker group, so it is kept small (one file, no network, CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH only, to resolve bind mounts in the worker's folders); a container the worker starts can still bind-mount the worker's own folders (its clones and scratch space, which it can read anyway); and the builds and runs of different scans share Docker's bridges. The boot test (appliance/ci/vm-checks.sh) builds an image whose RUN step tries SQL Server, the k3s API (node and service address), the kubelet, the registry, Grafana, Prometheus, the web UI and SSH on the host, and fails if any of them answers.

For local development outside the appliance, CONTAINERIZER_BUILD_HOST_NETWORK=1 lets builds and scanner containers use the host network again, for a proxy that listens only on 127.0.0.1.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Something does not start systemctl --failed, journalctl -b -u <unit>; units are containerizer-*, k3s, caddy, docker A scan cannot reach a host Admin → Firewall → Refused names; or journalctl -u containerizer-dns \| grep REFUSED The firewall did not load the SSH-only fallback ruleset is active; systemctl status containerizer-firewall shows why Status of the system agent /run/containerizer/system/status.json, journalctl -u containerizer-sysagent Planned restart (Admin → System) /var/lib/containerizer/system/restart-plan.json, journalctl -u containerizer-restart Locked out of SSH the console of the VM: GRUB menu → recovery, or a previous snapshot

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text: Containerizer ships as one virtual machine, the appliance: an immutable OS image with the web UI and API, the scan worker, SQL Server, a sandbox cluster and monitoring. You install it, set up sign-in, and do everything else in the web UI. This page is the short path from download to the first scan; what the appliance runs and how to operate it is in Running the appliance.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text:
• x86-64 VM (or server) with UEFI firmware (Secure Boot works: the shim and GRUB are Debian's signed ones). Hyper-V: generation 2 with the Secure Boot template Microsoft UEFI Certificate Authority, installed from the ISO. VMware: EFI firmware.
  • 4 vCPU and 16 GB memory or more (SQL Server takes 4 GB, CZ_MSSQL_MEMORY), more for parallel builds.
  • One disk of 64 GB or more: 16 GB for the OS snapshots, the rest is the persistent partition.
  • Optional, for the built-in LLM (off by default, for sites without an LLM server of their own): 40 GB memory or more (16 GB for the appliance, about 24 GB for the model) and about 20 GB more disk for the model file. 48 GB and 64 GB let it answer two and three requests at once.
  • Outbound HTTPS to the hosts on the Firewall page (the image registries the appliance uses are allowed by default) and DNS servers from DHCP or CZ_DNS_SERVERS.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Every minor or major release (vX.Y.0) has the files below. A patch release (vX.Y.Z, Z > 0) has none: it is an app update that appliances of its series install from Admin → System, so install a new appliance from the series' vX.Y.0 and let it update itself.

File For containerizer-vX.Y.Z.iso Installer: boot it, answer the questions on the console. SHA256SUMS, SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json Check the downloads (command in the release notes).

Every hypervisor installs from the ISO, KVM, Proxmox and OpenStack too (releases before 0.20.0 also had a qcow2 disk image).

Check what you downloaded:

cosign verify-blob --bundle SHA256SUMS.sigstore.json \
  --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github\.com/olljanat-ai/containerizer/\.github/workflows/release\.yml@refs/tags/' \
  --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com SHA256SUMS
sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS --ignore-missing

Boot the ISO: the console (screen or serial) shows the installer: the disk to install to (it is erased), an SSH public key for root (optional), and a host name. It installs and restarts; remove the ISO.

For unattended installs, see Running the appliance.

docs.title: First boot
docs.text:
Sign in as root with the password containerizer, over SSH (ssh root@<appliance>) or on the console. In 0.3.4 the default password is not expired, so change it yourself with passwd after the first sign-in (it is kept like any change). Otherwise, the first sign-in asks for the current password once more and then a new one; SSH closes the connection after the change if the login did not continue, so sign in again with the new password. Until the password is changed, an SSH key alone may be refused too. The new password is kept on the persistent partition, so it survives restarts, upgrades and roll backs.

The first boot created /etc/containerizer/ with the configuration files (configuration files). Then:

  1. Set CZ_HOSTNAME in appliance.env to the DNS name users will open (usually the FQDN), and register https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>/auth/callback as the redirect URI of an app registration at your identity provider (Entra ID, Okta, Keycloak, ...).
  2. Fill in web.env (issuer, client id and secret, CONTAINERIZER_ADMINS; sign-in and roles). Allow the identity provider's host on the Firewall page once you are in (or add it to egress.json now: e.g. login.microsoftonline.com), since the web UI fetches its keys.
  3. systemctl reboot (or systemctl restart containerizer-web caddy).
  4. Open https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>/admin. With the default certificate from the appliance's own CA, browsers warn until you trust its root: /var/lib/caddy/.local/share/caddy/pki/authorities/local/root.crt. With CZ_ACME_EMAIL, allow acme-v02.api.letsencrypt.org on the Firewall page first; the name must resolve to the appliance from the internet (TLS-ALPN challenge on 443). For a certificate from your own CA, see HTTPS certificate.
  5. Admin → Firewall: allow the hosts your scans need (Git servers, package feeds, registries).
  6. Admin → Source control & LLM: a read-only token for each organization to scan and a write token for each output repository (source-control.md), and the LLM if scans should ask one.
  7. Admin → Organization scans: define the scans (organization scans), and fill in sandbox.env so the sandbox cluster deploys what they generate.

The sandbox apps' secret values (connection strings, API keys, release-pipeline settings) are entered in OpenBao at https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>/ui/, user admin, password in /etc/containerizer/secrets/openbao-admin: every value an app reads is already there, empty (Secret values in OpenBao).

Grafana is at https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>/grafana/, user admin, password in /etc/containerizer/secrets/grafana-admin (change it in Grafana, or set up sign-in in grafana.env: Grafana sign-in). It opens on the Containerizer: organization scans dashboard.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Organization scans: what a scan does and where its results go.
  • Rule review: approve what the learning loop proposes.
  • How it works: how applications are assessed and what is generated.

docs.title: Build pipelines
docs.text:
Containerizer generates the Dockerfiles that build an application's components, and builds them itself during a scan. For the application team to build the images themselves, from their own repository, it also generates a container image build pipeline for the CI system the code lives on: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI/CD or Azure Pipelines.

The pipeline is made without an LLM, from what the assessment generated: the same Dockerfiles, the same image names as the generated Kubernetes manifests, and the same tag scheme the sandbox's GitOps image automation follows. Containerizer never writes to the application's repository: an organization scan commits the files to its output repository, and you copy them (or apply a patch made with git am) and open the pull request yourself.

docs.title: Where to get it
docs.text:
• The output repository of an organization scan: <organization>/<project>/<repository>/pipeline/, next to the generated manifests. pipeline/<provider>/ mirrors the application's repository: copy its contents to the repository root. pipeline/README.md says what to do.
  • The command line, on a checkout:
containerizer pipeline <app-path> [--provider github|gitlab|azure-devops] [--registry R] \
    [--sign none|keyless|key] [--out DIR] [--patch]

Without --patch it writes DIR/pipeline/<provider>/...; with --patch a git am patch made on a scratch copy of the checkout's HEAD commit and checked by applying it to another clean copy.

docs.title: Which provider
docs.text: The provider comes from, in this order: the organization scan that has the repository (its Provider: GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps, also self-hosted ones through its API URL: GitHub Enterprise Server, GitLab self-managed, Azure DevOps Server / TFS); then the repository URL: github.com, *.ghe.com or a host named github/ghe; gitlab.com or a host named gitlab; dev.azure.com, *.visualstudio.com, or a URL with /_git/ or /tfs/. An organization scan always knows its provider, so its output repository gets that one pipeline only. When neither tells (the command line, on a folder whose remote is not known), all three folders are written. --provider overrides it on the command line.

docs.title: What it adds to the repository
docs.text:
File containerizer/<component>/Dockerfile The generated Dockerfile, as the scan built it containerizer/<component>/Dockerfile.dockerignore The generated context filter, plus containerizer/ containerizer/README.md The components, images, what to set up first, the pins .github/workflows/containerizer-images.yml GitHub Actions .gitlab-ci.yml, or containerizer.gitlab-ci.yml GitLab CI/CD: when the repository has a .gitlab-ci.yml, a file to include: from it (add include: [{local: containerizer.gitlab-ci.yml}], and the stage build if your stages: list lacks it) azure-pipelines.containerizer.yml Azure Pipelines

For an application in a subfolder of its repository, the containerizer/ folder is in that subfolder; the CI file is at the repository root. If the application already has an entry called containerizer, the folder is containerizer-build/.

The build context is the application's folder, as in the scans (docker build -f <generated>/<component>/Dockerfile <application folder>): the generated Dockerfiles copy paths relative to it. Dockerfile.dockerignore next to the Dockerfile is the context filter: BuildKit (the default builder of current Docker, and of all three pipelines) reads <Dockerfile>.dockerignore instead of the context's .dockerignore. It leaves out bin/, obj/, node_modules/, secrets files, the pipeline's own containerizer/ folder and the settings of environments the container does not run as: it runs as Production, so appsettings.Development.json, appsettings.Release.json, appsettings.Staging.json and the like stay out, unless the code or a project file names one (AddJsonFile("appsettings.Release.json")) or builds the name ($"appsettings.{env}.json", appsettings.$(Configuration).json), when they are all kept. PowerShell scripts (*.ps1) stay out as well, unless a project file or the code names one. Build locally the same way:

DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1 docker build -f containerizer/<component>/Dockerfile .

docs.title: What the pipeline does
docs.text:
Pull / merge requests The default branch Build Yes, each changed component Yes, each changed component SBOM (Syft, CycloneDX JSON) Kept as a pipeline artifact Kept as an artifact (and attested to the image when signing) Vulnerability scan (Trivy) Fails the job on the gate's severities Fails the job before anything is pushed Push No 1.<yyyymmdd>.<hhmm> and sha-<commit> (and latest when asked) Sign (cosign) No Optional: keyless or with a key
  • Monorepos: one job per component. A component is rebuilt when its project folder, the folders of the projects it references, the application folder's shared build files (Directory.Build.props, global.json, NuGet.config, root package.json, ...) or its own containerizer/<component>/ files change. GitHub: a first job compares the push or pull request with its base and starts the components that changed (a change to the workflow, a new branch or a manual run builds all). GitLab: rules: changes: per job. Azure Pipelines has no per-job path filters: the trigger's path filter is the union, and every component is built.
  • Scanning uses the security gate's settings (rules/60-security.yaml scan): it fails on fail_on and above (default CRITICAL), only for vulnerabilities with a fix (ignore_unfixed). Change it per repository without editing the file: GitHub repository variables CONTAINERIZER_TRIVY_SEVERITY and CONTAINERIZER_TRIVY_IGNORE_UNFIXED, GitLab CI/CD variables or Azure pipeline variables TRIVY_SEVERITY and TRIVY_IGNORE_UNFIXED. Trivy and Syft run as containers that read the image from the job's Docker daemon (on GitLab: from the Docker-in-Docker service), so nothing is installed on the runner.
  • The image is <registry>/<app>/<component>, the name in the generated manifests.
