The registry is --registry on the command line when given (never the appliance's own localhost:5000, where the scans push for the sandbox); otherwise GitHub Container Registry (ghcr.io/<owner>), the GitLab project's registry ($CI_REGISTRY_IMAGE), or on Azure a placeholder (REPLACE-ME.azurecr.io) that fails the push job with a message until you set it. The variable CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY overrides it in each provider.
  • Tags: 1.<yyyymmdd>.<hhmm> (UTC, when the pipeline started) is the same semver scheme as the scans' own images, and sha-<first 12 characters of the commit>. latest is off by default (CONTAINERIZER_PUSH_LATEST=true).

docs.title: GitHub Actions
docs.text:
• permissions: {} for the workflow, and per job only what it needs: contents: read for the change detection and the pull request builds; the push job adds packages: write (only when the registry is GitHub Container Registry) and id-token: write (only with keyless signing). Pull requests from forks get no secrets, and the pull request job uses none.
  • GitHub Container Registry: nothing to set up, the job's GITHUB_TOKEN pushes. After the first push, link each package to the repository (package settings) and make it public, or give the cluster a pull secret.
  • Another registry: repository secrets CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY_USERNAME and CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY_PASSWORD; the repository variable CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY for another registry or path.
  • Key-based signing: secrets COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY (the contents of cosign.key) and COSIGN_PASSWORD.
  • Actions are pinned by full commit SHA with the version in a comment (actions/checkout, actions/upload-artifact; the rest is plain docker). Checkouts do not keep the token (persist-credentials: false). Protect the default branch so that only reviewed changes publish images.

docs.title: GitLab CI/CD
docs.text:
• The jobs run docker:<version>-cli with a docker:<version>-dind service (both pinned by digest): the runner needs a privileged Docker executor (GitLab.com's hosted runners have one).
  • The project's registry: nothing to set up, the job token (CI_REGISTRY_USER, CI_REGISTRY_PASSWORD) pushes. Another registry: CI/CD variables CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY_USER and CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY_PASSWORD, protected and masked, and CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY.
  • Push jobs run only for the default branch when it is protected ($CI_COMMIT_REF_PROTECTED); merge request jobs never push, and protected variables do not reach them.
  • Keyless signing: the push jobs get an id_tokens: SIGSTORE_ID_TOKEN (audience sigstore); the merge request jobs do not. Key-based: a protected File variable COSIGN_PRIVATE_KEY and a masked COSIGN_PASSWORD.
  • The template jobs set their variables on the jobs only, so an including .gitlab-ci.yml is not changed.

docs.title: Azure Pipelines
docs.text:
• Push with a Docker Registry service connection named containerizer-registry (Project settings → Service connections; change the name in the registryConnection variable): Docker@2 logs in with it, so no password or PAT is in the YAML or the variables. Allow the pipeline to use it.
  • Create the pipeline from azure-pipelines.containerizer.yml (Pipelines → New pipeline → Existing Azure Pipelines YAML file). Azure Repos pull requests: add it as a build validation policy of the default branch (the pr: trigger applies to GitHub and Bitbucket repositories only).
  • Signing is key-based only (Azure Pipelines has no OIDC token Sigstore accepts): upload cosign.key as the secure file cosign.key (Pipelines → Library) and set the secret variable COSIGN_PASSWORD.
  • pool: vmImage: ubuntu-latest. Self-hosted agents: replace it with pool: name: <your pool>; the agent needs Linux, bash and Docker. Tasks are pinned to their major version (Docker@2, DownloadSecureFile@1): Azure Pipelines cannot pin a task by digest.

docs.title: Signing
docs.text:
--sign on the command line, Signing in the box:

  • none (default): no signature.
  • keyless: cosign signs with the pipeline's OIDC identity (GitHub id-token: write, GitLab id_tokens); Fulcio issues a short-lived certificate and the signature is recorded in the public Rekor transparency log. Verify with, for example, cosign verify --certificate-identity-regexp '^https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/' --certificate-oidc-issuer https://token.actions.githubusercontent.com <image>. Not for images whose names must not appear in a public log.
  • key: cosign signs with your key (cosign generate-key-pair). The signature is recorded in Rekor unless pipelines.cosign_tlog_upload in rules/60-security.yaml is false (then --tlog-upload=false). This is the same key the generated clusters/<cluster>/platform/verify-images.yaml (Kyverno) can enforce.

When signing, the SBOM is also attached to the image as a signed CycloneDX attestation (cosign attest --type cyclonedx). cosign is the release binary, checked against the release's SHA-256.

docs.title: The sandbox and GitOps
docs.text:
The generated GitOps files follow new images by tag: Flux's gitops/flux/git/image-automation.yaml (an ImageRepository and an ImagePolicy per component, semver range >=1.0.0, and an ImageUpdateAutomation that writes the new tag to the kustomization.yaml setters of the output repository). The pipeline's version tag 1.<yyyymmdd>.<hhmm> is that scheme, the same as the scans' own pushes (org.default_tag), so:

  1. a merge to the default branch pushes <registry>/<app>/<component>:1.20261101.1530;
  2. Flux sees it within the ImageRepository interval (10 minutes) and commits the tag to the output repository within the automation interval (30 minutes); the sandbox then rolls it out.

The automation pins by digest: the ImagePolicy has digestReflectionPolicy: Always (Flux 2.5 or newer), and each image in kustomization.yaml has a name, a tag and a digest setter:

images:
  - name: registry.local/shop/web
    newName: registry.local/shop/web # {"$imagepolicy": "shop:web:name"}
    newTag: 1.20261101.1530 # {"$imagepolicy": "shop:web:tag"}
    digest: "sha256:…" # {"$imagepolicy": "shop:web:digest"}

so the workloads run <image>:<tag>@sha256:<digest>, and a tag moved in the registry later does not change what runs. Until the automation first ran, digest is empty and kustomize deploys by tag; an organization scan writes the digest of each image it pushed into it itself, so the sandbox runs by digest from the first deploy. HARDENING.md reports Images are deployed by digest as applied for these images (lint check image-digest-setter instead of image-digest).

Each publish job also keeps the pushed digest: digests.txt (<image>:<version>@sha256:<digest>) as the artifact digests-<component>, and the step output digest (GitHub, step push), the dotenv variable DIGEST_<COMPONENT> (GitLab) or the output variable push.DIGEST (Azure Pipelines). A deploy pipeline that does not use the Flux image automation pins by digest with kustomize edit set image $(cat digests.txt).

This needs the pipeline and the generated manifests to use the same registry. The sandbox runs the scans' images from the appliance's own registry, so for the real environment set the manifests' images to the registry the pipeline pushes to (CONTAINERIZER_REGISTRY). The sha-<commit> tag does not match the policy and is never rolled out by itself: it is for finding the image of a commit. No pipeline step writes to the output repository.

docs.title: Pins and updates
docs.text:
What Pinned to Trivy aquasec/trivy:0.67.2@sha256:e2b22eac59c02003d8749f5b8d9bd073b62e30fefaef5b7c8371204e0a4b0c08 (the security gate's version) Syft anchore/syft:v1.33.0@sha256:f94e5d9fce1f2278491a8e3a63bd5f6ddb81fdfdbb8bf7a1637565c1d5344357 (pipelines.syft_image in rules/60-security.yaml) Docker CLI and Docker-in-Docker (GitLab) docker:29.9.2-cli@sha256:5e6baf67…, docker:29.9.2-dind@sha256:9e79b879… actions/checkout 3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 (v7.0.1) actions/upload-artifact cf430e030ddbb5b0abf93d22962f4752f3646cd9 (v7.0.2) cosign v2.6.1, cosign-linux-amd64 SHA-256 064954c5d8c7e3b2…

Digests are of the multi-architecture index. To update: generate the pipeline again with a newer Containerizer, or by hand: docker buildx imagetools inspect <image>:<tag> for an image's digest, git ls-remote https://github.com/<action> refs/tags/<tag> for an action's commit (a Dependabot or Renovate configuration keeps both current). In Containerizer itself the pins are in containerizer/pipelines.py; the Trivy and Syft versions come from rules/60-security.yaml, and a test fails when a version there has no digest in the code.

docs.title: How the patch is made
docs.text: containerizer pipeline --patch makes a git am patch on the checkout's HEAD commit and checks it with git am on a clean copy. The patch only adds files; if one of them exists in the repository already, the output repository's pipeline/README.md names it: copy the files and merge that one by hand. Nothing is cloned and no LLM is asked: the files come from what the scan generated.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text:
• It does not run on Windows runners: containerizer generates Linux images only.
  • It does not include the scan's last-minute changes that are not in the generated Dockerfile at assessment time (the security gate's OS package upgrades); the output repository's pipeline/ copy does have them. The pipeline's own scan catches what they fixed.
  • It is not tested on GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps by Containerizer's CI: the files are checked against the providers' schemas and linters, and the build, SBOM, scan, push and key-based signing steps are run locally with Docker (docs: the tests in tests/test_pipelines.py).

docs.title: Clusters: sandbox, development, acceptance, production
docs.text:
The output repository is laid out for several clusters, all under clusters/: the sandbox (clusters/sandbox/, the appliance's own k3s) and by default development, acceptance and production. Every cluster deploys the same app folders and the same images with Flux. What differs per cluster lives in that cluster's own folder.

clusters/
  README.md                           the clusters and how many apps each runs
  sandbox/                            the sandbox (docs/scheduled-scans.md#the-sandbox-cluster)
  <cluster>/
    cluster.yaml                      which apps it runs, the registry it pulls from        yours
    README.md                         its apps and how to bootstrap it                      generated
    flux/bootstrap.yaml               the root GitRepository + Kustomization                generated
    flux/apps/kustomization.yaml      each app's gitops/flux, pointed at its overlay below   generated
    apps/<namespace>/
      kustomization.yaml              the app folder, the cluster's registry, custom/       generated
      custom/kustomization.yaml       the cluster's settings of this app (kustomize Component) yours
<org>/<project>/<repo>/gitops/sandbox/kustomization.yaml
                                      the app's Flux objects (../flux) with the sandbox's patch  generated

The sandbox's flux/apps/kustomization.yaml only lists each app folder's gitops/sandbox/. What the sandbox changes about an app (no waiting for every object, no Gateway API routes, the settings read from OpenBao, debug mode) is in that app's own folder, next to the gitops/flux the other clusters deploy unchanged.

"Yours": Containerizer writes it once and no later run rewrites it. cluster.yaml is written with the cluster's folder, and custom/ when the cluster first runs the app. "Generated": every containerizer org run rewrites it.

docs.title: Which apps a cluster runs
docs.text:
# clusters/production/cluster.yaml
deploy: listed          # all: every app in the repository; listed: only the namespaces below
apps:
- containerization-challenge-shop
registry: registry.example.com/apps   # images become <registry>/<namespace>/<component>; empty: as built
Cluster deploy by default Images development all: every app, new ones as soon as a scan writes them follow every new build acceptance, production listed, with an empty list: nothing until you list an app pinned when the cluster first runs the app

Taking an app off the list prunes it from the cluster. Its custom/ stays, so listing it again brings back the same settings. The sandbox's on/off switch (Admin -> Applications -> Sandbox) applies to the sandbox only.

docs.title: Promoting a build
docs.text:
In acceptance and production, apps/<namespace>/custom/kustomization.yaml starts pinned to the image tags and digests the app had when the cluster first ran it:

apiVersion: kustomize.config.k8s.io/v1alpha1
kind: Component
images:
- name: localhost:5000/sandbox/containerization-challenge-shop/api
  newTag: 1.20261107.200
  digest: sha256:...

A cluster that pinned a component of the shared Helm chart (before 0.43.0) with a HelmRelease patch here gets that pin as an images: entry like the one above when the app is converted back to manifests.

Promoting a build is a commit that changes the tag and digest there, for example from what acceptance runs to production. The scan's tags and digests are in the app folder's containerizer.json. An empty digest deploys by tag.

docs.title: Other per-cluster settings
docs.text:
Anything else that differs per cluster goes into the same custom/ Component as kustomize patches: replicas, resources, Ingress hosts. The cluster's Pod Security (restricted) keeps the hardening: no cluster can loosen it.

patches:
- target: {kind: Deployment, name: api}
  patch: '[{"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/replicas", "value": 3}]'
- target: {kind: Ingress, name: api}
  patch: '[{"op": "replace", "path": "/spec/rules/0/host", "value": "shop.example.com"}]'

docs.title: Bootstrapping a cluster
docs.text:
The prerequisites are those of the sandbox: Flux, External Secrets Operator with the ClusterSecretStore app-secrets (platform/secret-store.yaml in the cluster's folder), and the output repository's read-only token in the store under flux-system--cz-git and <namespace>--cz-git of every app the cluster runs (docs/external-secrets.md). The rest of the cluster's platform/ (signed images with Kyverno, the API server's audit policy) is meant for it too; Flux does not apply that folder. Then:

kubectl apply -f clusters/production/flux/bootstrap.yaml

Unlike the sandbox, the clusters keep each app Kustomization's wait: true (a secret missing from the store stops the rollout), deploy the Gateway API HTTPRoutes, and have no sandbox identity provider. The secrets of the apps' settings, and of the lab services they used in the sandbox (<namespace>--cz-lab-*), are remote keys in the cluster's own secret store: put the real values there. The health read-back (containerizer sandbox verify) is for the sandbox only.

docs.title: Cluster names
docs.text: CONTAINERIZER_CLUSTERS (a site setting) names the clusters, comma separated: the default is development,acceptance,production, and none writes no clusters/. A new name gets deploy: listed, except development, which runs every app. The folder of a cluster that is no longer named stays as it is.

docs.title: Where the sandbox was
docs.text:
Before 0.41.0 the sandbox's folder was sandbox/ at the repository's root. It is now clusters/sandbox/, next to the other clusters. Until 0.44.0 a pointer stayed in sandbox/ for the appliance's Flux; since 0.44.0 the appliance reads ./clusters/sandbox/flux/apps and the scans remove sandbox/. A cluster you bootstrapped yourself from the old sandbox/flux/bootstrap.yaml needs kubectl apply -f clusters/sandbox/flux/bootstrap.yaml once. The patches are written as YAML, not as JSON strings, and since 0.42.0 the sandbox's are in each app folder's gitops/sandbox/kustomization.yaml.

The cluster-level kit (ClusterSecretStore, signed-images policy, audit policy) was in cluster/ at the root until 0.44.0; it is now each cluster's platform/.

docs.title: Dev database backups for the sandbox
docs.text:
Many applications don't start without their database. Operators can upload a backup of an application's development database (SQL Server, PostgreSQL or MySQL) on the admin pages, together with instructions for the AI on how to point the application at it. The next scan of the application restores the backup into a database that runs next to the application in the sandbox namespace, and sets the application's connection settings. The application's code is not changed: only the generated Kubernetes manifests are.

On the appliance, the backup's engine must be on under Admin → Lab services. SQL Server is on by default. An app without a backup gets an empty database of its own on the lab's server instead.

Engine Files Restored with SQL Server .bak made with BACKUP DATABASE ... TO DISK, compressed or not RESTORE DATABASE ... WITH MOVE PostgreSQL pg_dump custom format (-Fc), or a plain SQL dump (.sql, .sql.gz) pg_restore, or psql MySQL mysqldump or mariadb-dump output (.sql, .sql.gz) mysql

The file's first bytes decide what it is: TAPE or MSSQLBAK (SQL Server), PGDMP (pg_dump custom format), or the dump header -- PostgreSQL database dump, -- MySQL dump or -- MariaDB dump (also inside a gzip file). A plain dump made from another database name is restored into the name you give. For PostgreSQL and MySQL, its CREATE DATABASE, USE and \connect lines are left out.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
operator ──upload backup + instructions──> web UI ──> /var/lib/containerizer/devdb/<sha256>.<bak|dump|sql|sql.gz>
                                           └──> DevDatabase row (name, size, SHA-256, instructions, who)
scan worker ──reads DevDatabase──> builds <registry>/<app>/devdb:<tag> (backup inside) ──push──> registry
            └──> generated manifests: devdb Deployment + Service + NetworkPolicy, app env → devdb
  1. Upload (Admin → Dev databases, admins and operators). The file is streamed to disk, so it is never held in memory. The page checks the session, the role and the Origin header before it reads the request body. It checks the form's CSRF token, which is the first field, before it writes any of the file. The file must start with the signature of the selected engine (see above). It is stored under its SHA-256, readable only by the web UI and the scan worker, and the web UI never serves it back. The size limit is 2048 MB.
  2. Instructions. The form starts from a template. Name the setting that holds the connection string (for example ConnectionStrings:Shop), test users, and anything else the AI needs. Never put a password here. You can edit the instructions later without uploading the file again.
  3. The scan. When an application has a backup, the scan:
  4. checks the file against its SHA-256;
  5. builds an image that contains the backup, FROM mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2025-latest, postgres:18-alpine or mysql:8.4 (override them with devdb: <engine>: in rules/images.yaml). SQL Server 2025 restores backups from older versions too (SQL Server 2008 and later), and upgrades the database as it restores it;
  6. pushes the image as <registry>/<app>/devdb:<tag>, also tagged sha-<first 12 of the SHA-256>.

Each time the database pod starts, it: - restores the backup. SQL Server moves every data and log file into its data volume. PostgreSQL and MySQL restore it through the image's own /docker-entrypoint-initdb.d, while the server listens only on its local socket; - creates the user app, which owns the restored database and nothing else. On SQL Server it is a member of db_owner, not sysadmin. On PostgreSQL it owns the database, and the dump is restored as app without the dump's owners and grants. On MySQL it has all rights on that database only, and root can log in only from inside the container; - only then reports ready, because it listens on TCP only after the restore.

Nothing is kept on a persistent volume. The database is a disposable copy, and it is restored again whenever its pod starts. 4. The application's settings. - With the LLM (Ask the LLM on the scan): the AI reads the instructions and the configuration the scan found. It answers with environment variables written as templates (only {host} {port} {database} {user} {password}). Every answer is validated, and anything that contains a literal password (in a connection string or in a URL), a $(...) reference or an unknown placeholder is dropped. - Without the LLM (or when its answer has nothing usable): every connection string the scan found in appsettings*.json points at the database. If it found none, the scan sets ConnectionStrings__DefaultConnection. A Java, Node.js, Python or Go component that has a client of the database's engine gets the variables of its own conventions, as for the lab services: SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL with a JDBC URL and the user name and password next to it, the variables its code reads (DB_HOST, PGPASSWORD, ...), else DATABASE_URL.

The LLM is told the same conventions for each component, with the variables the component's code reads.

The password is never written into a manifest. The container gets CZ_DEVDB_PASSWORD from the Secret devdb, and the connection string refers to it with Kubernetes' $(CZ_DEVDB_PASSWORD) expansion.

These settings replace any secret reference with the same name that the generator made for the connection string. devdb/README.md in the generated folder lists what was set, and why.

docs.title: What runs in the sandbox
docs.text:
Object What it does Deployment devdb One replica, Recreate strategy. Pod Security "restricted": runs as a non-root user (SQL Server 10001, PostgreSQL 70, MySQL 999), read-only root filesystem, all capabilities dropped, no privilege escalation, RuntimeDefault seccomp, no service account token. A 4 GiB emptyDir for the data folder and small ones where the server writes its socket and temporary files. Memory: SQL Server 2 to 3 GiB, PostgreSQL 256 MiB to 1 GiB, MySQL 512 MiB to 1 GiB (fits the namespace LimitRange; the ResourceQuota counts it). Service devdb The engine's port (1433, 5432 or 3306), so the application connects to devdb. NetworkPolicy devdb Ingress on that port only from the application's own pods (app.kubernetes.io/part-of); egress to DNS only. Password + ExternalSecret devdb, devdb-admin External Secrets Operator's Password generator creates the app and admin (sa, postgres or root) passwords in the cluster, once (refreshInterval: "0"). They never leave the cluster and need nothing in the secret store (external-secrets.md).

Two details of the SQL Server image:

  • setcap -r /opt/mssql/bin/sqlservr. The SQL Server binary carries the file capability cap_net_bind_service. Linux refuses to start a binary like that in a container that drops all capabilities ("Operation not permitted"). The server listens on 1433, so it doesn't need the capability, and the image removes it instead of adding the capability back to the pod.
  • MSSQL_PID=Developer. SQL Server Developer edition is free for development and test use, and not licensed for production. These databases only run in the sandbox.

docs.title: Browse and fix the data
docs.text:
On the appliance, Admin → Dev databases also opens the databases the applications have in the sandbox, to look at and fix their data while you debug them: a restored dev database (above), or the application's own database on a lab service's shared SQL Server, PostgreSQL or MySQL. Only administrators and operators see the page (product owners and viewers do not, not even the link).

  • Which database. The list at the top names every application with a database in the sandbox. On an application's page, pick the database and the namespace: the application's own (also while a Make it A patch runs there in place: it uses the application's lab database), the latest first. MongoDB, Redis and the other lab services are not browsed here.
  • Tables. The tables and views, with their approximate row counts.
  • Rows. 50 a page, sorted by any column (the primary key by default), filtered on one column (equals, contains, is NULL, is not NULL). Values are shown as text: binary columns as hex, NULL as NULL.
  • Edit. Change a row, add one or delete one, always picked out by its primary key. Only the values you change are written; tick NULL for no value, and default on a new row to leave a column to the database (identity, auto-increment and columns with a default start ticked). Computed columns, rowversion and binary columns are not written here. A table without a primary key, or with a binary one, and a view are read-only, and the page says why.
  • SQL. Run one statement (on SQL Server one batch, without GO): the result table (at most 500 rows), the number of rows affected, or the database's error. A SQL Server statement whose result cannot be captured as a table (temporary tables, several result sets) shows sqlcmd's text output instead.
  • Delete the database, after typing its name:
    • a lab-service database is dropped (its open connections closed first) and the lab agent creates it again straight away, empty, with the same login and password; then the application's Deployments restart, so an application that creates its own tables (Entity Framework EnsureCreated, migrations, seed data) fills it again;
    • a restored dev database restarts. It keeps its data in its pod only, so it is restored again from the uploaded backup, which takes as long as the first restore. To stop restoring the backup, remove the backup instead.

docs.title: How a statement reaches the database
docs.text:
web UI (cz-web) --requests/<id>.json--> system agent (root) --kubectl exec -i--> the server's own client
        ^                                    |                                   (psql, mysql, sqlcmd)
        └──────── answers/<id>.json ─────────┘                                    as the application's login

The web UI has no access to the cluster. It hands each step to the system agent as a request carrying the signed-in user, the application, the namespace and the statements, and waits up to 45 seconds for the answer in /run/containerizer/system/answers/<id>.json (readable by root and the web UI only); otherwise it says the appliance did not answer. The agent trusts nothing in the request:

  • the namespace must be one that the results database maps to that application, and not a system namespace;
  • lab service: the lab agent must have provisioned that namespace's database. The login, password and database come from the secret store (containerizer-secrets/<ns>--cz-lab-<service>), and the agent checks them against the names it derives itself;
  • restored dev database: the ready devdb pod in that namespace; its engine and database name come from the pod, the password from the namespace's devdb Secret, the login is app.

The statement then runs through the engine's own client inside the server's container, as the application's own login, in its own database: whatever SQL a request holds, it can only do what the application itself can do there. The password is the first line of the client's standard input, read by a fixed script into the client's environment: it is never on a command line, in a request or answer file, or sent to the web UI. Nothing in a statement reaches the client's own command language: psql -c (no backslash commands), mysql --binary-mode (no client commands, no local files), and on SQL Server the statement travels hex-encoded into sp_executesql (no : commands, no $(variables)). Values typed into the row editor are quoted for the engine (SQL Server N'…', PostgreSQL '…'/E'…', MySQL hex literals), never pasted in raw. Each statement stops after 15 seconds; an answer holds at most 500 rows and 1 MB.

Deleting a lab-service database runs DROP DATABASE as the shared server's admin (from its own environment, as provisioning does) on the database name the agent derives itself; the typed name must match it.

docs.title: What the change history records
docs.text: Every change, before it runs: a row changed, added or deleted, a SQL statement (even a SELECT), a database deleted. It is recorded with who, when, the application, the namespace, the engine and the statement with its values (these are lab databases), in DatabaseEdit and the change history (Change history → Sandbox databases); the outcome (rows affected or the error) follows on the application's database page. If it cannot be recorded (a results database older than schema 38: run containerizer db init), it does not run. Looking at tables and rows is not recorded, unless the access log is on (CONTAINERIZER_VIEW_AUDIT): then each page is logged like other results pages.

docs.title: Setting it up
docs.text: Nothing to set up: the appliance keeps the backups on its data partition in /var/lib/containerizer/devdb, where the web UI writes them and the scan worker reads them. To allow larger uploads than 2048 MB, set CONTAINERIZER_DEV_DB_MAX_MB in /etc/containerizer/web.env and restart the web UI.

docs.title: Security notes
docs.text:
• The backup is data. It is stored on the web UI's volume and in the registry, inside the devdb image. Use backups with test data only. Treat the registry repository <registry>/<app>/devdb like the database itself, and restrict who can pull it.
  • What the audit log records. Uploads, instruction edits and removals go to the change history (AuditLog, table DevDatabase): engine, database name, file name, size, SHA-256 and a SHA-256 of the instructions, with who made the change and in which role. The instructions themselves stay only in DevDatabase.Prompt.
  • No security gate on this image. The security gate does not scan the database image. Its base is the engine's official image, which you can pin and update through rules/images.yaml.
  • Removing a backup deletes the stored file once no application refers to it. The next scan deploys the application without the database.

docs.title: Developers and ownership
docs.text: Mapping hundreds of Git repositories to products and business units by hand is slow, and the repositories rarely say who owns them. The people who commit to them usually do. Admin → Developers (administrators) lists everyone who committed to the organizations' repositories in the last six months, and uses the business units you give them to suggest where the repositories and products nobody mapped belong.

docs.title: Where the list comes from
docs.text:
At the end of every organization scan run, full or Discover, the worker reads the commit authors of the last six months from the provider's API (Azure DevOps, GitLab, GitHub), for every repository of the scan with a commit in that time. Nothing extra is cloned. It keeps:

  • one developer per e-mail address (lower case), with the name of their latest commit;
  • the repositories each developer committed to, the number of their commits there in the six months, and their latest commit there. That date only moves forward; someone whose commits are older than six months stays listed with 0 commits.

A repository is read again when it has a newer commit than the last time, or once a week (the counts age), so most runs ask the API about few repositories. Archived and empty repositories are left out. A disabled one (itself or its project, or a new repository that starts disabled) is read only while its latest commit is in the six months, so the page shows whom to ask before enabling it, and a deprecated one nobody touches costs nothing. Automation is left out as it is read ([bot] accounts, noreply addresses, build services without an e-mail address); tick Ignore for any other service account. Why reading a repository failed is in OrgRepository.HistoryError.

docs.title: Map developers to business units
docs.text:
Pick each developer's Business unit and press Save changes (once, for every row you changed). Suggested is the business unit of the products of the repositories they commit to, weighed by commits: it says matches when it is the one set, differs when it is another. Apply suggestions sets it for every developer without a business unit whose suggestion is at least 60% sure. Filter by No business unit or Ignored, or search by name, e-mail, repository or business unit.

So start from what is mapped already: map a few products to business units, apply the developers' suggestions, check them, then turn to the repositories.

docs.title: Suggestions for what nobody mapped
docs.text:
Suggestions weighs the business units of each repository's developers (not ignored) by their commits:

  • Products without a business unit, such as the ones made from projects (below): Set the suggested one, or Apply suggestions for all that are at least 60% sure.
  • Repositories without a business unit: their applications have no product, a product without a business unit, or the repository was not assessed at all (no application code, say). Map their applications on Admin → Applications to a product of the suggested business unit.

docs.title: One product per project
docs.text:
As a starting point, an Azure DevOps project (a GitLab subgroup) is one product. After every run the worker:

  1. makes a product named after each project that has an assessed application and that nobody decided on yet (an existing product of that name is used instead);
  2. maps the applications of the project's repositories that nobody mapped to it. Each application is mapped automatically once only: if someone changes its mapping, that stays.

On Projects → products change a project's product, or choose No product (a project with several products: map its applications yourself) or Automatic. The applications that were mapped automatically follow the project's product; the ones people mapped stay. Map now runs the step at once. Disabled projects are left alone, and GitHub organizations have no projects. The change history records every change the scan or people make (Via: scan for the automatic ones).

docs.title: In the database
docs.text:
Table What Developer one row per e-mail address: BusinessUnitId, Ignored and Note are set by people DeveloperRepository developer × repository: Commits (six months), LastCommitAt OrgRepository.HistoryAt, HistoryCommitAt, HistoryError when its authors were read, its newest commit then, why it failed OrgProject.ProductId, ProductMappedAt the project's product; ProductMappedAt NULL: not decided (automatic) Application.ProductAutoAt when the application was mapped to its project's product automatically

The procedure AutoMapProjects does the mapping; the scan worker's login (<schema>_writer) may run it, and may not change products or mappings otherwise.

docs.title: Egress and network connectivity
docs.text:
The sandbox is isolated. Containerizer generates a default-deny NetworkPolicy for every component that opens egress only on the ports it can infer from packages, code and configuration (a SQL Server client opens 1433, an HTTP client 443 and 80, a configured Server=db,14330 its port), and on the appliance nothing leaves the sandbox at all unless an administrators' egress rule allows it (Admin → Firewall: its firewall drops everything else and its DNS filter refuses every other name), whatever a NetworkPolicy says. A dependency of an application is then blocked in the sandbox, and someone has to find out what the application needs, and write the real environment's firewall rules for it.

Containerizer finds and documents it; agents only propose, people approve:

  1. The egress observer records what the sandbox blocks, at every layer: the NetworkPolicies, the appliance's firewall and its DNS filter, with the name a pod looked up just before.
  2. The egress review (an LLM queue job) looks at the new ones of applications rated A that run in the sandbox. A deterministic pre-filter decides first, then the LLM: is the destination named by the application's configuration or code (it quotes the file and line), and why does the application need it? It proposes, reports or flags it as suspicious.
  3. Administrators, operators and the application's product owners approve or reject each proposal. Approving documents the destination for the real environment: the queue runner writes it to the application's connectivity.yaml in the output repository. It opens nothing in the sandbox.

Links between applications connect the components that call each other across repositories and products; those calls stay inside the sandbox cluster, and a confirmed link opens them there.

Network connectivity brings everything together: on the application's results page as a diagram with the details, and next to the manifests in the output repository as connectivity.yaml, CONNECTIVITY.md and connectivity.svg, which the platform or firewall team uses to write the real environment's rules.

docs.title: Network connectivity
docs.text:
Every application has a Network connectivity section on its results page, whether it runs in the sandbox or not. It shows what the application needs from the network, from every source, each marked by where it comes from:

Source What Configuration, code URLs and connection strings in the configuration (appsettings.json, web.config, .properties, .yaml, .env) and the code, with the file and line. Development settings, comments, documentation and schema URLs are left out. A connection string without a port has its provider's default (SQL Server 1433, PostgreSQL 5432, MySQL 3306, RabbitMQ 5672); a named SQL Server instance (host\instance), whose port SQL Server Browser gives, is not listed. Package A dependency the generated NetworkPolicy opens a port for (a SQL Server client, an HTTP client, a message broker) when no configuration names its destination. NetworkPolicy What the generated policy allows: the inferred ports to any address but the blocked ranges, the application's own pods, DNS. Lab service The lab services the components need. Observed in the sandbox Connections the sandbox blocked (the egress observer), with the dropped packets, when, and from which pods. Approved A destination a person approved for the real environment (documented; the sandbox stays as it is). Ingress, service port Who reaches the components: the sandbox HTTPS host, the service port from the ingress controller's namespace (Inbound).

The diagram has the inbound side on the left, the components in the middle and the destinations on the right, one line per connection, styled by its status:

Status Meaning Allowed The generated NetworkPolicy allows it. Approved (documented) A person approved it for the real environment after the egress review. The sandbox still blocks it unless its NetworkPolicy and, on the appliance, an egress rule allow it (the Sandbox column). Proposed The egress review proposes it: waiting for a person. Blocked The sandbox blocked it; not reviewed yet, or reported (nothing to propose: an IP address without a name, a platform service). Not allowed (will time out) The configuration or code names it, and nothing allows it. Suspicious The review flagged it (a paste or file-sharing site, a tunnel, a metadata endpoint, ...): never proposed. Rejected A person rejected it.

The table under the diagram has the details: the component, the destination with port and protocol, the status, the sources, why (the review's reason, or the dependency the policy opens the port for), the evidence (the quoted lines, the flows and pods), Sandbox (below) and, for staff, Approve and Reject. A destination whose name the appliance's DNS filter refused has no port (nothing was connected): it is shown with port unknown, or on the entry of the same name that the configuration names with its port.

Sandbox: whether the sandbox can reach a destination, and what blocks it:

  • the component's NetworkPolicy: it allows the ports the assessment inferred (and confirmed links), nothing else;
  • on the appliance, its egress rules (Admin → Firewall: the system rules of the OS image and the administrators' rules, read from the same files, the same way as the firewall itself, and never changed from here): allowed by the rule that covers it, refused by the appliance's DNS filter (a name no rule covers), or dropped by the appliance firewall (an address or port no rule covers); in log mode everything is allowed and logged;
  • without an appliance (a lab): no appliance firewall (lab).

In the diagram, an allowed or approved destination the sandbox cannot reach is drawn with a thin dotted line.

Findings under the table point at what to look at:

  • Missing: the configuration or code names a destination that nothing allows. The connection fails in the sandbox, and behind a default-deny firewall in the real environment, until a rule allows it.
  • Unexplained: a port the NetworkPolicy opens to any address for a package or code pattern, but no configuration names a destination on it; or an approved destination that the configuration no longer names. Keep it only if the application needs it.

An application that is not in the sandbox (yet) shows what the assessment inferred, and says that nothing was observed. Assessments made before this version have no inferred network: scan the application again.

docs.title: Inbound
docs.text:
A component's service port is open to the ingress controller's namespace only (namespaceSelector on kubernetes.io/metadata.name), not to every namespace of the cluster: a pod of another tenant cannot call the application directly, around the ingress (TLS, sign-in proxies, rate limits). Its sibling components reach it through their own rule, and so do the callers of confirmed links (the caller's namespace and pods). CONNECTIVITY.md names the namespace in its Inbound table (namespace ingress-nginx (Service)), and HARDENING.md in its network policies row.

The namespace is a site setting: network.ingress_namespace in rules/60-security.yaml (default ingress-nginx), overridden by the environment variable CONTAINERIZER_INGRESS_NAMESPACE or --ingress-from <namespace> (containerizer generate, analyze, gate, org). The appliance sets kube-system, where k3s runs Traefik for the sandbox (its scan worker, LLM queue runner and web UI, containerizer-*.service); so does the lab sandbox (ci/lab-sandbox/env.sh).

A web component's port is also open to the Gateway's namespace, where its HTTPRoute traffic comes from: gateway.parent.namespace (--gateway <namespace>/<name>), or gateway.proxy_namespace when the implementation runs its proxies elsewhere (Envoy Gateway: envoy-gateway-system).

--ingress-from any keeps the old rule (namespaceSelector: {}, every namespace) and says so in the NetworkPolicy (containerizer.io/ingress-from: any). Without it, the gate's lint warns about an ingress rule with an empty namespaceSelector (check ingress-namespace). Where the controller runs in the host network (hostNetwork: true, some bare-metal installations), its connections come from the node's address, which no namespace selector matches: generate with --ingress-from any and replace that rule's from with an ipBlock of the node CIDR, for example from: [{ipBlock: {cidr: 10.0.0.0/24}}].

With the service ports closed to other namespaces, the egress observer also records the drops at a component's ingress whose source is another application's pod: as that caller's blocked call to <component>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local, so the link is proposed as before.

docs.title: The egress observer
docs.text:
containerizer egress-observe runs on the sandbox node. It is deterministic: no LLM.

  • What it reads, the three places the sandbox blocks a connection:
  • NetworkPolicies. k3s's network policy controller (kube-router) logs every packet a NetworkPolicy drops to the netlink log group 100 with the prefix DROP by policy <namespace>/<policy>, at most 10 packets a minute per policy. The observer binds to that group (NFLOG over a NETLINK_NETFILTER socket, no packages and no tcpdump), asks for the first 128 bytes of each packet and reads the IPv4 or IPv6 header and the TCP or UDP ports. Nothing else of the packet is kept. A drop of a cluster address on port 53 is the controller catching up with a pod that just started (every generated policy allows the cluster's DNS): it is left out.
  • The appliance firewall. Its egress chain logs what it drops to the kernel log (cz-egress-drop: IN=cni0 OUT=eth0 ... SRC=<pod> DST=<address> ... PROTO=TCP ... DPT=443, at most 30 a minute). The observer reads those lines from /dev/kmsg (--kernel-log), takes the ones whose source is an application pod (looked up across the application namespaces) and ignores the rest.
  • The appliance's DNS filter. It refuses every name no egress rule covers; CoreDNS passes the refusal on and logs it. A name an application pod asked for and was refused is a blocked destination by itself, with no port (nothing was connected).
  • Egress only. A drop counts when its source is a pod of the namespace; a drop of a pod's incoming traffic is not a dependency. Drops in the platform's namespaces (kube-system, flux-system, containerizer-*, ...) are left out.
  • Names. CoreDNS logs every query (log in the coredns-custom ConfigMap: the appliance ships it, the lab script turns it on). The observer follows that log and remembers which names each pod looked up in the last 10 minutes. When a pod's connection to an address is dropped, the address is matched to a name the same pod, or another pod of the namespace, looked up: the observer resolves those names (through the cluster's DNS on the appliance) and takes the one that resolves to the address. A destination without such a name stays an IP address, which the review reports and never proposes. An address a named flow had is explained by it and left out.
  • Which pod. The pods of the namespace through the Kubernetes API (address, pod name, the component from its app.kubernetes.io/name label).
  • Stored every minute in the results database, added up per namespace, component, destination, port and protocol: the dropped packets, first and last seen, a few pods, the policy, and the layer that blocked it (network-policy, appliance-firewall, dns-filter; cz.EgressFlow, through the procedure cz.RecordEgressFlow, with the scanner's writer login). Because kube-router logs at most 10 packets a minute per policy, the count is a lower bound.
  • Which application. A namespace belongs to the application whose sandbox check last read it, or to the "Make it A" order whose patched copy runs in it, in place (cz.vSandboxNamespace).

--dry-run prints each blocked connection (with its layer) and stores nothing:

sudo -E containerizer egress-observe --dry-run --kubeconfig ~/.kube/config --seconds 60

docs.title: On the appliance
docs.text:
containerizer-egress-observer.service runs it with the least it needs:

  • User containerizer, not root, with two capabilities: CAP_NET_ADMIN, which binding to an NFLOG group needs (the socket only reads), and CAP_SYSLOG, which reading the kernel log needs (kernel.dmesg_restrict=1): the appliance firewall's drops. Of the devices, only /dev/kmsg is visible (read only); ProtectKernelLogs is off for that reason, since it would hide it. NoNewPrivileges, a read-only system, no home directories, and only the address families it uses (netlink, IPv4, IPv6, Unix). It changes no firewall rule.
  • Kubernetes: its own ServiceAccount, containerizer-egress-observer (in containerizer-verify), with get and list on pods and get on pods/log in kube-system (the CoreDNS query log) and get and list on pods in every namespace Containerizer generated. No Secrets, no write verbs, nothing cluster-wide. cz-sandbox applies the Roles every 2 minutes and writes the kubeconfig (/run/containerizer/egress-observer.kubeconfig, root:containerizer 0640, a 24-hour token renewed every 12 hours).
  • CoreDNS query log: /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/containerizer-coredns-log.yaml (the coredns-custom ConfigMap, log.override). The log has the names pods look up and their addresses in the cluster, no answers and no payloads; it stays in the cluster's log (kubectl -n kube-system logs).
  • Database: the scanner's writer login (cz.RecordEgressFlow).

docs.title: In the lab
docs.text:
ci/lab-sandbox/egress-observer.sh install    # Roles and kubeconfig, CoreDNS query log, systemd unit lab-egress-observer
ci/lab-sandbox/egress-observer.sh remove

The unit runs as the lab user with CAP_NET_ADMIN only, writes to the lab's results database with the scanner login (results/.env) and restarts every 12 hours with a fresh token; sync.sh gives it the Roles of new namespaces. The lab has no appliance firewall or DNS filter: only NetworkPolicy drops are seen there.

docs.title: The egress review
docs.text:
The LLM queue runner looks for new blocked flows every minute (part of its housekeeping, with the job kind egress; containerizer llm-queue --kinds chooses the kinds a runner takes). A flow is new when no decision exists for its application, component, destination, port and protocol. Only applications rated A whose namespace is healthy in the sandbox, and applications a "Make it A" patch runs for (in their own namespace), are reviewed.

The pre-filter decides first and is never overruled by the LLM. Its lists are in rules/60-security.yaml (network.egress_review):

Verdict When Suspicious A metadata endpoint or one of the blocked_cidrs (169.254.169.254, ...), a wildcard name, a paste, file-sharing, tunnelling or request-capture service (suspicious_domains: pastebin, transfer.sh, ngrok, webhook.site, ...) Reported: platform A drop in a platform namespace, a service of the cloud platform (platform_domains: Key Vault, the container registry, ...) Reported: IP address No pod of the namespace looked the address up by name Reported: in the cluster A pod or service address of the cluster (a call to another namespace: allow it with a NetworkPolicy, not egress) Reported: unusual port A port that is not in ports (443, 80, the usual database and broker ports, ...): a person decides

The LLM gets the rest, one job per application (at most 10 destinations a call): each destination with its port, protocol, component, the dropped packets and when, the pods, and the lines of the application's source that name it, from the assessed commit (the source is loaded as for a refactoring patch: the scan worker's clone). Without the source, the lines the assessment recorded. It answers per destination, in a fixed JSON schema:

{"destinations": [{"destination": "api.github.com", "port": 443, "verdict": "propose",
  "reason": "The application configures its upstream API URL (Upstream:Url) ...",
  "file": "src/Egress.Demo/appsettings.json", "line": 4, "quote": "\"Upstream\": { \"Url\": \"https://api.github.com/zen\" }"}]}
  • propose: the configuration or code names it, or it is an ordinary public API the application plainly uses with a steady flow;
  • report: nothing explains it, or a person should decide;
  • suspicious: exfiltration, command and control, a hard-coded destination unrelated to what the application does.

The answer is checked: a quoted line must be in the source (near the line it names), else the evidence is dropped and the reason says so; a proposal with no such line and fewer than 3 dropped packets is reported instead. A destination the LLM did not answer for is reported. The job goes through the queue's approval policy like the other kinds (egress in Jobs that wait for approval).

docs.title: Approving
docs.text:
Admin → Egress lists the decisions of the applications one may decide for, open ones first; the results page has the same buttons in its Network connectivity table.

Role Approve, Reject Administrator, Operator Every application Product owner The applications of their products Viewer, anyone without sign-in Sees the decisions, not the buttons
  • Approve is possible for named destinations the review proposed or reported, never for suspicious ones, the platform's or IP addresses. A rejected proposal can be approved later.
  • Reject: connectivity.yaml records the decision.
  • An approved destination stays approved: Containerizer never rewrites or removes it. To take one back, remove it from connectivity.yaml in a commit of your own.

Every decision records who made it and when (DecidedBy, DecidedAt, and the change history).

docs.title: What approving changes
docs.text:
Approving documents; it opens nothing. Within a minute the LLM queue runner, which holds the output repository's write token (the one registered for the organization scan's output repository, as for Make it A patched copies), commits the application's connectivity.yaml, CONNECTIVITY.md and connectivity.svg with the approved destination: the FQDN, port and protocol, why, the evidence and who approved it. That is what the real environment's firewall rules are written from.

The sandbox stays isolated. The NetworkPolicies keep allowing only what the assessment inferred, and on the appliance only the administrators' egress rules let anything out of the sandbox. If an application must reach a destination in the sandbox too, an administrator adds an egress rule on Admin → Firewall; the Sandbox column then shows the rule (the NetworkPolicy still has to allow the port: it allows the inferred ones).

Later organization scans keep approved entries: the generator reads the application's connectivity.yaml from the output repository and the new connectivity.yaml keeps every approved entry as it was (its sandbox status is computed again). A Make it A patched copy runs in the application's folder and keeps them too. New decisions (also reported and suspicious ones) and rejections are written to connectivity.yaml the same way.

docs.title: connectivity.yaml
docs.text:
Next to the application's manifests in the output repository (<Org>/<Project>/<Repo>/connectivity.yaml), written by every organization scan with the manifests, and refreshed by the queue runner when there are new decisions, approvals or rejections. CONNECTIVITY.md is the same as a page, with the diagram as a Mermaid block (Azure Repos, GitHub and GitLab draw it in the file preview; Azure Repos does not show SVG images there) and as an image, connectivity.svg (light and dark), linked from it.

apiVersion: containerizer.eu/v1
kind: Connectivity
application: egress-demo
namespace: egress-demo                # in the sandbox
generatedAt: '2026-11-02T03:45:01Z'
observed: true                        # false: inferred only, nothing observed in the sandbox
note: Approved destinations are documented for the real environment ...
components:
- {name: egress-demo, component: Egress.Demo, role: web, port: 8080, service_port: 80}
inbound:
- {component: egress-demo, from: 'https://egress-demo.sandbox.lab.test/', port: 80, protocol: TCP, source: ingress, target_port: 8080}
- {component: egress-demo, from: namespace kube-system (Service), port: 80, protocol: TCP, source: service, target_port: 8080}
internal: []                          # component to component, lab services
outbound:
- component: egress-demo
  destination: api.github.com
  type: fqdn                          # fqdn, ip, any (a port open to any address), component (another application)
  port: 443
  protocol: TCP
  status: approved                    # allowed, approved, proposed, blocked, not-allowed, suspicious, rejected, reported
  sources: [config, observed, approved]
  reason: The application configures its upstream API URL ...
  evidence:
  - {file: src/Egress.Demo/appsettings.json, line: 4, quote: '"Upstream": { "Url": "https://api.github.com/zen" }'}
  observed: {packets: 3, first_seen: '2026-11-02T03:38:59Z', last_seen: '2026-11-02T03:38:59Z', pods: [...], ips: [140.82.121.6]}
  approved_by: john.doe@example.com
  approved_at: '2026-11-02T03:43:46Z'
  blocked_by: [network-policy]        # the layers the sandbox blocked it at: network-policy, appliance-firewall, dns-filter
  sandbox:                            # whether the sandbox can reach it (computed on every write)
    network_policy: blocks port 443
    appliance: 'refused by the appliance''s DNS filter: no egress rule allows it'   # lab: no appliance firewall (lab)
    reachable: false
    blocked_by: network-policy
- component: egress-demo
  destination: orders-demo.orders-demo     # as the configuration names it
  type: component                          # another application's component (links between applications)
  port: 80
  protocol: TCP
  status: linked                           # linked, link-proposed
  sources: [config, link-config]
  target: {application: orders-demo, application_id: 1011, component: orders-demo, namespace: orders-demo,
           service: orders-demo.orders-demo.svc.cluster.local, port: 8080}
  link: {id: 1, status: confirmed, method: config, confidence: 0.95, reason: the configuration names ...}
  linked_by: john.doe@example.com
  linked_at: '2026-11-02T04:12:59Z'
- component: egress-demo
  destination: pastebin.com
  type: fqdn
  port: 443
  protocol: TCP
  status: suspicious
  category: file-sharing
  sources: [code, observed]
  reason: pastebin.com is a paste, file-sharing, tunnelling or request-capture service ...
findings:
- {kind: unexplained, component: ..., text: ...}
Field Meaning outbound[].destination, port, protocol What a firewall rule needs. type: any is a port the generated policy opens to any address (a package needs it; name the destination for production). status As on the results page (table above). approved entries are never rewritten or dropped by Containerizer. sources config, code, package, policy, observed, approved, lab-service. evidence The lines that name the destination (file, line, the line itself). observed What the sandbox blocked: dropped packets (a lower bound), first and last seen, pods, addresses. blocked_by The layers the sandbox blocked it at: network-policy, appliance-firewall, dns-filter. sandbox Whether the sandbox can reach it: what its NetworkPolicy does, the appliance's egress rule that allows it (rule) or what blocks it (blocked_by), reachable. port_unknown The appliance's DNS filter refused the name, so no port was seen and the configuration names none (port: 0). approved_by, approved_at, rejected_by, rejected_at Who decided, when. inbound, internal Who reaches the components (the Ingress host, the service port, and confirmed callers from other applications: source: link, with their application, component and namespace), component to component and lab services. target (type: component) The other application's component a destination is: application, component, namespace, service name and container port. findings missing and unexplained, as on the results page.

docs.title: Links between applications
docs.text:
A real application is often several Containerizer applications: components in different repositories, owned by different teams or products, calling each other. An outbound destination can then be another component assessed here, and connectivity says so: the destination is linked to that component (type: component in connectivity.yaml), the diagram draws it as a teal box with the other application's name, and the table links to its page.

How links are found (cz.ComponentLink, every minute by the LLM queue runner's housekeeping), each recorded with how it was found and its evidence:

Found by When Configuration matches (config) A configured host is another application's component: its service in the sandbox (<component>.<namespace>, ...svc, ...svc.cluster.local) or its sandbox Ingress host. Confidence 0.95. Observed in the sandbox (observed) The sandbox blocked a call from one application's pod to another application's pod (the observer names such a destination <component>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local). Not recorded again when the configuration already links it. LLM (llm) A configured destination that looks internal (one label, or .local, .internal, .corp, .lan, .intranet, .svc, ..., or a host of one of your own internal domains, see below) and that nothing matched. A link job of the LLM queue (with its approval policy) gives the LLM the destination, its configuration lines and a shortlist of 15 candidate components of other applications (name, application, product, project, role, repository) and asks for the best match, its confidence and why, or none. Answers below 0.5 or outside the shortlist are not taken. By hand (manual) Link manually on the results page: pick one of the components assessed here.

Every link is a proposal until a person confirms it: Confirm and Reject on the calling application's results page, for administrators, operators and the calling application's product owners; a link made by hand is confirmed at once. A destination that looks internal and is not linked shows as Looks internal, not linked, with Link manually. Every decision is recorded with who made it (and in the change history).

Your own internal domains. Many organizations name internal servers under a registered domain (orders.corp.contoso.com, sql01.ad.company.net), which does not look internal by its name. List those domains in network.internal_domains of rules/60-security.yaml, or set the environment variable CONTAINERIZER_INTERNAL_DOMAINS (comma separated) for the worker and the web UI. Hosts under them are then candidates for links, and for the calls between the Linux and the Windows part in a migration plan.

A confirmed link is written by the queue runner to both applications in the output repository, in one commit:

  • the caller's connectivity.yaml names the other application, component, namespace, service and port (type: component, target), and the caller's NetworkPolicy gets an egress rule to that namespace and those pods on the component's container port;
  • the callee's connectivity.yaml lists the caller under inbound (source: link), and its NetworkPolicy gets an ingress rule from the caller's namespace and pods.

Later scans keep both (the generator reads them from connectivity.yaml), as they keep approved egress.

The callee's page shows its callers:

How the applications connect (/connectivity, linked from each application's section; ?product=<id> or ?bu=<id> for one product or business unit): the applications as groups of their components, the links between them (confirmed solid, proposed dashed), each application's decided outbound destinations summed up, and the links in a table. The other side of a link outside the product is shown too, with a dashed frame.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• Only what is blocked is seen. The observer reads the drop log; allowed traffic is not recorded, so Containerizer cannot tell whether an allowed or approved destination is still used.
  • Names come from DNS. A connection to an address no pod of the namespace looked up (a hard-coded IP, a name looked up more than 10 minutes before, a DNS-over-HTTPS client) stays an address. Shared CDN addresses can serve several names; the observer takes the name the namespace's own pods looked up.
  • Rate limit. kube-router logs at most 10 packets a minute per policy: a burst is counted as at most 10.
  • The LLM can be wrong. It only proposes; the quoted line is checked against the source, and a person approves.
  • The appliance's signals are rate limited too: its firewall logs at most 30 drops a minute.
  • Approval is documentation. It never changes the sandbox: a destination an application needs in the sandbox as well needs an administrators' egress rule (and a port its NetworkPolicy allows).

docs.title: Secrets: External Secrets Operator
docs.text:
Nothing containerizer generates is a Kubernetes Secret, and no generated file holds a secret value. Every Secret a workload, a Flux source or an image pull needs is an External Secrets Operator (ESO) ExternalSecret. ESO reads the value from a secret store and creates the Secret in the cluster. The store can be a vault, a cloud secret manager, or on the appliance a locked-down namespace of the same cluster. Git only holds the references.

What ExternalSecret Remote key Properties Connection strings, secret settings and secret-looking settings with release-pipeline tokens (#{X}#, __X__; the others are in the ConfigMap <component>-settings) of a component <component>-secrets <namespace>--<component> one per environment variable, e.g. ConnectionStrings__Main Key and certificate files: .pfx/.p12 next to the code (mounted where the app reads them), files named by a Windows path (under /secrets), every file when the repository mounts them all (Admin → Repositories) <component>-files <namespace>--<component>-files the file names; values base64 Kerberos keytab <component>-keytab <namespace>--<component> the file name Flux GitRepository credential <namespace>-git <namespace>--cz-git username + password, or identity + known_hosts Flux commit verification keys <namespace>-git-gpg <namespace>--cz-git-gpg the public keys Registry read credential (Flux OCIRepository/ImageRepository; the image pull secret of an organization scan) <namespace>-registry, the pull secret's name <namespace>--cz-registry .dockerconfigjson cosign public key for signed OCI artifacts <namespace>-cosign-pub <namespace>--cz-cosign-pub cosign.pub Sandbox root sync (clusters/sandbox/flux/bootstrap.yaml) containerizer-sandbox-git flux-system--cz-git username + password Dev database passwords (dev-databases.md) devdb, devdb-admin none: ESO's Password generator creates them in the cluster

<namespace> is the app's namespace. Each app's HARDENING.md lists the exact remote keys and properties under Secret store keys. The <namespace>--<name> form is valid as a Kubernetes Secret name, an Azure Key Vault secret name, an AWS Secrets Manager name and a Vault path, so the same generated files work with every store below.

docs.title: Isolation: each namespace reads only its own keys
docs.text:
All ExternalSecrets use one ClusterSecretStore, app-secrets. The store names its identity, the ServiceAccount app-secrets-reader, without a namespace. ESO then authenticates as app-secrets-reader in the namespace of the ExternalSecret ("referent" authentication). So namespace shop reads the store as shop:app-secrets-reader and can get only what that identity is granted:

  • kubernetes provider (appliance, default): a Role in containerizer-secrets with get on exactly the remote Secrets of shop (resourceNames, no list, no watch). It is generated in gitops/flux/tenant.yaml (with containerizer generate on a single app, also in its cluster/secret-store.yaml).
  • Vault / OpenBao: a policy that allows <mount>/data/<namespace>--* for the namespace of the caller.
  • AWS Secrets Manager: an IAM role per namespace (IRSA) limited to secret:<namespace>--*.
  • Azure Key Vault: a workload identity per namespace with Key Vault Secrets User on its own secrets.

The reader ServiceAccount runs no pod and mounts no token. ESO asks the API server for a short-lived token of it (TokenRequest, one hour) each time it reads. Every app namespace gets the ServiceAccount from the generated security.yaml; on Flux it is in the platform-owned tenant.yaml instead, because the Git source's own ExternalSecret needs it before the first sync.

The rules behind this are in rules/60-security.yaml (secrets): store name and kind, refresh interval, key format, reader name and annotations, and the provider definitions. CONTAINERIZER_SECRET_STORE=kubernetes|vault|azurekv|aws in /etc/containerizer/worker.env chooses which store the scans write into each cluster's platform/secret-store.yaml (default kubernetes, the appliance's own store).

docs.title: Missing secrets
docs.text:
A component's settings, connection strings, secret files and keytab are optional references in its workload: a pod starts without them when the store has no value (or not every property: ESO then creates none of that Secret's keys). Their ExternalSecret stays not ready (SecretSyncedError) until the values are in the store. The Secrets a pod cannot start without are not optional: the Data Protection key ring (made in the cluster by ESO's Password generator, no store), the image pull credential, the Flux Git credential.

  • Real clusters: the app's gitops/flux/git/sync.yaml has wait: true, so Flux waits for every applied object and the Kustomization stays not ready (health check timeout naming the ExternalSecret) until each secret is in the store. Fill the keys of HARDENING.md before the first sync.
  • The sandbox: nobody fills the components' own keys there, so each app folder's gitops/sandbox/ patches the app's Kustomization to wait: false with healthChecks of its Deployments and StatefulSets and the ExternalSecrets of the Secrets a pod needs. The Kustomization is ready when the workloads are; a missing required secret still fails it (the pod never starts, or its ExternalSecret is not ready).

docs.title: Hardening checks
docs.text:
The security gate and HARDENING.md (NSA/CISA "Secrets", CIS 5.4.2 and 5.1.2) check:

Check Severity Fails when plain-secret error a Secret object is in the manifests secret-literals error a Secret, an env variable with a secret-looking name, or an ExternalSecret template carries a literal value secret-source error a workload references a Secret (env, envFrom, volume, projected volume, imagePullSecrets) that no ExternalSecret of the app produces external-secret-store error an ExternalSecret names no SecretStore/ClusterSecretStore (generators excepted), or the app ships its own store

A component that needs a different Secret source declares a waiver in its exception (containerizer.io/waives), and the waiver appears in the report.

docs.title: The appliance sandbox
docs.text:
The appliance installs ESO 2.14.0 in its k3s cluster at boot. The chart is part of the OS image, checked against its digest, and the images are pinned by digest. PushSecret, ClusterExternalSecret and ClusterGenerator are switched off. Every 2 minutes cz-sandbox:

  1. creates namespace containerizer-secrets (Pod Security "restricted", a ResourceQuota of zero pods, so nothing can run next to the values) and ClusterSecretStore app-secrets (kubernetes provider over that namespace, referent ServiceAccount app-secrets-reader);
  2. puts the read-only Git token of sandbox.env there as flux-system--cz-git and as <namespace>--cz-git for every app that the output repository deploys. Flux reads them through the generated ExternalSecrets.

Administrators and operators enter the apps' values in OpenBao (https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>/ui/, Secret values in OpenBao): the appliance makes an empty entry for every value a sandbox app reads and copies the filled ones here. The rest of this section is for the appliance's own writers and for doing it by hand.

Other appliance scripts write values with the helpers in /usr/lib/containerizer/lib/secret-store.sh:

k() { k3s kubectl "$@"; }; . /usr/lib/containerizer/lib/secret-store.sh
cz_store_put shop--web ConnectionStrings__Main='Server=db;...'   # or key=@file
cz_store_grant some-platform-namespace some-key                  # app namespaces get theirs from tenant.yaml

cz_store_put uses server-side apply with its own field manager (--manager NAME), so two writers can own different keys of the same remote Secret without removing each other's. The values reach kubectl on standard input, never on a command line. To set a component's secret settings by hand on the appliance, as root:

kubectl -n containerizer-secrets create secret generic shop--web \
  --from-literal=ConnectionStrings__Main='Server=...' --dry-run=client -o yaml | kubectl apply -f -

k3s encrypts Secrets at rest (secrets-encryption: true), and the audit policy logs Secret access at metadata level only.

docs.title: Real clusters
docs.text: Install ESO (the Helm chart), apply clusters/<cluster>/platform/secret-store.yaml of the organization scan's output repository (the store is the same for every app; each app's Role is in its gitops/flux/tenant.yaml), and put the remote keys from HARDENING.md in the store. Then deploy as usual. To use another backend, set CONTAINERIZER_SECRET_STORE for the scans, or edit the store. The app manifests stay the same.

docs.title: HashiCorp Vault or OpenBao
docs.text:
secrets.providers.vault in the rules (KV version 2 at secret/, Kubernetes auth at kubernetes/):

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata: {name: app-secrets}
spec:
  provider:
    vault:
      server: https://vault.example.com:8200
      path: secret
      version: v2
      auth:
        kubernetes:
          mountPath: kubernetes
          role: app-secrets
          serviceAccountRef: {name: app-secrets-reader, audiences: [vault]}   # no namespace: the caller's

On the Vault side, one role for every namespace, and a policy templated on the caller's namespace so shop reads only secret/data/shop--*:

ACCESSOR=$(vault read -field=accessor sys/auth/kubernetes)
vault policy write app-secrets - <<EOF
path "secret/data/{{identity.entity.aliases.$ACCESSOR.metadata.service_account_namespace}}--*" {
  capabilities = ["read"]
}
EOF
vault write auth/kubernetes/role/app-secrets bound_service_account_names=app-secrets-reader \
  bound_service_account_namespaces='*' audience=vault policies=app-secrets token_ttl=10m
vault kv put secret/shop--web ConnectionStrings__Main='Server=...'

Vault must be able to call the cluster's TokenReview API (Vault's Kubernetes auth documentation covers kubernetes_host and the system:auth-delegator binding). OpenBao uses the same vault provider.

docs.title: Azure Key Vault
docs.text:
secrets.providers.azurekv (workload identity of each namespace's reader):

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata: {name: app-secrets}
spec:
  provider:
    azurekv:
      authType: WorkloadIdentity
      vaultUrl: https://contoso-apps.vault.azure.net
      serviceAccountRef: {name: app-secrets-reader}     # no namespace: the caller's
  • Store each remote key as one secret whose value is a JSON object, e.g. secret shop--web with value {"ConnectionStrings__Main": "Server=..."}. ESO reads the properties from the JSON.
  • Give each app namespace its own user-assigned managed identity. Add a federated credential for subject system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:app-secrets-reader, and set the identity's client id on that namespace's reader. secrets.reader.annotations / readerAnnotations in the rules set one client id for all namespaces; use a kustomize patch per app for one identity each.
  • Grant Key Vault Secrets User to each identity on its own secrets only (role assignments scoped to .../vaults/<vault>/secrets/<namespace>--<name>), or give each app its own vault. A vault-wide assignment lets every namespace read every key.

docs.title: AWS Secrets Manager
docs.text:
secrets.providers.aws (IRSA role of each namespace's reader):

apiVersion: external-secrets.io/v1
kind: ClusterSecretStore
metadata: {name: app-secrets}
spec:
  provider:
    aws:
      service: SecretsManager
      region: eu-north-1
      auth:
        jwt:
          serviceAccountRef: {name: app-secrets-reader}  # no namespace: the caller's
  • The reader of each namespace carries eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn. The rules template it as arn:aws:iam::<account>:role/app-secrets-{namespace}, so create one IAM role per app namespace, trusted by the cluster's OIDC provider for system:serviceaccount:<namespace>:app-secrets-reader.
  • Allow that role secretsmanager:GetSecretValue (and DescribeSecret) on arn:aws:secretsmanager:<region>:<account>:secret:<namespace>--* only.
  • Store each remote key as a JSON secret (shop--web → {"ConnectionStrings__Main": "..."}).

docs.title: Other stores
docs.text: Any ESO provider works: add it under secrets.providers, keep the store named app-secrets, and, where the provider supports it, name app-secrets-reader without a namespace so each namespace keeps its own identity. A namespaced SecretStore per app (secrets.store.kind: SecretStore) is the alternative when a provider has no referent authentication. Apply it in each app namespace, and drop the namespaces from its references (a namespaced store may only refer to its own namespace).

docs.title: Gateway API routes
docs.text: Every web component (a component that serves HTTP: web and spa) gets an HTTPRoute in its <component>/k8s.yaml. The route carries what IIS or App Service did for the application: timeouts, sticky sessions, rewrite rules, redirects and response headers. They are set in standard Gateway API fields, so the application code stays as it is. The route does not use vendor annotations. The mapping is data in rules/60-security.yaml (gateway:).

docs.title: The platform owns the Gateway
docs.text:
The routes attach to a Gateway that the platform team runs. Containerizer does not generate it per app.

  • Its HTTPS listener holds the certificate. TLS terminates at the Gateway, and the pods stay on plain HTTP.
  • Its HTTP listener only redirects to HTTPS. No route attaches to it.
  • The routes attach to the HTTPS listener only (sectionName).

The default parent is gateway-system/platform-gateway, listener https. Change it with --gateway <namespace>/<name> and --gateway-listener <listener> (containerizer generate, analyze, gate, org). The environment variables are CONTAINERIZER_GATEWAY and CONTAINERIZER_GATEWAY_LISTENER, or gateway.parent in the rules.

An example Gateway (the class and the certificate Secret are the platform's own):

apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: platform-gateway
  namespace: gateway-system
spec:
  gatewayClassName: example        # the implementation's class
  listeners:
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      hostname: "*.apps.example.com"
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs: [{name: apps-example-com-tls}]
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces: {from: All}    # or a selector on the applications' namespaces
    - name: http                   # only redirects; no route attaches here
      protocol: HTTP
      port: 80
      allowedRoutes:
        namespaces: {from: Same}
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: HTTPRoute
metadata:
  name: https-redirect
  namespace: gateway-system
spec:
  parentRefs: [{name: platform-gateway, sectionName: http}]
  rules:
    - filters: [{type: RequestRedirect, requestRedirect: {scheme: https, statusCode: 301}}]

docs.title: Host names
docs.text: A route's host is <component>.<app>.<domain>, or <app>.<domain> when the component has the app's name. The domain is --ingress-domain (or the organization's setting). Without a domain, the placeholder example.invalid is used, and MIGRATION.md says so. A wildcard certificate covers one label only: a listener for *.apps.example.com matches web.shop.apps.example.com, but its certificate does not. Give the Gateway a certificate per application (*.shop.apps.example.com), or change gateway.host to '{component}-{app}.{domain}' so that one wildcard certificate covers every route.

docs.title: What maps to which field
docs.text:
Finding or configuration HTTPRoute host-long-request-timeout (executionTimeout, ANCM requestTimeout) rules[].timeouts.request and backendRequest (the longest timeout, at most 3600 s). The pod's terminationGracePeriodSeconds covers it too (at most 600 s). signalr-scaleout, host-blazor-server timeouts of at least 3600 s for the long-lived connections in-memory-session-scaleout, state-session-in-memory, host-arr-affinity, signalr-scaleout, host-blazor-server cookie session affinity at the Gateway implementation (listed in MIGRATION.md), or sessionPersistence on the rule with gateway.session_persistence.emit: true <rewrite> rule, HTTP to HTTPS ({HTTPS} off, X-Forwarded-Proto, port 80) nothing: the Gateway's HTTP listener does it <rewrite> rule, prefix rewrite or redirect (^old/(.*) to new/{R:1}) URLRewrite or RequestRedirect with ReplacePrefixMatch on a PathPrefix match <rewrite> rule, one path (^about$ to about/, so trailing slashes too) ReplaceFullPath on an Exact match <rewrite> rule, whole site to another host RequestRedirect with hostname.
