With a {HTTP_HOST} condition, it is a route of its own for the old host, which needs a listener and a certificate for that host. <httpRedirect> RequestRedirect <httpProtocol><customHeaders> ResponseHeaderModifier (set, remove) HSTS ResponseHeaderModifier sets Strict-Transport-Security on every rule that reaches the app

Redirects use 301 or 302, the codes in the standard channel, so every generated route deploys on a cluster with the standard-channel CRDs.

sessionPersistence is in Gateway API's experimental channel. With only the standard-channel CRDs installed, server-side apply (Flux) rejects a route that has it (field not declared in schema). So it is opt-in. By default the route has no such field, and MIGRATION.md and HARDENING.md say the component needs cookie session affinity at the Gateway implementation. They name the cookie (CZAFFINITY) and the findings that call for it. On a cluster with the experimental CRDs, set gateway.session_persistence.emit: true in the rules, and the route carries the cookie sessionPersistence itself. The findings are not marked resolved either way: one replica keeps working, but scaling out needs the affinity.

docs.title: What the Gateway implementation sets
docs.text:
Gateway API has no standard field for some settings. MIGRATION.md and HARDENING.md list them with their values, to set in the implementation's own policy:

  • request body limits: <requestLimits maxAllowedContentLength>, <httpRuntime maxRequestLength>, and file uploads (IFormFile), which need at least the IIS and Kestrel default of 30,000,000 bytes;
  • URL and query string limits (maxUrl, maxQueryString);
  • client IP allow and deny lists (<ipSecurity>, as CIDRs).

docs.title: What is not translated
docs.text:
These rules are listed in MIGRATION.md with their original XML, to re-create at the Gateway or with ASP.NET Core's UseRewriter, which reads IIS rules:

  • rules with conditions on other server variables ({HTTP_USER_AGENT}, {QUERY_STRING}, {REQUEST_FILENAME} file checks);
  • rules that set server variables, use rewrite maps or back-references other than {R:1};
  • outbound rules;
  • request filtering other than the limits;
  • configuration scoped to a <location path>.

The web-config-rewrite finding is marked resolved (resolved_by: gateway-httproute) only when every item translated and nothing is left for the implementation.

Gateway API picks the most specific match (an exact path, then the longest prefix), while IIS runs its rules in order. Path matches are case-sensitive, and IIS rules ignore case by default. Review overlapping rules.

docs.title: Checks and permissions
docs.text:
• The gate's lint checks every HTTPRoute. route-parent: it attaches to a Gateway. route-listener: it attaches to an HTTPS listener (gateway.https_listener, or the configured listener), never by port and never without a sectionName. route-hostname: it names its hosts, with no wildcard and no address. HARDENING.md reports these checks in its Gateway row.
  • The component's NetworkPolicy lets the Gateway's namespace call the service port (Inbound).
  • The built-in admin role does not cover Gateway API resources. The Flux tenant (gitops/flux/tenant.yaml) therefore gets a Role for httproutes in the app's namespace.
  • The sandbox keeps its Traefik Ingress (Sandbox HTTPS). The appliance's Traefik has no Gateway API provider, so the sandbox's copy of each app's Flux Kustomization drops the HTTPRoutes.

docs.title: Java and Node.js
docs.text: The rule engine assesses Java (Maven and Gradle, Spring Boot, Quarkus, Micronaut, plain JVM programs and WAR files) and Node.js (npm, yarn and pnpm; Express, Fastify, Koa, NestJS, Next.js, Nuxt and others) the same way as .NET: rules first, every finding explained with references, the same ratings, and the same stateless requirement for an A. Nothing from the repository is built or run during the assessment.

docs.title: What is read
docs.text:
Java (containerizer/scan_java.py)

  • pom.xml: coordinates, packaging (jar, war, ear, pom), properties and ${...} references, in-repository parents (<relativePath>), inherited dependencies and plugins, profiles, dependencyManagement versions, the Spring Boot line, the Java version and the main class.
  • build.gradle / build.gradle.kts: plugins (id, apply plugin, alias(libs.plugins.x)), dependencies by configuration (string, map and version catalog notations), project(':x') references, subprojects {} and allprojects {} blocks, toolchains and settings.gradle includes; gradle/libs.versions.toml is resolved, bundles included.
  • A folder with both pom.xml and build.gradle is one project (Maven's).
  • Dependencies are named groupId:artifactId. Test-scoped dependencies (Maven test, Gradle test* configurations) are kept apart, and src/test/ is not searched by code rules.

Node.js (containerizer/scan_node.py)

  • package.json: dependencies (devDependencies kept apart), scripts and the start command, main, bin, engines.node, packageManager, library markers (exports, files, peerDependencies) and npm/yarn workspaces or pnpm-workspace.yaml.
  • Workspace packages that depend on each other become project references, so a finding in a shared package reaches the applications that use it.
  • The lockfile (package-lock.json v2/v3 or pnpm-lock.yaml) is walked from the package's own runtime dependencies: packages that install only on Windows ("os": ["win32"], not optional) and packages that compile a native addon are recorded.
  • Test files and folders (__tests__/, test/, *.spec.ts, ...) are not searched by code rules.

A front end inside a Java module (src/main/webui, frontend-maven-plugin, the Gradle node plugin, a build that writes into the module) is served by that module, like a ClientApp in an ASP.NET Core project.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text: Role Java Node.js web @SpringBootApplication with a web stack (also through a shared module), Quarkus/Micronaut/Helidon HTTP, Javalin/Dropwizard/Vert.x with a main, a WAR or EAR a server framework among the runtime dependencies and a start script, .listen() or a self-starting framework (Next.js, Nuxt, NestJS) worker a Spring Boot/Quarkus application with listeners or schedulers and no HTTP a start script and a queue, scheduler or bot package console Spring Batch, other Spring Boot applications, a declared main class a start script that runs node spa React/Angular/Vue/Svelte apps with an index.html or app tooling desktop Swing, JavaFX, SWT, Android Electron, React Native, Ionic, Tauri library Maven aggregators and BOMs, modules without an application workspace roots, component libraries, middleware packages tool command line packages (bin)

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
Rules are in rules/12-java.yaml, rules/13-node.yaml and rules/14-java-node-common.yaml.

  • Blockers and rewrites: COM automation (JACOB, com4j, winax), Windows API calls through JNA, FFI or NodeRT with no OS check, native libraries shipped only as DLLs, the JDBC-ODBC bridge. Each has an entry in the migration assistant (rules/migrations.yaml).
  • Refactoring: Windows integrated authentication (WAFFLE, node-sspi), the Windows registry, Windows-only helper packages and dependencies, Edge.js, starting Windows programs, Java 7 or older, Node.js 17 or older, node-sass, full Jakarta EE servers (EJB, EAR) and vendor server APIs.
  • Configuration: SQL Server integrated security from JDBC, msnodesqlv8, iisnode, Windows service wrappers (procrun, WinSW, node-windows), file-only logging, schedulers that run in every replica, Quartz's in-memory store, Socket.IO without an adapter, headless browsers, Oracle Thick mode, process managers, Windows environment variables and drive paths in code.

docs.title: Stateless
docs.text:
As for .NET, an application is A only when every server component keeps its data in external services. These keep a component stateful (rated B when otherwise ready):

  • an embedded database in file mode (H2/HSQLDB file URLs, Derby, SQLite, LowDB, NeDB, LevelDB) with no server database driver in the repository;
  • an embedded in-memory database (H2, HSQLDB, Derby) as the only database;
  • HTTP sessions in process memory (HttpSession, form login, Vaadin/JSF without Spring Session; express-session's default store) or in local files;
  • uploads and data files written to the local disk without an object storage client;
  • a local Lucene index (FSDirectory, the Hibernate Search Lucene backend).

Not counted: an embedded database next to a server database driver (the deployment can choose the server one), and in-memory test databases.

docs.title: Confidence
docs.text: Java runtime dependencies that are not in rules/packages-java.yaml lower the confidence, as do Node.js native addons and Windows-only packages not in rules/packages-node.yaml (pure JavaScript packages are portable and do not count). Low confidence triggers verification and the optional LLM review, as for .NET.

docs.title: Containers
docs.text:
The scan generates Java and Node.js components the same way as .NET ones: a multi-stage Dockerfile that uses the application folder as build context, a hardened Kubernetes manifest (non-root, read-only root file system, no capabilities, seccomp, resource limits, NetworkPolicy) and a plan.json that explains every non-default decision. Base images are in rules/images.yaml, with patched tags pinned in rules/images.lock.yaml.

Java (containerizer/gen_jvm_node.py)

Java line the version the build declares (maven.compiler.release, java.version, toolchains), rounded up to an LTS line: 8, 11, 17, 21 or 25. The build and the runtime use the same line. Build Maven from the image (-pl <module> -am from the in-repository aggregator), or the repository's Gradle wrapper (bootJar, quarkusBuild, installDist, shadowJar, war). Tests are skipped in the image build. A CA bundle passed as the ca build secret is added to the build JDK; HTTPS_PROXY is passed to Maven and Gradle. Runtime distroless Java 17/21/25, or the Temurin JRE for Java 8 and 11, as uid 65532. Spring Boot and executable jars or WARs run with java -jar; Quarkus runs its fast-jar; a plain program runs its main class with its dependencies on the class path; a WAR without an embedded server is unpacked into Tomcat 9 (javax.servlet) or 10.1 (jakarta.servlet). Port SERVER_PORT, QUARKUS_HTTP_PORT, MICRONAUT_SERVER_PORT or PORT set to 8080; a port fixed in code is kept. Probes Spring Boot Actuator liveness and readiness groups (not when Spring Security protects them and the code does not open them), SmallRye Health, Micronaut management; a TCP probe otherwise. The context path is taken into account. Configuration Windows paths in application.properties/.yml (and the prod profile) are overridden through environment variables (Spring relaxed binding, MicroProfile names) to folders under /data. Credentials (passwords, secrets, JDBC URLs) become optional Secret references; a ${DB_PASSWORD} placeholder references that variable. Memory -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75, request 512Mi, limit 1Gi.

Node.js

Node.js line the newest supported LTS line (22 or 24) that engines.node allows. Install npm ci, pnpm install --frozen-lockfile or yarn install (classic or Berry, with the node-modules linker) through corepack, at the workspace root. Packages with native addons build on the full Debian image (Python, make, g++). Build the build script of the package and of the in-repository packages it uses, dependencies first (pnpm orders a filtered run itself). devDependencies are pruned afterwards with npm and pnpm (not in pnpm or yarn workspaces, where that means a reinstall). Start the production start script (start:prod, start, ...), parsed without a shell: node <file>, a package's command (next start, resolved at build time to the file it runs), nest start and nx serve mapped to their compiled output. Without a start script: server.js, main or index.js. A start command that needs a shell runs with npm run on the slim image. Runtime distroless Node.js as uid 65532, NODE_ENV=production, PORT=8080, HOST=0.0.0.0. Probes a /health-style route on the application object, a NestJS Terminus controller; a TCP probe otherwise. Configuration variables listed in .env.example that hold credentials or connection URLs become Secret references; Windows paths in node-config files (config/default.json) are overridden with NODE_CONFIG.

Single-page apps build with the repository's package manager and are served by unprivileged nginx.

docs.title: Verification
docs.text: The scan builds and runs Java and Node.js images hardened, as for .NET. Failure rules in rules/50-failures.yaml recognise Java and Node.js build and start failures: a dependency that needs a newer Java line, Maven version enforcement (the build switches to the Maven wrapper), a lockfile out of sync, missing native toolchains, the V8 heap during builds, a devDependency needed at run time, writes to read-only folders, and databases, brokers, config servers or variables that only the real environment provides. Unknown failures go to the optional LLM, which gets a language-specific evidence pack and plan vocabulary; what works is learned for review, as for .NET.

docs.title: Organization scans
docs.text: Organization scans treat Java and Node.js repositories like .NET ones: each buildable component (a Maven or Gradle jar/war, a Node.js server or single-page app) gets its Dockerfile, hardened manifests and GitOps entries. Repositories without .NET, Java or Node.js code are still skipped and say so.

docs.title: Validation corpus
docs.text:
bench/realworld.yaml holds 17 public Java (jv-*) and Node.js (nd-*) repositories, pinned to a commit, with ratings and roles judged by reading each repository. Run them with python -m containerizer.realworld --root <dir> --clone jv-petclinic nd-ghost ....

All 17 match. Jenkins and Ghost are the two that need a volume for state that is easy to miss: Jenkins keeps jobs, configuration and history in its home directory (JENKINS_HOME, by default ~/.jenkins), found by java-app-home-directory; Ghost unpacks uploaded themes into content/themes, which its S3 adapter does not cover, found by node-local-extensions.

Images were built and run hardened (verify) for Spring PetClinic, Quarkus rest-heroes (Java 25), PiggyMetrics account-service (Java 8), Halo, RealWorld Express (Nx), Node-RED, Uptime Kuma and the React RealWorld single-page app; each either served or stopped only at a database or config server it needs from the real environment. Taxonomy's build needs its runtime variables (reported as a finding) and the NestJS RealWorld app fails on its own outdated dependencies.

docs.title: Lab services
docs.text:
Many applications need a database, a cache, a message broker, object storage or a file server before they start. On the appliance, administrators can turn on lab services: backing services that run in the sandbox cluster next to the apps that the organization scans deploy. When an app depends on a service that is on, the generated manifests point the app at it. The app's code does not change: only its configuration, through environment variables.

Service What runs What each app gets On by default SQL Server SQL Server 2025, Developer edition (the appliance's own pinned image) Its own database and login, owner of that database only yes PostgreSQL PostgreSQL 18 Its own database and role, owner of that database only no Redis Redis 8.8 Its own instance and password no S3 object storage Versity S3 Gateway (Apache 2.0) Its own S3 endpoint and access key no Azure Blob storage Azurite, blob service Its own Azurite endpoint and account key no MySQL MySQL 8.4 LTS Its own database and user, with all rights on that database only no MongoDB MongoDB 8.0 Community Its own database and user, dbOwner of that database only no RabbitMQ RabbitMQ 4.4 Its own virtual host and user, with rights on that virtual host only no Kafka Apache Kafka 4.4, one node (KRaft) Its own broker no SFTP SFTPGo, SFTP only Its own SFTP server, user and password, on port 22 no Mail (SMTP) Mailpit (MIT), a catch-all mailbox that never sends on Its own mailbox on port 25, which takes any login or none; read under Admin → Lab mail yes

MongoDB 8.0 does not start on Linux 6.19 and newer (a tcmalloc bug, SERVER-121912). The appliance runs Debian 13's kernel, so this only matters on a self-built cluster with a newer kernel.

SQL Server is on by default because the appliance already ran SQL Server for dev database restores. Mail (SMTP) is on by default because it only catches: an app that sends mail would otherwise fail against a relay the sandbox cannot reach, or write files nothing sends. An app with an uploaded backup (SQL Server, PostgreSQL or MySQL) still gets that backup restored next to it, and the lab's server for that engine is not used for it. Turning the engine off stops those restores too.

docs.title: Turn a service on or off
docs.text:
Administrators turn each service on or off under Admin → Lab services, with a note for the change history. A service that is on starts only when the first app asks for it, so a service nobody uses costs nothing. Turning off a service that apps use takes it from them at once (the page asks first), and the next scan generates them without it. Needed but off lists the apps whose latest scan found that they need a service that is off (each application of a repository split into several, since 0.16.1), and the repository's page shows the same warning: turn the service on, then scan again.

Everyone sees it on the application's results page too: Lab services at the top lists what the application needs in the sandbox, what the lab provides and what is turned off, with the components that run without it (they keep their own settings, and an app without its message broker or database often just stops). The Sandbox column marks those components ("needs RabbitMQ: turned off in the lab"), and the sandbox check of a component that fails says first that it needs a service the lab has turned off.

The other direction is on Admin → Lab services: Applications that need each service lists, per service, every application whose latest scan found that it needs it, with the components that do and whether the scan gave it the lab's service (Provided) or the service was off (Without it). Each application links to its results page. Use it to see what turning a service on brings into the sandbox, or what turning it off takes away.

docs.title: What the scan changes in an app
docs.text:
The scan decides, for each component, which services the component needs:

  • Packages, the component's own or those of the projects it references (rules/lab-services.yaml):
    • SQL Server: Microsoft.Data.SqlClient, System.Data.SqlClient, Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore.SqlServer, Hangfire.SqlServer, dbup-sqlserver
    • PostgreSQL: Npgsql*, Hangfire.PostgreSql, dbup-postgresql
    • Redis: StackExchange.Redis, Microsoft.Extensions.Caching.StackExchangeRedis, the SignalR and Data Protection Redis packages
    • S3: AWSSDK.S3, Minio
    • Azure Blob storage: Azure.Storage.Blobs, Microsoft.Azure.Storage.Blob, WindowsAzure.Storage
    • MySQL: MySqlConnector, MySql.Data, Pomelo.EntityFrameworkCore.MySql, MySql.EntityFrameworkCore, Hangfire.MySqlStorage, dbup-mysql
    • MongoDB: MongoDB.Driver*, MongoDB.Entities, MongoDB.EntityFrameworkCore, Hangfire.Mongo
    • RabbitMQ: RabbitMQ.Client, MassTransit.RabbitMQ, EasyNetQ*, NServiceBus.RabbitMQ, RawRabbit*, Rebus.RabbitMq
    • Kafka: Confluent.Kafka, MassTransit.Kafka, KafkaFlow*, Silverback.Integration.Kafka, Rebus.Kafka
    • SFTP: SSH.NET, Renci.SshNet*, WinSCP
    • Mail (SMTP): MailKit, FluentEmail.Smtp, FluentEmail.MailKit, NETCore.MailKit, or code that creates an SmtpClient or sets SmtpDeliveryMethod

The Aspire client packages for these services count too.

Java, Node.js, Python and Go components are found by the client packages of their own ecosystems, for example:

Service Java (Maven, Gradle) Node.js Python Go SQL Server mssql-jdbc mssql, tedious pyodbc, pymssql go-mssqldb PostgreSQL org.postgresql:postgresql pg, postgres psycopg, psycopg2, asyncpg pgx, lib/pq MySQL mysql-connector-j, mariadb-java-client mysql2, mysql pymysql, mysqlclient go-sql-driver/mysql Redis spring-boot-starter-data-redis, jedis, lettuce-core redis, ioredis, bullmq redis go-redis, redigo MongoDB spring-boot-starter-data-mongodb, mongodb-driver-* mongodb, mongoose pymongo, motor mongo-driver RabbitMQ spring-boot-starter-amqp, amqp-client amqplib pika, aio-pika amqp091-go Kafka spring-kafka, kafka-clients kafkajs, node-rdkafka kafka-python, confluent-kafka kafka-go, sarama S3 software.amazon.awssdk:s3, io.minio:minio @aws-sdk/client-s3, minio aws-sdk-go-v2/service/s3, minio-go Azure Blob storage azure-storage-blob @azure/storage-blob azure-storage-blob azblob SFTP jsch, sshj, sshd-sftp ssh2-sftp-client pysftp pkg/sftp Mail (SMTP) spring-boot-starter-mail, Jakarta Mail nodemailer smtplib, aiosmtplib net/smtp, gomail

Packages that only tests and builds use (Maven test scope, npm devDependencies) do not count. The whole list is in rules/lab-services.yaml. - Settings in appsettings.json (.NET, with appsettings.Production.json on top). Each connection string and setting is classified by its value: - Initial Catalog= or Server=host,1433 means SQL Server; - Host=...;Username= means PostgreSQL; - host:6379,abortConnect=false means Redis; - UseDevelopmentStorage=true or AccountName=...;AccountKey= means Azure Storage; - ServiceURL, AccessKey and similar keys under an AWS, S3 or Minio section mean S3; - Server=...;Uid= or Port=3306 means MySQL, but Server=host:50000 (a port after a colon) is Db2 or Informix, which the lab does not run. A component with a Db2 or Oracle driver (Net.IBM.Data.Db2*, IBM.Data.DB2*, Oracle.ManagedDataAccess*, ...) and no driver of a lab database gets no lab database from its settings; - mongodb:// means MongoDB, and DatabaseName under a Mongo... section is its database; - amqp://, or host= under a key that names RabbitMQ or EasyNetQ, means RabbitMQ. So do HostName, UserName, Password, Port and VirtualHost under a RabbitMQ section; - BootstrapServers (or bootstrap.servers) means Kafka; - Host, Port, Username and Password under an Sftp or Ssh section mean SFTP; - Host, Server, Port, EnableSsl (UseSsl, StartTls), SecureSocketOptions, PickupFolder (PickupDirectory, PickupDirectoryLocation), DeliveryMethod and Mode under a section whose name has Mail or Smtp in it (Mail, Smtp, EmailSettings, DocControl:Mail), or a key that says it (SmtpHost, SmtpPort, MailPickupFolder), mean Mail (SMTP). Sections of HTTP mail APIs (SendGrid, Mailgun, Microsoft Graph, ...) do not count.

For each service that the component needs and that is on, the scan writes the following.

  • Environment variables that override the component's configuration. For a .NET component:
Service Settings that are overridden SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL Each connection string of that engine, from the Secret lab-<service> (key connection-string). If no connection string says which engine it is and the component needs only this database, the unclassified ones are used. If there are no connection strings at all, ConnectionStrings__DefaultConnection is set. Redis Each Redis connection string or setting (Redis:Configuration, ConnectionStrings:Cache, ...). If none is found, ConnectionStrings__Redis is set. S3 AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID, AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY, AWS_REGION, and AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3, which AWSSDK.S3 3.7.300 and later read. The ServiceURL, access key, secret key and region settings that were found are overridden too. Azure Blob storage Each Azure Storage connection string, from the Secret (key connection-string). MongoDB Each MongoDB connection string (key connection-string) and each database name setting (key database). The database name has to change too: the app's user may use only its own database. RabbitMQ Each AMQP URI or EasyNetQ connection string (key connection-string), and each host, port, user name, password and virtual host setting (keys host, port, username, password, vhost). Kafka Each bootstrap servers setting (key bootstrap-servers). A SecurityProtocol setting becomes Plaintext. SFTP Each host, port, user name and password setting (keys host, port, username, password). Mail (SMTP) Each SMTP host and port setting (keys host, port). TLS settings become false (SecureSocketOptions: None); a pickup folder setting becomes empty, DeliveryMethod SpecifiedPickupDirectory or PickupDirectoryFromIis becomes Network, and Mode: Pickup becomes Smtp, so the app sends over SMTP. The sender, the recipients and the credentials stay as they are: the mailbox takes any login, or none.

The whole connection string, or each part of it, comes from the Secret, so no password appears in a manifest. When no setting is found for a service the component needs, lab/README.md names the Secret and its keys. Entries with the same name that the generator made before (references to the component's own secrets) are replaced.

A Java, Node.js, Python or Go component gets the variables of its own conventions instead of Section__Key names:

1. **The variables its framework binds.** Spring Boot: `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` (a JDBC URL),
   `SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME` and `SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD`, `SPRING_DATA_REDIS_HOST`, `_PORT` and
   `_PASSWORD` (and `SPRING_REDIS_*`, which Spring Boot 2 reads), `SPRING_DATA_MONGODB_URI`,
   `SPRING_RABBITMQ_HOST`, `_PORT`, `_USERNAME`, `_PASSWORD` and `_VIRTUAL_HOST`,
   `SPRING_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS`, `SPRING_MAIL_HOST` and `_PORT`. Quarkus: `QUARKUS_DATASOURCE_JDBC_URL`,
   `_USERNAME` and `_PASSWORD`, `QUARKUS_REDIS_HOSTS`, `QUARKUS_MONGODB_CONNECTION_STRING`,
   `KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS`, `QUARKUS_MAILER_HOST` and `_PORT`. Micronaut: `DATASOURCES_DEFAULT_URL`,
   `_USERNAME` and `_PASSWORD`, `KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS`.
2. **The variables its code reads**: `process.env.X`, `os.environ["X"]` / `os.getenv("X")`,
   `os.Getenv("X")`, `System.getenv("X")`, `${X}` in a Spring configuration file, and the names in
   `.env.example`. The name says the service and what the variable holds: `REDIS_HOST`, `PGPASSWORD`,
   `MYSQL_DATABASE`, `MONGO_URI`, `RABBITMQ_VHOST`, `KAFKA_BROKERS`, `SMTP_PORT`. Names that only say
   "the database" (`DATABASE_URL`, `DB_HOST`, `DB_NAME`, `DB_USER`, `DB_PASSWORD`) are used when the
   component needs exactly one database.
3. **A common name**, when neither says anything: `DATABASE_URL`, `REDIS_URL`, `MONGODB_URI`, `AMQP_URL`,
   `KAFKA_BROKERS`, `SMTP_HOST` and `SMTP_PORT`, `AZURE_STORAGE_CONNECTION_STRING`. `lab/README.md` then
   says that the name is a guess, and names the Secret and its keys.

A URL is written in the form the component's client takes: jdbc:postgresql://... for Java, postgresql://user:password@host:5432/db for Node.js and Python (?sslmode=disable for Go), mysql://... (mysql+pymysql://... with PyMySQL, user:password@tcp(host:3306)/db for Go), mssql://..., mssql+pyodbc://... or sqlserver://... for SQL Server, redis://:password@host:6379. The user name and password in it are references to the Secret (CZ_LAB_<SERVICE>_USERNAME, CZ_LAB_<SERVICE>_PASSWORD, expanded by Kubernetes), so no password appears in a manifest here either. The S3 variables are the same for every stack.

When the scan cannot tell (a component with two databases whose variables do not say which is which, an SFTP client without a variable for its host), nothing is set and lab/README.md says that the service is not wired for the component, with the Secret and the keys to point its settings at. - lab/k8s.yaml: an ExternalSecret lab-<service> for each service. It reads remote key <namespace>--cz-lab-<service> from the store app-secrets (External Secrets). The namespace's reader Role grants exactly these keys, like every other key of the app. - NetworkPolicy egress from the component to the service's port. Only the service's pods are allowed (for a per-app service, only the app's own instance), in namespace containerizer-lab. - lab/README.md lists the host names, the Secrets, which settings were overridden, and the services that were needed but off. The scan result has the same, as lab_services in containerizer.json.

docs.title: Things the scan cannot see
docs.text:
• Settings made in code. A RabbitMQ ConnectionFactory without a user name in the configuration uses guest, which the lab does not allow, and a Kafka client that sets SASL in code cannot log in to the lab broker, which has no logins. An S3 client built with new AmazonS3Client(new AmazonS3Config { ServiceURL = "..." }) uses the URL in the code. A Node.js, Python or Go client whose host is written in the code, or read from a configuration file and not from a variable, is not changed either. The AWS SDK reads AWS_ENDPOINT_URL_S3 only when the code does not set an endpoint. The same is true for Azure clients created from a serviceUri with managed identity: the lab gives each app a connection string, not an identity. lab/README.md says when no setting was found.
  • Database schema. The databases start empty. Run the app's migrations at start-up, as most EF Core apps do, or upload a dev database backup for SQL Server, PostgreSQL or MySQL.
  • The repository's SQL setup scripts (SQL Server). Many apps are set up by a DBA with scripts in the repository rather than by migrations. The scan finds them: in the order the deploy scripts run them (Invoke-Sqlcmd -InputFile ..., sqlcmd -i ...), else every .sql file of a folder named db, database, sql, sqlscripts, schema or migrations (Flyway's db/migration too: versions in order, repeatable migrations last, undo and down scripts never), by name; of several such folders side by side (billing/db, crm/db) all of them. sqlcmd variables get the values the script sets itself (:setvar Schema "app"), and a database-name variable ($(DatabaseName)) the app's lab database; a variable without a value stays as written and its batch fails. It leaves out what the lab does itself or what needs server-wide rights (a database, a login, server configuration, another database, sqlcmd directives such as :on error exit) and a script's own BEGIN TRANSACTION / COMMIT batches, and puts the rest into the ConfigMap cz-lab-sqlserver-init of the app's namespace (lab/k8s.yaml; lab/README.md lists the scripts and what was left out). The lab agent runs them once into the app's database, as the app's own login (the owner of that database only), batch by batch: a batch that fails (a user for a production login, say) is reported on Admin -> Lab services and the rest goes on. They run again when they change, or when the database is made again (Admin -> Dev databases -> Delete); the database keeps the hash of what ran (extended property containerizer.lab-init). A script that only some deploy step runs later (reference data "after the first import") is not picked up: run it yourself if the app needs it.

docs.title: Mail
docs.text:
Many applications send mail: order confirmations, password resets, reports. On the Windows server they sent it to the company's SMTP relay, or wrote it as .eml files to a pickup folder that the IIS SMTP service emptied. In the sandbox neither exists, so the app fails to send, or writes files that nobody sends. The lab's Mail (SMTP) service gives each such application its own catch-all mailbox instead: the scan points the application's SMTP settings at it (see the tables above), every message it sends is kept, and none leaves the appliance. The mailbox has no relay or forwarding settings, whatever address a message is for.

Administrators and operators read the caught mail under Admin → Lab mail: one inbox over all the applications' mailboxes, the newest first, with the application each message came from, or one application's mailbox at a time. Opening a message shows its addresses, its text and the names of its attachments. An HTML message is never rendered: the page shows its text, with links written out, and its HTML source. The application's results page links to the inbox from its Lab services line. Each mailbox keeps the newest 1,000 messages, for at most 30 days. Each read is in the access log when the view audit is on.

What the scan cannot fix: mail that the code always writes to a folder, or sends to a host set in code. lab/README.md says when no SMTP host setting was found, and when the code writes to a pickup folder that no setting turns off. For production the application still needs a real SMTP relay in its settings (cfg-smtp-pickup-iis).

The page reads the mailboxes through the system agent, as the database browser does: the agent checks that the namespace is one the lab runs a mailbox for, and runs only wget against the mailbox's API, which listens on the pod's own loopback (127.0.0.1:8025) and cannot be reached over the network.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Admin -> Lab services --(cz.LabService, audited)--> system agent --> lab-services.json
                                                                      │            │
           scan worker: needs + overrides + ExternalSecret <──────────┘            │
                                                                                   ▼
app namespace: ExternalSecret lab-<service> ──ESO──> containerizer-secrets/<ns>--cz-lab-<service>
                                                                                   ▲
lab agent (root, every 2 min) ──finds the ExternalSecrets──> creates database/login or instance,
                                                             writes the credentials ─┘
containerizer-lab: sqlserver, postgres, mysql, mongodb, rabbitmq (shared)
                   redis-<ns>, s3-<ns>, azure-blob-<ns>, kafka-<ns>, sftp-<ns>, smtp-<ns> (per app)

The lab agent (python -m containerizer.labagent reconcile, containerizer-lab.timer) runs as root with the k3s admin kubeconfig. Each time it runs, it does the following.

  1. It applies namespace containerizer-lab with Pod Security restricted, a default-deny NetworkPolicy, a LimitRange and a ServiceAccount without a token.
  2. It finds the apps that asked for a service: every ExternalSecret labelled containerizer.io/lab-service. It accepts one only if it reads its own namespace's key, <namespace>--cz-lab-<service>. A namespace therefore can never ask for another app's credentials, and system namespaces cannot ask at all.

  3. For each service that is on and asked for:

    • Shared server (SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, MongoDB, RabbitMQ). It runs one Deployment with a data volume. The admin password (not for RabbitMQ, which rabbitmqctl manages through its Erlang cookie) is created once, in the Secret <service>-admin in containerizer-lab. For each app, it creates the app's credentials once and stores them in the secret store. Then it runs the provisioning script in the server's container (kubectl exec, script on stdin). The script is idempotent:
      • SQL Server: login <ns> (hyphens become underscores) with CHECK_POLICY = ON, database <ns> owned by that login, DENY VIEW ANY DATABASE and DENY VIEW SERVER STATE.
      • PostgreSQL: role <ns> with NOSUPERUSER NOCREATEDB NOCREATEROLE, database <ns> owned by it, CONNECT revoked from PUBLIC on every database (including postgres and template1), and schema public owned by the app.
      • MySQL: user '<ns>'@'%' with all privileges on database <ns> only. root can log in only from inside the server's container.
      • MongoDB: user <ns> in database <ns> with role dbOwner on that database only. mongod runs with authentication on.
      • RabbitMQ: virtual host <ns> and user <ns> with configure, write and read rights on it only. The guest user is deleted, and the lab's configuration replaces the image's, which lets guest log in from anywhere. The node name is fixed (rabbit@localhost), so the data survives a new pod.

    The script runs again only when the server's pod or the password changes. - Per-app instance (Redis, S3, Azure Blob, Kafka, SFTP, Mail). It runs a Deployment, a Service and a data volume named <service>-<ns>. Their config Secret is built from the app's credentials: - Redis keeps only the SHA-256 of the password in its ACL. Commands in @admin are denied, and the append-only file is on. - Azurite's AZURITE_ACCOUNTS holds only the app's account, so the emulator's well-known devstoreaccount1 key does not work. Telemetry is off. - Versity S3 Gateway runs with the app's root key. Objects are under /data/buckets, and their metadata is in a sidecar folder. - Kafka is one node that is both broker and controller. The controller listens on localhost only, and the broker advertises the instance's Service name. Clients connect without a login: an app reaches only its own broker, so the NetworkPolicy is the access control. - SFTPGo serves SFTP only. The web admin, REST API, FTP, WebDAV and telemetry listeners are off, and the brute-force defender is on. Its user store is the app's one user, read from the config Secret. The Service listens on port 22, so a client that uses the default port works. The host keys are on the data volume, so they stay the same. - Mailpit listens for SMTP on port 1025 (the Service's port 25) and keeps the messages in a SQLite file on the data volume. It takes any login or none, has no relay or forwarding configured, does no reverse DNS lookups and no version check, and its web UI and API listen on the pod's loopback only. Like Kafka, the NetworkPolicy is the access control: only the app's own namespace reaches its mailbox. - A NetworkPolicy per app lets in only that app's pods (app.kubernetes.io/part-of: <ns> in namespace <ns>), on the service's port. - When the store gets new credentials, the agent annotates the app's ExternalSecret, so ESO syncs it straight away. 4. For each service that is off, it deletes the Deployments, Services, NetworkPolicies and config Secrets. It keeps the volumes, the admin passwords and the apps' credentials in the store. Turning the service on again brings back the same data with the same passwords. Instances of apps that no longer ask are stopped the same way. 5. It writes /run/containerizer/system/lab-status.json for the page. The file holds no secrets.

Secret values never appear on a command line. They reach kubectl on stdin, the provisioning scripts reach the server's own client on stdin, and the admin passwords stay in the servers' environment (SQLCMDPASSWORD for sqlcmd, MYSQL_PWD for mysql, and mongosh reads it from the environment). psql connects over the local socket with peer authentication. For RabbitMQ, the shell's printf builtin pipes the app's password to rabbitmqctl.

docs.title: Hardening
docs.text:
The lab follows the same baseline as the generated apps (NSA/CISA Kubernetes Hardening Guide, rules/60-security.yaml):

  • Pods. They run as non-root users: SQL Server as 10001, PostgreSQL as 70, MySQL, MongoDB and Redis as 999, RabbitMQ as 100, Azurite, Kafka, SFTPGo and Mailpit as 1000, the S3 gateway as 10001. The root file system is read-only, with emptyDir folders (size limited) where the server needs to write. All capabilities are dropped, privilege escalation is off, seccomp and AppArmor use RuntimeDefault, no service account token is mounted, and service links are off. There are memory requests and limits and ephemeral-storage limits. SQL Server keeps NET_BIND_SERVICE in its bounding set, the only capability Pod Security restricted allows, because its binary carries that file capability. With no_new_privs the capability is never raised.
  • Network. Default deny, in and out. Each app gets an ingress rule to its own service, and lab pods make no outgoing connections. The apps' own NetworkPolicies allow only the service's pods and port.
  • Secrets. Credentials are in the secret store only, read by each namespace's own reader. The store namespace runs no pods. The admin passwords are in containerizer-lab Secrets. k3s encrypts Secrets at rest (secrets-encryption: true).
  • Images. They are pinned by digest in /usr/lib/containerizer/images.env, and an OS upgrade brings new pins. SQL Server uses the same pinned image as the results database.
  • Least privilege in the data. Each app is the owner of its own database only, and on SQL Server cannot even list the others. An app cannot reach another app's Redis, S3 or Azurite instance on the network, and the same goes for Kafka and SFTP.

Encryption in transit. SQL Server connections are encrypted (Encrypt=True) with the server's own certificate (TrustServerCertificate=True, as for the dev databases). The SQL Server and PostgreSQL connection strings name the app (Application Name=<app>), so the shared server shows whose session it is; the database browser's sessions are containerizer-db-browser (PostgreSQL; sqlcmd sets none). MySQL connections are encrypted too (SslMode=Required, with the certificate MySQL makes at first start). SFTP is SSH. PostgreSQL, MongoDB, RabbitMQ, Kafka, Redis, S3, Azurite and Mail (SMTP) use plain connections. The sandbox is a single-node cluster, so lab traffic never leaves the appliance: it stays on the node's pod network, and the NetworkPolicies limit who can open a connection.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Each service keeps its data on a PersistentVolumeClaim of the default StorageClass. On the appliance, this is k3s local-path, under /var/lib/rancher/k3s/storage on the persistent partition, so the data survives restarts and OS upgrades. The requested sizes are 20 GiB for SQL Server, 10 GiB each for PostgreSQL, MySQL and MongoDB, 5 GiB for RabbitMQ, 1 GiB for each Redis or Mail and 5 GiB for each S3, Azurite, Kafka or SFTP instance. local-path does not enforce these sizes: the appliance's disk is the limit.

To delete an app's data for good, delete its volume and its credentials:

k3s kubectl -n containerizer-lab delete pvc -l containerizer.io/lab-app=<namespace>
k3s kubectl -n containerizer-secrets delete secret -l containerizer.io/lab-app=<namespace>

On a shared server, drop the app's database and login with the server's tools.

To look at or fix an app's data in its SQL Server, PostgreSQL or MySQL database, or to start it again empty, use the database browser under Admin → Dev databases (Browse and fix the data). It runs every statement as the app's own login, in its own database, and records every change.

docs.title: Resources
docs.text: When it is in use, SQL Server takes 2 to 3 GiB of memory, on top of the appliance's own SQL Server. PostgreSQL, MySQL and MongoDB take up to 1 GiB each, and RabbitMQ up to 768 MiB. Each Kafka instance takes 512 MiB to 1 GiB. Each Redis, S3, Azurite, SFTP or Mail instance takes 32 to 512 MiB. Size the VM for the services you turn on.

docs.title: Licences
docs.text:
• SQL Server Developer edition is free for development and test, and not licensed for production. The lab is a sandbox.
  • PostgreSQL: PostgreSQL License.
  • Redis 8: AGPLv3, RSALv2 or SSPLv1, at your choice. It runs unmodified as a service.
  • Versity S3 Gateway: Apache 2.0.
  • Azurite: MIT.
  • MySQL Community Server: GPLv2.
  • MongoDB Community Server: SSPL. It runs unmodified as a service for the lab's own apps.
  • RabbitMQ: MPL 2.0.
  • Apache Kafka: Apache 2.0.
  • SFTPGo: AGPLv3. It runs unmodified.
  • Mailpit: MIT.

The appliance downloads each image from its publisher when the service is first used. Nothing is redistributed in the OS image.

docs.title: Local development server
docs.text:
How to set up a Debian 13 (trixie) server where Claude Code (or you) can develop Containerizer and run the whole end-to-end test suite locally, instead of pushing and waiting for GitHub workflows. Everything the workflows in .github/workflows do, except publishing (GHCR push, cosign signing, release assets, gh-pages), runs here with one command:

ci/local.sh            # the fast set, about 10-15 minutes
ci/local.sh all        # everything, including the one-shot assessment and the appliance boot test

docs.title: What the workflows need
docs.text:
Derived from the workflows themselves, so the local run matches CI:

Workflow job Needs on the server ci/local.sh job ci.yml test Python 3.12, requirements.txt, pytest, pytest-xdist test docs.yml build mkdocs==1.6.1, mkdocs-material==9.8.0 docs ci.yml containerizer, containerizer-head Python, git (the composite action is python -m containerizer check) gate ci.yml action-selftest git, network access to github.com/onek8s/containerization-challenge selftest security.yml gate Docker; Trivy and Grype run as containers (aquasec/trivy, anchore/grype, pinned in rules/60-security.yaml) security ci.yml sql Docker, mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2025-latest, requirements-sql.txt (pymssql) sql ci.yml sandbox Docker, kind, kubectl sandbox ci.yml assess-oneshot Docker with BuildKit (builds and runs every generated container), a lot of disk assess release.yml appliance Docker + buildx, KVM, qemu-system-x86, qemu-utils, ovmf, zstd, expect (the boot test changes the expired root password over SSH); the Elemental toolkit is built inside appliance/Dockerfile, so it needs no install appliance

Not needed: Node.js (the repository has no JavaScript build), Syft as a binary (it runs as the anchore/syft container, in the generated build pipelines' tests), and cosign unless you test release signing by hand.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
x86_64 only: the SQL Server image, OVMF and the appliance are amd64.

Fast set Everything (all) With Ollama CPU 4 cores 8+ cores 8+ cores, or a GPU RAM 16 GB 32 GB 64 GB on CPU, or a 24 GB GPU for a 30B model (Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B on CPU: + 20 GB) Disk (SSD/NVMe) 100 GB 250 GB + 20-40 GB per model

The appliance boot test gives its VM all CPUs and the free memory less 1 GiB (at most 11 GiB, at least 4 GiB; SQL Server inside it needs 2 GiB), and grows the disk image to 96 GB (sparse). The one-shot assessment builds .NET images for three apps; Docker's build cache grows quickly, so prune it now and then (docker system prune -af --volumes when nothing else runs).

If the server is itself a VM, turn on nested virtualization so /dev/kvm exists: CPU type host on Proxmox / libvirt, Set-VMProcessor -VMName <vm> -ExposeVirtualizationExtensions $true on Hyper-V. Check with ls -l /dev/kvm.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
Start from a minimal Debian 13 install with SSH. As root (or with sudo), once:

# a dedicated, unprivileged user for development; Claude Code runs as this user
adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" dev
install -d -m 700 -o dev -g dev /home/dev/.ssh
cp ~/.ssh/authorized_keys /home/dev/.ssh/ && chown dev:dev /home/dev/.ssh/authorized_keys

apt-get update
apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends ca-certificates curl git jq make openssh-client \
  qemu-system-x86 qemu-utils ovmf zstd expect nftables unattended-upgrades

# Docker Engine with BuildKit / buildx, from Docker's repository (Debian's docker.io has no buildx plugin)
install -m 0755 -d /etc/apt/keyrings
curl -fsSL https://download.docker.com/linux/debian/gpg -o /etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc
echo "deb [arch=$(dpkg --print-architecture) signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/docker.asc] https://download.docker.com/linux/debian trixie stable" \
  > /etc/apt/sources.list.d/docker.list
apt-get update
apt-get install -y docker-ce docker-ce-cli containerd.io docker-buildx-plugin

# kind and kubectl for the sandbox test (ci.yml uses helm/kind-action; any recent kind works)
curl -fsSLo /usr/local/bin/kind https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/kind/releases/download/v0.26.0/kind-linux-amd64
curl -fsSLo /usr/local/bin/kubectl https://dl.k8s.io/release/v1.32.0/bin/linux/amd64/kubectl
chmod 0755 /usr/local/bin/kind /usr/local/bin/kubectl

# kind's kubelet watches files with inotify; with the lab k3s and builds beside it Debian's 128 instances
# run out ("unable to create inotify: too many open files") and the sandbox test's cluster never starts
echo 'fs.inotify.max_user_instances = 1024' > /etc/sysctl.d/90-inotify.conf && sysctl --system >/dev/null

# docker: run containers without sudo (see Security); kvm: the appliance boot test
usermod -aG docker,kvm dev

Debian 13 ships Python 3.13; the workflows use 3.12. ci/local.sh creates its environment with uv, which fetches 3.12 for the user, so the system Python is left alone. As dev (log in again first, so the new groups apply):

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh      # installs to ~/.local/bin
uv python install 3.12
docker run --rm hello-world && ls -l /dev/kvm        # both must work without sudo

Without uv the script falls back to python3 -m venv with Debian's 3.13 (install python3-venv for it), which works for development but is not exactly what CI runs. If .venv-ci/ was created that way and uv is installed later, the next ci/local.sh run notices the version and recreates it with 3.12.

docs.title: Optional: cosign
docs.text:
Only for testing release signing by hand. The same pinned version and checksum as release.yml:

curl -fsSLo /tmp/cosign https://github.com/sigstore/cosign/releases/download/v3.1.4/cosign-linux-amd64
echo "424e2c97d0b45fd7a6b608a87f090f35633f4c23ece5f092d48bba11aaf4bbfa  /tmp/cosign" | sha256sum -c -
sudo install -m 0755 /tmp/cosign /usr/local/bin/cosign

docs.title: Optional: Ollama for the self-hosted LLM backend
docs.text:
To test --ai against a local model (the LLM):

curl -fsSL https://ollama.com/install.sh | sh       # a systemd service on 127.0.0.1:11434
ollama pull qwen3:32b                                # or a smaller model for quick checks, e.g. qwen3:8b

export CONTAINERIZER_LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:11434/v1
export CONTAINERIZER_MODEL=qwen3:32b
.venv-ci/bin/python -m containerizer assess examples/ci-demo --ai

docs.title: Optional: Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B on CPU only (no GPU)
docs.text:
For a lab server without a GPU. This is for development and testing only: real environments use an external LLM, or the appliance's built-in LLM, which runs the same model and server with the settings below (on port 8082, sized from the machine's memory). ByteShape publishes quantized builds of Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B tuned for CPUs (Apache 2.0). The model is a mixture of experts with only 3B of its 30B parameters active per token, so it is several times faster on a CPU than a dense model of similar quality. Their dense Devstral Small 2 24B builds stay under 10 tokens/s on CPUs.

Build (file) Size Quality (vs. baseline) Intel Core i7 Memory with a 32K context Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-IQ4_XS-4.20bpw.gguf 16 GB 99.0% 15.9 tokens/s about 20 GB Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-Q3_K_M-3.31bpw.gguf 12.7 GB 97.5% 18.3 tokens/s about 16 GB

The quality and speed figures are ByteShape's. Generation speed follows memory bandwidth, so a dual-channel desktop is slower than a many-channel server. Reading the prompt is slower too: the evidence packs are 5,000 to 15,000 tokens, so expect up to a few minutes per answer. LLM-heavy mode makes many calls and turns a scan into hours. Use the 4.20 bpw build when the memory is there, and stay above about 3 bpw.

Run llama.cpp's server on loopback, as an unprivileged container. The model file is read-only:

sudo install -d -m 0755 /srv/llm
cd /srv/llm
f=Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-IQ4_XS-4.20bpw.gguf
sudo curl -fL -C - -o $f \
  https://huggingface.co/byteshape/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF/resolve/0436a5b1e12e051e8a8568d56a1526734d3ed572/$f
echo "618f0a45a5a85f099106c80e44e0eb8ce9ee094b6268395b84e8b5b729f865dd  $f" | sha256sum -c -
sudo chmod 0644 $f

docker run -d --name llm --restart unless-stopped --network host \
  --volume /srv/llm:/models:ro --memory 24g --cpu-shares 256 \
  --user 65534:65534 --read-only --tmpfs /tmp:size=64m --cap-drop ALL --cap-add IPC_LOCK --ulimit memlock=-1:-1 \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  -e LLAMA_ARG_HOST=127.0.0.1 -e LLAMA_ARG_PORT=8081 \
  --health-cmd 'curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8081/health' --health-start-period 5m \
  ghcr.io/ggml-org/llama.cpp:server-b12030@sha256:e67d88af487390098c76d7982b1761484339fa147b7e41d3c64ae1318759f78b \
  --model /models/$f --alias qwen3-coder-30b-a3b \
  --ctx-size 32768 --parallel 1 --jinja --load-mode mmap+mlock --lazy-mode off \
  --cors-origins localhost --no-cors-credentials --cache-ram 1024
curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8081/health                 # {"status":"ok"} once the model is loaded
sudo grep VmLck /proc/$(docker inspect llm --format '{{.State.Pid}}')/status   # about 15 GB: the model is pinned

Why the options:

  • --load-mode mmap+mlock with IPC_LOCK and an unlimited memlock keeps the model in RAM. The file is memory-mapped, so its 16 GB is page cache, not container memory (docker stats shows only the 3 GB or so of context buffers), and without the lock the kernel drops it when the test suite's builds fill the cache, so the next answer first reads the model from disk again. --lazy-mode off keeps large tensors resident too. This build has no --mlock: it fails with invalid argument.
  • The image sets LLAMA_ARG_HOST=0.0.0.0 and LLAMA_ARG_PORT=8080. Setting the variables, instead of --host and --port, avoids a warning that they are overridden, and --health-cmd replaces the image's health check, which probes port 8080 and would mark the container unhealthy.
  • --cache-ram 1024: llama.cpp keeps up to 8 GiB of earlier prompts in RAM by default (its RSS grows from about 6 to 11 GiB and more over a scan). Review prompts rarely repeat, so a small cache is enough.
  • --cors-origins localhost --no-cors-credentials: by default any web page can call the server (the no API key is set and CORS allows all origins warning). Containerizer is not a browser, so it is not affected. The remaining warning, control-looking token: 128247 '</s>' was not control-type, comes from the model file's metadata and is harmless.

--threads N limits the CPU it takes (the default is about one thread per core). --cpu-shares 256 gives the test suite's builds the CPU first when both want it. For several scans at once (one shard of apps per process, or an organization scan with several workers), --parallel N with --ctx-size N times as large decodes N answers together for about the cost of one, since speed follows memory bandwidth; keep the context per slot (n_ctx_slot in the log) above about 20,000 tokens, use a multiple of 256 per slot to avoid a rounding warning (--parallel 3 --ctx-size 66048), and raise --memory by about 3 GB per extra slot. Restarting the container while a scan runs is safe: requests are retried while the model loads. Then point Containerizer at it. Raise the timeout, because the default of 15 minutes per call is tight on a CPU:

export CONTAINERIZER_LLM_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8081/v1
export CONTAINERIZER_MODEL=qwen3-coder-30b-a3b
export CONTAINERIZER_LLM_TIMEOUT=3600
.venv-ci/bin/python -m containerizer assess examples/ci-demo --ai

--ai asks the LLM only about server and platform components with a confidence below 0.85, and examples/ci-demo has none, so the command above checks the configuration but never calls the model. To see a real answer, scan a challenge scenario with a low-confidence component, for example freight-rates (after ci/local.sh selftest or assess has cloned the challenge repository):

cp -r .work/ci-local/challenge/scenarios/freight-rates /tmp/freight-rates
.venv-ci/bin/python -m containerizer assess /tmp/freight-rates --ai -v

Answers are cached in .work/ai-cache/ (CONTAINERIZER_AI_CACHE), so delete the entry, or point the variable at an empty folder, to make the model answer again.

To test it from an appliance VM on the same server, enter the same server URL (the server's address instead of localhost, with LLAMA_ARG_HOST set to match) and model on Admin → Source control, and allow the address on Admin → Firewall. Plain http is accepted only when there is no API key: put TLS and a key (llama.cpp --api-key, behind a reverse proxy) in front of it otherwise.

With Ollama instead of llama.cpp, run ollama pull hf.co/byteshape/Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-GGUF:Qwen3-Coder-30B-A3B-Instruct-IQ4_XS-4.20bpw.gguf and use that name as the model, with the base URL http://localhost:11434/v1.

docs.title: Claude Code
docs.text:
As dev:

curl -fsSL https://claude.ai/install.sh | bash        # native installer, to ~/.local/bin/claude
claude                                               # first start: choose a login method

Ways to sign in on a headless server:

  • Claude subscription: start claude, pick the Claude account login, open the URL it prints in a browser on your own machine, and paste the code back into the SSH session.
  • Long-lived token: on a machine with a browser run claude setup-token, then put export CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN=... in ~dev/.bashrc (mode 600) on the server.
  • API key: export ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... from the Anthropic Console.

claude doctor checks the install. With claude on PATH, Containerizer's --ai option can also use it as its backend (CONTAINERIZER_AI_BACKEND=cli).

docs.title: Clone and run
docs.text:
# GitHub access for git push and pull requests: a fine-grained token for this one repository
# (Contents and Pull requests: read and write), or an SSH deploy key with write access
git clone https://github.com/olljanat-ai/containerizer.git ~/containerizer
cd ~/containerizer
ci/local.sh --list
ci/local.sh

The first run creates .venv-ci/ with Python 3.12, the requirements, pytest, pytest-xdist and the pinned MkDocs. Use that environment for ad hoc runs too: .venv-ci/bin/python -m pytest -q tests/test_engine.py, or the whole unit suite in parallel: .venv-ci/bin/python -m pytest -q -n auto (a few minutes instead of more than twenty in one process).

Command Runs ci/local.sh test docs gate selftest security sql sandbox ci/local.sh all the above, then assess (up to about an hour) and appliance (one to two hours) ci/local.sh sql sandbox only the jobs named, in that order CI_LOCAL_WORKERS=1 ci/local.sh test the unit tests in one process (default: one worker per CPU) CI_LOCAL_PARALLEL=0 ci/local.sh every job in turn (default: sql runs in the background after test) KEEP=1 ci/local.sh sql leaves SQL Server (cz-ci-mssql) and the web UI (cz-ci-web) running for debugging

The unit tests run in parallel (pytest-xdist), and sql, the longest job, runs in the background once they are done, next to the other jobs; its output is only in its log. Each job keeps going after another fails; the summary at the end lists pass / FAIL and the time per job, and the exit code is non-zero if any failed. Logs are in .work/ci-local/logs/<job>.log, and reports, SARIF files, the kind kubeconfig and the appliance images in .work/ci-local/ (git ignores .work/).

Differences from the GitHub runners, on purpose:

  • SQL Server is published on 127.0.0.1:11433 only (CI_LOCAL_SQL_PORT), and the web UI smoke test uses port 18080 instead of 8080, so nothing on the server's network can reach them, and the sql job runs while the web UI without an appliance holds 1433 and 8080.
  • The kind cluster is called cz-sandbox, as in CI; it is deleted after the test unless it already existed or KEEP=1 is set. Keep one running between runs to save a minute or two.
  • The appliance job builds, boots and tests the image but never pushes, signs or publishes it. It hands the root-owned Elemental output back to dev through a container, so it needs no sudo.
  • The gate job compares HEAD with its merge base on origin/main, as containerizer-head does on a pull request.

docs.title: Telling Claude Code about it
docs.text:
Put this in ~dev/.claude/CLAUDE.md on the server (your own instructions, not committed), so every session tests locally before pushing:

This server can run the whole CI suite locally: see docs/local-dev-server.md.
Before pushing, run `ci/local.sh` (and `ci/local.sh assess` or `ci/local.sh appliance` when the change
touches the assessment or the appliance). Use .venv-ci/bin/python for ad hoc test runs.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Use a dedicated machine or VM, not your workstation, and keep no other credentials on it. The tests build and run third-party code (the challenge apps, base images, scanner images), and Claude Code runs commands as dev.
  • The docker group is root. Anyone in it can start a privileged container and mount /, and the appliance and kind jobs need exactly that (--privileged). So dev is effectively root on this machine: that is acceptable only because the machine is dedicated to this. Do not add other users to docker, and do not give dev sudo as well; nothing here needs it after the install. Rootless Docker does not work for the appliance build or kind.
  • Docker bypasses the host firewall for published ports. -p 1433:1433 would open SQL Server to the network even with ufw or an nftables input policy of drop, because Docker inserts its own rules. ci/local.sh binds everything to 127.0.0.1; do the same in anything you run by hand.
  • Firewall: allow only SSH in, for example with nftables:
cat > /etc/nftables.conf <<'EOF'
#!/usr/sbin/nft -f
flush ruleset
table inet filter {
  chain input {
    type filter hook input priority 0; policy drop;
    iif lo accept
    ct state established,related accept
    ip protocol icmp accept
    ip6 nexthdr icmpv6 accept
    udp dport 68 accept     # DHCP client (offers and acknowledgements can be broadcasts)
    udp dport 546 accept    # DHCPv6 client
    tcp dport 22 accept
  }
}
EOF
systemctl enable --now nftables && systemctl restart docker   # Docker re-adds its own tables

The DHCP lines matter on a server that gets its address by DHCP: renewals are answered as established traffic, but a new lease (after a reboot or a lost lease) can arrive as a broadcast that conntrack does not match, and the server would lose its address. Restarting Docker restarts the containers that have a restart policy; give long-running ones you started by hand one (docker update --restart unless-stopped <name>), or they stay stopped. A kind cluster does not survive it: the sandbox job creates it again.

  • SSH: key login only. In /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/hardening.conf set PasswordAuthentication no and PermitRootLogin no, then systemctl reload ssh.
  • Ollama listens on 127.0.0.1:11434 only, and the llama.cpp container on 127.0.0.1:8081; leave OLLAMA_HOST unset unless you put TLS and a key in front of it.
  • GitHub: give the server a fine-grained token (or deploy key) scoped to this repository only, with no admin or workflow permissions, so a mistake on the server cannot change other repositories or the release workflow's secrets.
  • Claude Code permissions: on this dedicated VM it is reasonable to allow the commands the suite needs (ci/local.sh, docker, kind, kubectl, git, .venv-ci/bin/python) in ~/.claude/settings.json instead of approving each one. Keep git push behind a prompt if you want to review before anything leaves the machine.
  • The SQL Server and web passwords in ci/local.sh are the throwaway values from ci.yml; the database is recreated on every run and is reachable from localhost only.
  • Keep the OS patched: dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades.

docs.title: The web UI without an appliance
docs.text:
results/compose.yaml runs SQL Server 2025 Developer edition, creates the database, the schema and the three logins (cz_scanner, cz_web, cz_admin), and starts the web UI hardened, all on 127.0.0.1:

cp results/.env.example results/.env          # four strong passwords, and sign-in (docs/sign-in.md)
docker compose -f results/compose.yaml up -d --build
# http://127.0.0.1:8080/ shows the (empty) portfolio

# scan an app into it, static analysis only (mount it under its real folder name)
docker compose -f results/compose.yaml run --rm -v "$PWD/../my-app:/apps/my-app:ro" scan assess /apps/my-app

docs.title: Admin pages without sign-in
docs.text:
The admin pages need sign-in through an OpenID Connect provider. For development, a lab or your own machine, development mode skips it: set in results/.env

CONTAINERIZER_DEV_NO_AUTH=1
CONTAINERIZER_PUBLIC_URL=http://127.0.0.1:8080   # the address you open in the browser (forms check it)
# optional: who you are and your roles (admin, operator, viewer); default John Doe, admin
CONTAINERIZER_DEV_USER=john.doe@example.com
CONTAINERIZER_DEV_NAME=John Doe
CONTAINERIZER_DEV_ROLES=admin

and restart the web UI (docker compose -f results/compose.yaml up -d). Opening /admin then signs you in as that person at once. Everything else works as with sign-in: the roles decide what you see, every form needs its CSRF token, and the change history records the changes as made by that person in development mode. A red banner on every page says so. The JSON API works with API keys made on Admin → API (access tokens need sign-in).

Never on a shared network

Everyone who reaches the web UI is an administrator. The web UI refuses to start in development mode on the appliance, and when sign-in (CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_ISSUER) is set as well. Keep it on 127.0.0.1, or limit who reaches it with the firewall, as for the rest of this server.

docs.title: Building the appliance image
docs.text:
docker build -f appliance/Dockerfile --build-arg VERSION=v0.0.0-dev -t containerizer-appliance:dev .
# disk image (expandable), ISO
docker run --rm --privileged -v /dev:/dev -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v "$PWD/build:/build" \
  --entrypoint /usr/bin/elemental containerizer-appliance:dev build-disk --expandable --local \
  --system containerizer-appliance:dev -n containerizer -o /build
docker run --rm --privileged -v /dev:/dev -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock -v "$PWD/build:/build" \
  --entrypoint /usr/bin/elemental containerizer-appliance:dev build-iso --local --bootloader-in-rootfs \
  --extra-cmdline "console=tty1 console=ttyS0" -n containerizer -o /build containerizer-appliance:dev

A fork that publishes its own images sets --build-arg IMAGE=ghcr.io/<owner>/containerizer-appliance --build-arg SIGNER_REPO=<owner>/<repo>, so its appliances accept only its own signed releases. .github/workflows/release.yml builds, boot-tests (QEMU: firewall, DNS filter, services, sandbox cluster, registry, roll back) and, on a vX.Y.Z tag, pushes, signs and publishes.

docs.title: Lab sandbox (k3s, Flux, Git server)
docs.text:
A persistent copy of the appliance's sandbox deployment path on this server, for testing features that deploy applications to the sandbox through GitOps end to end: the same k3s, Flux and External Secrets versions and settings as the appliance, a Git server for the output repository, and what the appliance's cz-sandbox timer does. It is not the sandbox job of ci/local.sh (a throwaway kind cluster cz-sandbox): the two run side by side. The scripts are in ci/lab-sandbox/; its state lives in LAB_DIR (default /home/dev/lab-sandbox):

mkdir -p ~/lab-sandbox && cp -r ci/lab-sandbox/. ~/lab-sandbox/   # the timer runs sync.sh from where up.sh ran
~/lab-sandbox/up.sh        # install or start everything; idempotent, needs sudo; about 3 minutes the first time
~/lab-sandbox/status.sh
~/lab-sandbox/smoke.sh     # the end-to-end test below
~/lab-sandbox/down.sh      # stop, data kept (--purge: remove the cluster, Gitea and all state)

docs.title: What runs where
docs.text:
What How Reached at k3s v1.37.1+k3s1, the appliance's binary and checksum, single node lab systemd k3s-lab, config /etc/rancher/k3s-lab/config.yaml API https://127.0.0.1:6443; admin kubeconfig $LAB_DIR/kubeconfig (mode 600) Flux v2.10.0 (the appliance's install.yaml and checksum, images pinned by digest in lib.sh) k3s, flux-system External Secrets Operator 2.14.0 (the appliance's chart digest and values), ClusterSecretStore app-secrets over namespace containerizer-secrets k3s; the store is made by the appliance's own lib/secret-store.sh secret.sh <remote-key> <json-or-literal> Gitea 28.3 (rootless, pinned by digest), HTTPS with a certificate from the lab CA container lab-git, runs as dev, data in $LAB_DIR/state/gitea https://lab-git:3001/: published on 127.0.0.1:3001 and on the Docker bridge address 172.17.0.1:3001 Output repository Gitea organization lab, private https://lab-git:3001/lab/sandbox-deployments.git Traefik (k3s's, as on the appliance) NodePorts 30080 / 30443 on loopback only, default certificate *.sandbox.lab.test from the lab CA https://<component>-<app>.sandbox.lab.test through 127.0.0.1:30443 The cz-sandbox equivalent (sync.sh) systemd lab-sandbox-sync.timer, every 2 minutes, as dev systemctl status lab-sandbox-sync.timer; sudo systemctl stop lab-sandbox-sync.timer to pause it Read-only verifier for containerizer sandbox verify ServiceAccount from the output repository's clusters/sandbox/verify-rbac.yaml $LAB_DIR/verifier.kubeconfig (24-hour token, renewed every 12 hours)

$LAB_DIR/secrets.env (mode 600) holds the Gitea administrator lab-admin's generated password, a write token for the output repository (write:repository) and a read-only token (read:repository, read:organization) that Flux uses.

The Git URL is the same everywhere because the GitOps files name it: /etc/hosts maps lab-git to the Docker bridge address, CoreDNS in k3s does the same (ConfigMap coredns-custom), and Gitea is published on that address. git on the host trusts the lab CA for this one URL (http.https://lab-git:3001/.sslCAInfo in ~/.gitconfig); Flux gets it as ca.crt next to the token in <namespace>--cz-git (on the appliance the Git servers have public certificates). The appliance's cz-sandbox accepts only https URLs, so the lab uses HTTPS too.

docs.title: Differences from the appliance
docs.text:
• Images come from Docker's image store, not a registry. k3s runs with docker: true (its embedded cri-dockerd), so a pod can run any image docker build made on this host, and the manifests containerizer generates use imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent: nothing is pushed or pulled. The kubelet's image garbage collection is off, because the store is shared with the builds and ci/local.sh. Pods show up in docker ps as k8s_* containers. The appliance still pushes to its registry at localhost:5000/<path>.
  • The appliance's k3s settings are kept (servicelb off, secrets encryption, no anonymous API access), except resolv-conf, the audit log and protect-kernel-defaults, which depend on the appliance's OS.
  • Traefik is on loopback NodePorts instead of behind Caddy on 443, without the HTTP-to-HTTPS redirect.
  • Flux is the only GitOps tool, as on the appliance.
  • The k3s system images (pause, CoreDNS, Traefik, metrics-server, local-path, klipper-helm) are pinned by the k3s release's tags, as on the appliance, not by digest.

docs.title: Firewall
docs.text:
k3s runs on the host network. Its pods reach the host (the API server, Gitea through the Docker bridge) through cni0, so the input chain of /etc/nftables.conf gets two accept rules, which up.sh adds to the file and to the running rule set (with nft add rule, not by loading the file again: its flush ruleset would also remove Docker's and k3s's tables):

    iifname { "cni0", "flannel.1" } accept
    ip saddr { 10.42.0.0/16, 10.43.0.0/16 } accept

The API server (6443) and the kubelet (10250) listen on every address and are kept off the network by the input chain's drop policy. NodePorts answer on loopback only (nodeport-addresses=127.0.0.1/32): Docker-style DNAT traffic to them would pass the forward chain, which accepts by default. Reach Traefik or Gitea from another machine with SSH port forwarding, e.g. ssh -L 30443:127.0.0.1:30443 -L 3001:127.0.0.1:3001 dev@<server>.

To open the sandbox's HTTPS entry to your own subnet instead, limit it in the forward chain first, then let k3s answer on the server's address too:

# /etc/nftables.conf, forward chain (and the same with `sudo nft add rule inet filter forward ...` to apply it now,
# without reloading the file: that would drop Docker's tables)
iifname "eth0" ct original proto-dst 30443 ip saddr != $LAB drop
iifname "eth0" ct original proto-dst 30443 meta nfproto ipv6 drop
# /etc/rancher/k3s-lab/config.yaml, then: sudo systemctl restart k3s-lab
kube-proxy-arg:
  - "nodeport-addresses=127.0.0.1/32,<server address>/32"

docs.title: Pointing a scan or a runner at it
docs.text:
. ~/lab-sandbox/env.sh
Setting Value Registry (image prefix) localhost/lab ($LAB_REGISTRY): images localhost/lab/<app>/<component>:<tag>, built and tagged locally, not pushed Output repository --output-repo $LAB_OUTPUT_REPO --output-username lab-admin, write token in OUTPUT_GIT_TOKEN sandbox.env equivalents CZ_SANDBOX_GIT_URL, CZ_SANDBOX_GIT_USERNAME, CZ_SANDBOX_GIT_TOKEN (read-only); sync.sh puts them in the store Sandbox verification --verify-sandbox --kubeconfig $LAB_VERIFIER_KUBECONFIG (or containerizer sandbox verify --kubeconfig ...) Ingress --ingress-domain sandbox.lab.test; verify with --ingress-address 127.0.0.1:30443 --ingress-ca $LAB_CA Secrets the apps need secret.sh <namespace>--<name> '{"key": "value"}'

Two things the lab does not cover yet: containerizer org has no Gitea provider (scan sources from GitHub, GitLab or Azure DevOps and write the output to the lab), and --no-push-images does not tag the gate's image as <registry>/<app>/<component>:<tag>, so for local images that tag has to be added (docker tag) by whatever replaces the push.

docs.title: The egress observer
docs.text: ci/lab-sandbox/egress-observer.sh install runs the egress observer for the lab, as the appliance does (but without the appliance firewall's signals: the lab has none): the systemd unit lab-egress-observer as this user with CAP_NET_ADMIN only, its own read-only ServiceAccount ($LAB_DIR/egress-observer.kubeconfig), the CoreDNS query log on (log.override in the lab's coredns-custom manifest), flows into the lab's results database with the scanner login of results/.env. sync.sh gives it the Roles of new namespaces; egress-observer.sh remove takes it all out again. For an egress review in the lab, a queue runner needs the output repository and, for apps not cloned by an organization scan, their checkouts: CONTAINERIZER_EGRESS_OUTPUT_REPO=$LAB_OUTPUT_REPO, CONTAINERIZER_EGRESS_OUTPUT_USERNAME=lab-admin, the write token in OUTPUT_GIT_TOKEN (env.sh) and CONTAINERIZER_EGRESS_SOURCES=<folder of checkouts named after the applications>; containerizer llm-queue --kinds egress,link --name <own name> runs one beside the lab's runner.

docs.title: The smoke test
docs.text:
smoke.sh checks the whole path without a scan: it builds localhost/lab/smoke:1 (nginx answering 200 on 8080) with docker build, writes an app smoke into a clone of the output repository in the layout containerizer org writes, generated by containerizer from examples/ci-demo with that image (smoke_app.py: lab/_/smoke/, its gitops/flux tenant, ExternalSecret, GitRepository and Kustomization, containerizer.json, and clusters/sandbox/ from write_sandbox), and pushes it. Then Flux syncs the root Kustomization, sync.sh puts smoke--cz-git in the store, the app's own Kustomization deploys it as smoke-reconciler, the pods become Ready with no Pulling event, and containerizer sandbox verify reads the result back as the verifier:

smoke/Demo.Web: healthy - 2/2 ready
sandbox health: healthy=1

smoke.sh --remove takes the app out of the repository again, and Flux prunes it.

docs.title: Secret values in OpenBao
docs.text:
The apps in the appliance's sandbox read their connection strings, secret settings and the settings a release pipeline used to fill (#{Api.Host}#, __Example.Mode__) from the secret store (see External Secrets). On the appliance you enter those values in OpenBao. It runs on the appliance and is served on its normal HTTPS port:

https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>/ui/. On the admin pages, Secrets ↗ links there.

You don't have to look up which keys an app needs. Every two minutes the appliance makes one entry for each component that has secrets, with an empty value for each key the component reads. You only type the values.

docs.title: Sign in as the administrator
docs.text:
User name admin (method Username). The password is in /etc/containerizer/secrets/openbao-admin (root only, like Grafana's). Change it in OpenBao after the first sign-in. The appliance doesn't need it afterwards.

The admin user can:

  • read and write every app's values;
  • create users, groups and policies (to give operators access);
  • turn on sign-in methods (for SSO).

It can't seal OpenBao, change its storage or create a root token.

docs.title: Fill in an app's values
docs.text:
1. Secrets engines → apps: one folder per app namespace, one entry per component (apps/<namespace>/<component>, KV version 2, so every save keeps the earlier versions).
  2. Open the entry and choose Create new version. Fill in the values; leave a key empty if the app should keep its own value from appsettings.json. Save.
  3. Within two minutes the appliance:
  4. copies the filled values into the store;
  5. has External Secrets Operator sync the app's Secret right away;
  6. restarts the app's Deployments and StatefulSets that read it, once, and only when what the app gets changed: the pod template's annotation containerizer.io/secrets is a fingerprint of the Secrets it reads (ESO's data hash, never a value). CronJobs pick the values up at their next run.

The key names are environment variable names: ConnectionStrings__Main sets ConnectionStrings:Main, Api__Url sets Api:Url. They match the Secret store keys in the app's HARDENING.md.

docs.title: Files (certificates)
docs.text:
Files an app reads, such as a certificate with its private key (.pfx), are in a second entry of the component: apps/<namespace>/<component>-files. Each key is a file name, its value the file in base64 (for example base64 -w0 app.pfx). Its password, when the app's settings have one (...__CertificatePassword), is a key of the component's own entry.

  • A .pfx or .p12 next to the app's code: the image leaves it out, and the scan mounts it read-only where the app reads it (/app/<path>). Its key starts with the repository's own file (a development certificate); put the environment's certificate in its place.
  • Any other file: turn on Files from the secret store for the app's repository (Admin → Repositories → the repository → Settings) with a folder, /secrets by default. After the next scan each component mounts all of its files there, and its -files entry exists, empty. Add a key per file and point the app's setting at it (/secrets/app.pfx), in settings.yaml or in the settings entry.

Saving a file restarts the app (a file mounted on its own does not change in a running pod).

What you see Where it comes from An empty key Nobody has filled it yet. The app runs without it (with its appsettings.json value). A key with a value you didn't type The app's own development value: the one appsettings.json (or appsettings.Development.json, ...) gives it in the app's repository, where a release pipeline replaces it. The scan leaves these values on the appliance only, never in the output repository, and each key is filled from there once: empty it and it stays empty. Or someone put it in the store by hand before OpenBao was there: it was taken over. A key that is not there although HARDENING.md lists it Another part of the appliance fills it (the sandbox identity provider's client secret, lab services' credentials): don't set it.

Settings that are not secret (a URL with a token in it, say) are in the component's ConfigMap <component>-settings, not in OpenBao: see overview.

docs.title: Give operators their own apps (delegated access)
docs.text:
For every app namespace the appliance writes the policy app-<namespace>. It allows reading and changing that namespace's entries (apps/<namespace>/*) and nothing else. An operator who has it sees the names of the other namespaces, never their values.

Give operators that policy as a user or, better, through a group of your identity provider (next section). With a user (Access → Authentication methods → userpass → Create user, or with the CLI):

export BAO_ADDR=https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>    # on a workstation; on the appliance just run `bao` (see Recovery)
bao login -method=userpass username=admin
