An answer over the budget is sent back once with the count (it is a rewrite, not a targeted change: renames, refactorings and modernizations are other tooling's job); if it is still over, the file is left unchanged and the order page says why. The edits may touch only the files shown with the question: the finding's file and the component's appsettings.json (in a repair round, the files the compiler errors name).

The order page's findings table has Lines changed per finding (with how many findings of the file share them, and what was put back), and the patch's commit message lists each finding fixed in code with its lines, under "Changed in code (no platform alternative)", and the findings handled by configuration.

The changes become one commit in a scratch copy ("Containerizer: <app>: <findings fixed>", author Containerizer <containerizer@localhost>), and the patch is git format-patch of it, so git am applies it as a commit with that message.

docs.title: How it is verified
docs.text:
The patch is applied to a second, clean copy at the assessed commit: git apply --check, then git am. Then:

  1. The rules run again on the patched copy. Each finding shows whether it is gone from this file, in fewer places or still found, and any new finding of the changed components is listed: check whether the patch caused it.
  2. Each changed component is built and run with the same build-and-run step as the scans (verify): the generated Dockerfile, a hardened container, an HTTP probe.

NuGet package versions are fixed without the LLM. The LLM sees only the file it edits, so it may add a package reference at a lower version than a project the component references (or a package it uses) needs. NuGet refuses that build (NU1605, Detected package downgrade). Right after the LLM's edits, a direct reference below the version of a referenced project is raised to it. A downgrade the build still reports is raised to the version NuGet names in the next repair round, without an LLM call. The patch's notes list each version raised. The prompt also lists the packages the referenced projects bring in, so that they are not added again. Since .NET Core 3.0, ASP.NET Core's own parts (Microsoft.AspNetCore.HttpOverrides, .Mvc, .Hosting, ...) come with the shared framework, and their NuGet packages end at 2.x. An answer that adds one to such a project does not add it, and when the build cannot find one (NU1101, NU1102), the reference is removed (outside the Web SDK, a FrameworkReference to Microsoft.AspNetCore.App replaces it), without an LLM call.

Status Meaning Queued Waiting in the LLM queue Generating The LLM is writing the changes (the page says which file) Verifying Applying the patch, running the rules, building and running Verified The patch applies cleanly, and every changed component builds and runs Applies only The patch applies cleanly, but a build or a run failed, or could not be done (no Docker, a component that is not built in a Linux container as it is): the log tail says why Failed No patch: the LLM made no usable edits, or the patch did not apply cleanly (never offered) Cancelled Skipped, or cancelled while it ran, on the LLM queue page

A failure to reach the LLM, or a source that is gone, is a failed attempt of the queue job: it is tried again up to three times (the LLM queue page shows the error), then the order fails. A commit that is no longer in the clone (the repository moved on, and the scan worker keeps shallow clones) fails with a message: scan the repository again and order a new refactoring.

The page shows every change as a coloured diff per file, here a real patch the dev server's CPU LLM wrote for the challenge app expense-claims:

docs.title: How to apply it
docs.text:
The order's page has Download .patch (<app>-<component>-containerizer.patch, or -all- for every component) and the steps:

git checkout -b containerizer-refactor <assessed commit>
git am --keep-cr < expense-claims-ExpenseClaims.Jobs-containerizer.patch
# or, if your branch has moved on since the assessed commit:
git apply --3way expense-claims-ExpenseClaims.Jobs-containerizer.patch

--keep-cr keeps Windows line endings in files that have them (without it git am drops them and the patch does not apply). Then review every change, build and run your tests, set the configuration the notes mention (paths, certificates, credentials as Kubernetes Secrets), push the branch and open a pull request yourself.

docs.title: Make it A
docs.text:
Make it A is one order for everything that keeps a B-rated application from A: its refactor findings, its configuration findings that name a file, and, for the server components that keep their own data, the move of that data to SQL Server. It runs on request only: Make it A in the Refactoring box of the results page (operators, administrators and the application's product owners, with the queue's estimate), or Make it A: every B application for administrators (below). A scan never orders one by itself.

Keeping its own data does not make an application B: it rates A, marked stateful, and the organization scan deploys it as it is with its data on a persistent volume and one replica (Application data on persistent volumes). Make it A moves the data of a B application's stateful components to SQL Server only along with the code changes that make it B in the first place, or when the data is in a folder Containerizer could not find.

The results page's migration plan points here from its second wave: the components that rate A once their code changes are made. For an application with components that cannot run in a Linux container (no Refactoring box), the plan lists the same changes with the findings to make them by hand, and shows the components that are ready already in the sandbox.

Where an order of the same kind is already waiting, running or has a patch, the box offers that order (its status, Open the patch, Download .patch and the commit it was made for) instead of a new one; Request a new one is for code that has changed since.

The order is one refactor job (goal rating-a) that loops in the queue runner:

  1. Generate. The LLM is asked about every file with findings, as for a refactoring patch; the files of a stateful component that open its embedded database get the stateless guidance.
  2. Apply and verify. Everything changed so far becomes one commit for the assessed commit; it is applied to a clean copy, and the changed components are built and run.
  3. Repair. When a build or run fails, a repair round in the same job gives the LLM the compiler errors (or the run log), the files they are in and the patch, and the combined patch is verified again: at most 2 repair rounds a pass.
  4. Assess again. The patched copy is assessed with every rule. A is reached when it rates A and builds and runs.
  5. Second pass. Still B with findings left (still found by the rules, or a component that still keeps its data) and LLM calls left: one more pass on what remains, then steps 2 to 4 again. At most 2 passes.

Every LLM call of the job, retries and repair rounds included, counts against its limit of 16 calls; files beyond it are not attempted. Each pass leaves a quarter of the calls (at most 4) for its repair rounds, so a patch that does not build always gets a repair round. The order page shows each pass and round (files, calls, changes, the build and run, the rating), the rating before and after (B → A: Rating A reached, or B → B: 4 of 6 fixed; still keeps data in Api (Embedded file database)), the result per finding as the rules see the final patched copy, and the one patch to download, as for any refactoring patch. Its statuses are the same (verified, does not build, does not start, ...).

Reading the order page. B → A: Rating A reached is the goal: the rules rate the patched copy A and it builds and runs, so it is deployed to the sandbox. B → A with A by the rules, but the patched copy does not build or run means the code changes remove what kept it from A, but the copy is not A yet and is not deployed: the errors are under Verification; Fix it with the LLM orders a repair. Findings left (they do not keep it from A) are configuration findings an A application may still have.

Build again (no LLM). A build or run can fail for a reason outside the code: the appliance's firewall blocks a package mirror (E: Unable to locate package ...), a registry was down. Once that is fixed, Build again (no LLM) on the order page (any finished Make it A order with a patch) places a new order with the same patch: it is applied, built, run and assessed, and deployed to the sandbox when it rates A and runs, as the first time. It makes no LLM call (no repair round either, and no LLM-heavy chain), so it needs no approval; it still waits for its turn in the LLM queue (its hours and free requests, as any job). When it still fails, Fix it with the LLM on its page is there as usual.

Newer code starts from the earlier patch. When the application has a working Make it A patch (it builds, runs and rates A) for an older commit, a new order for the newer code starts from it. The patch is applied file by file (with a 3-way merge where git can). The files it still applies to are kept as they are and the LLM is not asked about them; the files it no longer applies to are put back and edited again, with every file the newer code needs. Then the copy is verified and assessed as usual, and a second pass takes what is still found. When the newer code did not touch the patched files, the order makes no LLM call at all. The order page says which order's patch it started from, how many files were kept and which were edited again. A chain that starts over (below) does not use the earlier patch again.

Until it runs in the sandbox (LLM-heavy mode). With an LLM-heavy window on the whole application (Admin → Applications), a Make it A order may do more (40 LLM calls, 4 passes, 4 repair rounds a pass) and stops making LLM calls when the window ends. An order whose copy does not end up running in the sandbox queues the next one at once, approved and first in the queue, which continues from its patch with what went wrong: the compiler errors or the run log, or, when it was deployed but failed there, the sandbox's state and log of each failing component (its failing copy is taken out of the sandbox first: the scan's output goes back). The chain ends when a copy runs in the sandbox, when the window ends, after 30 orders, or when two orders in a row changed nothing. Each order's page links the one before and the next.

A chain stuck on the same errors starts over. Repairs build on the patch before them, so an early wrong edit is carried by every order after it. When 3 orders in a row fail with the same errors (the same compiler errors, or the same run or sandbox error, apart from times and line numbers), the next order starts again from the original code. Its prompt says what kept failing, and no answer of the stuck attempt is reused. A chain starts over at most twice; stuck a third time, it stops and says so. This applies to the refactoring orders below too.

Refactoring orders in an LLM-heavy window. With an LLM-heavy window on the whole application, or on the component of an order of one component, a refactoring order of chosen findings makes up to 40 LLM calls (files) instead of 8, and makes no LLM call after the window ends (the files left say not attempted: the LLM-heavy window ended). An order that does not finish the job queues the next one at once, approved and first in the queue:

  • its patch does not build or run: a repair order (as Fix it with the LLM), with the build errors or the run log, which carries the findings that are left for after the repair;
  • it builds and runs, but findings are left (not attempted, not fixed, or an LLM error): an order for the files of those findings, which continues from its patch, so the result is one patch with every change (its subject ends in (continued)).

The chain ends when every finding is fixed and the patched copy builds and runs, when the window ends, after 30 orders, or when two orders in a row changed nothing. Each order's page says where it is in the chain and links the one before and the next; the queue's result line ends with LLM-heavy: continues as #n.

Estimates. The button and the bulk page show the queue's estimate of the first pass (the size of what it sends, a typical file for each stateful component, at the speed the queue learned); repair rounds and a second pass, when needed, take more, up to the limit of 16 calls.

Make it A: every B application (Admin → Refactoring, administrators) lists every B-rated application with what changes and its order's estimate (tokens and LLM time), smallest first, with the running total of the LLM time up to each row, so the LLM's time goes to the cheapest wins first; a local LLM gets the most applications to A for its hours. Applications with an order in the queue already say so and link to it. The ones that a verified patch makes A already (Made A by a patch on the front page: it builds, runs and rates A, merged or not, for the commit the latest scan assessed) link to that patch and are not queued again from here (order one on its application page for a new patch). The ones that cannot be ordered (no commit recorded, source not kept on this machine) are at the bottom with the reason. Orders under a number of tokens each (20,000 to begin with) marks the ones that fit, and Queue … approved places one order for each of them, approved by you at once: they do not wait for approval, whatever the LLM queue's approval policy says, and run by the queue's settings (hours, idle, parallel requests). Nothing is queued by opening the page.

Tick Also LLM-heavy mode for these applications, for (8 hours to begin with, up to 7 days) to turn LLM-heavy mode on for each application ordered, with the same button: until the window ends, their orders and the LLM jobs that follow (egress and link reviews) go before every other job in the LLM queue, approved, and their scans review each of their components. Admin → LLM queue lists the windows, each with End now. Applications that already had an order waiting are not turned LLM-heavy.

docs.title: The sandbox variant
docs.text:
A Make it A order whose patched copy rates A and is verified is deployed to the sandbox in place of the application's scan output, the way an organization scan deploys (the same code): an organization scan deploys only an application's components that rate A on their own, so a B application has only those in the sandbox, often none; the patched copy takes the application's place. There is one folder, one Git history, one namespace, one set of URLs, IdP clients, lab databases and egress decisions per application.

  • Where. The application's own folder in the output repository of the organization scan that assessed it, <Organization>/<Project>/<Repository>/ (or <Repository>@<folder>/ for one application of a split repository), the folder the scan writes. The scan's output there is replaced, clusters/sandbox/ is regenerated, in one commit: sandbox: <app> runs the Make it A patch of order #<job> (commit <sha>); Flux rolls the application over to it. Its images go to the appliance's own registry, as the scan's do; the output repository and branch and the security gate are that scan's; the output repository's write token is its registered credential. An application that no organization scan with an output repository assessed here is not deployed, and the order page says so (no output repository: ...).
  • The application's name. Everything an organization scan derives from an application's name is the application's own: the namespace, the images <registry>/<app>/<component>, the Ingress hosts (so the application's sandbox URLs), the sandbox IdP clients, the lab services, the connectivity.yaml with its approved egress and confirmed links, and the NetworkPolicies. The image tag says it is the patch: 1.<yyyymmdd>.<hhmm>-refactor.<job>, a semver pre-release that the application's image automation never picks up.
  • What it records. containerizer.json in the folder has patched: the order (job), the source commit the patch was made for (commit), the tag, and previous_revision, the output repository's commit before the first patch ran there, whose folder is the scan's output. The scan's output is never lost: it stays in the output repository's history.
  • Data. Only the components that rate A are deployed, with no uploaded dev database: the patched copy uses the application's lab database (when the lab services are on), the one its scan output uses, as the lab services are per namespace.
  • Health. The runner reads the application's namespace back with a read-only kubeconfig (CONTAINERIZER_SANDBOX_KUBECONFIG, optional CONTAINERIZER_SANDBOX_CONTEXT; on the appliance the verifier account of clusters/sandbox/verify-rbac.yaml, below) and records it in the order: running in the sandbox, failing in the sandbox, or deployed, health not checked without a kubeconfig. From then on the scan's sandbox checks of the application see the patched copy, and the results page's Migration plan says the sandbox runs the patch.
  • Kept up to date. The queue runner checks again what runs: a copy whose health is not known yet (deployed, health not checked: the cluster could not be read in time, as after a restart) every 10 minutes, one running or failing every hour, a few per pass. While an administrator has the application's sandbox turned off, the order says sandbox turned off; when it is on again, the health is read at once. The application's folder in the output repository decides whether the copy is there: when it no longer runs the order's patch (a scan or another order wrote it), the order says removed from the sandbox; when the latest removed copy of an application turns out to run there after all, it is back, with the date (Back) on the order page.
  • Scans. A scan that assesses the commit the patch was made for leaves the folder as it is (the patch is newer than what the scan would write) and still records its assessment; its result says the folder runs the patch. A scan that assesses newer code writes its own output into the folder, and the order's state becomes replaced by newer code: the patch was made for code the application no longer is. Without scheduled scans, the code an order was made for stays the code the scans know, and so does the patched copy.
  • One per application. A newer order's patched copy overwrites the older one in place (on the same commit or another; it keeps the scan's commit to go back to), and the older order's state becomes replaced by newer code, with the newer order.
  • Try again on the application's results page (administrators and operators, when a component is not in the sandbox) builds the patched copy again: the same patch on the same commit, generated, built, checked and deployed with the version the appliance runs now (no LLM), within a few minutes by the queue runner. A scan does not: it leaves the patched copy as it is. Use it after an update that lets a component through, such as a gate fix. If the new build cannot be deployed, what ran stays and the page says why.
  • After an update the queue runner does the same by itself, once: the patched copy of each application's latest order that another Containerizer version built (or one from before 0.35.7, which recorded no version) is built again with the new version. So what the update changes in the generated files (settings, Secrets, ConfigMaps) reaches the applications that run a patch, too.
  • Remove from the sandbox on the order page (administrators, operators, the application's product owners) puts the scan's output back: the queue runner, within a few minutes, checks the folder out of previous_revision (no folder there, as when no component rated A on its own: the folder goes), regenerates clusters/sandbox/ and commits; the sandbox runs the application as the scan deployed it. The patch stays available on its order (in the results database), and a new Make it A order for the new code starts from it (above).

Variants of before: <app>-refactor-<job>. Until 0.10.0 patched copies ran beside the application, in a folder <Organization>/<Project>/<Repository>-refactor-<job>/ and a namespace of their own. The LLM queue runner's housekeeping moves them: the latest one of each application that still runs is generated again under the application's name from the source at its commit with its patch (its images as they were built: nothing is built again) into the application's folder, the -refactor- folders are deleted and clusters/sandbox/ regenerated, in one commit; Flux prunes the old namespaces (with their lab database). The order keeps its history; its sandbox namespace, folder and URL become the application's (the old ones under Before on the order page). One that cannot be moved (its source is gone) is taken out of the sandbox, and Build again (no LLM) on its order deploys it in place. Variants deployed before 0.9.1 had an expiry date, which no longer applies.

The folder also holds the order's patch, make-it-a.patch, so developers who look in the output repository find the code change next to its manifests (git am it on the commit it was made for).

The results page shows the patched copy's state next to the order, with its URL (open ↗, the application's own) while it runs; the front page lists it under Made A by a patch.

Images without a registry. In a lab whose sandbox cluster shares the image builder's Docker image store (k3s with --docker on the machine that builds), set CONTAINERIZER_LOCAL_IMAGES=1 for the scan worker and the LLM queue runner: each image is then tagged with its deploy reference (docker tag, no push) and the manifests run it with imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent. Such images have no digest or signature (they need a registry). Without the setting (the appliance), the images are pushed to the appliance's own registry.

docs.title: The command line
docs.text:
containerizer refactor path/to/app [--component NAME] [--out DIR] [--include-config] [--max-calls 8] [--no-verify]
containerizer refactor path/to/app --queue [--sql ...]

Without --queue it runs at once with the LLM of the environment (CONTAINERIZER_LLM_BASE_URL and CONTAINERIZER_MODEL for a self-hosted one; the LLM), and writes the patch and a summary (<app>-<component>-containerizer.json: every finding's result, the verification, the payload) to --out. The application folder must be a git checkout for git am to work: the patch is made for its HEAD commit, and uncommitted changes are not in it. A folder without git gets a patch for git apply -p1 in that folder. With --queue the order goes to the LLM queue in SQL Server (--sql or CONTAINERIZER_SQL), or to llm-queue.json in --out, which containerizer llm-queue --file works through.

--goal rating-a runs Make it A on the checkout (the loop, the repair rounds and the second pass; --max-calls is then the limit of the whole order, 16 by default); the command line never deploys a sandbox variant.

docs.title: On the appliance
docs.text:
The LLM queue runner (containerizer-llm-queue) carries out the orders. For them it

  • reads the scan worker's clones (/var/lib/containerizer/worker/scan-<id>/repos/<app>) read only, and makes its scratch copies with git clone --shared in /var/lib/containerizer/refactor, the only folder it may write to besides the LLM answer cache. It reads no other folder: a job that names another source is refused (CONTAINERIZER_REFACTOR_SOURCES), so a row in the database cannot make it read the machine's files;
  • reaches Docker through the Docker socket guard, like the scan worker, to build and run the patched components: it is not in the root-equivalent docker group, and the patched code is built and run in the same hardened, isolated containers as the scan worker's. Without Docker the patches are applies only.
  • for the sandbox deployment of patched copies: clones the scan's output repository into its scratch space with the registered write token, pushes the patched copy's images to the appliance's registry, reads the lab services that are on, and reads its health with the kubeconfig of the read-only verifier account, /run/containerizer/sandbox-verifier.kubeconfig. cz-sandbox (root, every 2 minutes) gives that account its Role in every namespace Containerizer generated (clusters/sandbox/verify-rbac.yaml: workloads, pods, their logs and events, the namespace's Flux Kustomization; no Secrets, nothing cluster-wide) and writes the kubeconfig with a 24-hour token (root:containerizer, 0640). A namespace new to the sandbox gets its Role at the next run of cz-sandbox; the runner waits for it within its health check (15 minutes, CONTAINERIZER_SANDBOX_VARIANT_TIMEOUT).

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
• The LLM can be wrong. A patch that builds and runs is not a patch that is correct: the build and a start-up probe do not run your tests. Review every change.
  • APIs the component cannot use. Models suggest APIs of newer frameworks than the component targets (on a net6.0 component, Qwen3-Coder used X509CertificateLoader, which is .NET 9 and later). The build catches it: such a patch is applies only, with the compiler error in the log tail. Fix it with the LLM on the order page asks again with the errors; Make it A does so by itself (at most 2 rounds a pass).
  • Speed. On the built-in CPU LLM each file takes five minutes or more, and the verification build takes minutes too; an order of a few files takes most of an hour. The queue runs it when its settings allow.
  • Small context. The LLM sees one file (or part of a large one) and the component's settings, not the whole application: changes that span several files (a new option class wired up in Program.cs) may be left as not fixed with a reason, or made in one file only.
  • What is verified is the component's container as Containerizer generates it, with the production services it needs missing (a smoke test in Development mode when they are), not the application in its real environment.
  • Make it A stops at its limits (16 LLM calls, 2 passes, 2 repair rounds a pass): an application whose findings need more stays B, and the order says what is left. The rating after is the rules' rating of the patched copy and the build and run of its components, not a test of the application.
  • A patched copy in the sandbox runs with the application's lab database (the one its scan output uses): it shows that the application starts and answers as a stateless container, not that its data or its integrations work.

docs.title: Rule review
docs.text:
The learning loop of a scan builds and runs applications, matches failures against the failure rules, patches the build plan and retries (how it works). Nothing it learns enters the ruleset until an administrator approves it under Admin → Rule review:

  1. The run uses what it learns, and nothing else does. A learning run works on a staging copy of the learned rules, so its own result is as good as it can be while the rules other runs read stay unchanged.
  2. What it learned waits as a candidate with its evidence: every new finding or plan rule, failure rule and Linux-safe package.
  3. A person decides: approve (after editing the rule in the text box, if needed) or reject with a reason. Rejected rules are not proposed again. Every decision is in the change history.
  4. Approved rules go into your internal rules repository, never into this tool's public rules/ folder: what your applications taught the tool stays inside your organization.

docs.title: What a candidate shows
docs.text:
Kind A finding or plan rule (70-reviewed.yaml), a failure rule of the build-and-run loop (55-reviewed-failures.yaml), or a package proven to work on Linux (packages-reviewed.yaml) Source learned (from a build and run) or ai (proposed by the LLM, with the model's name) Confidence The rule's own confidence if it has one (0.7 for LLM rules), else 0.9 when the container built and ran with it, 0.8 for a failure observed at runtime, 0.6 otherwise Seen How many runs learned the same rule. The same condition and effect learned again adds evidence to the existing candidate, whatever its id or wording Evidence For each run (the latest 20): repository and commit, application and component, every attempt (which failure rule matched, its outcome, the exit code, the diagnosis), and the tail of the failing log

Logs are stored with credentials masked (passwords and keys in connection strings, Authorization headers, user:password in URLs, JSON web tokens, private keys). The masking catches the common forms, not every secret an application can print, so rule review is for administrators only.

docs.title: What approval checks
docs.text:
A learned rule has to meet the same bar as the curated ones:

  • a unique id (lower-case letters, digits, ., -, _), not already used by a curated or approved rule;
  • every regular expression in when compiles; the condition is not empty;
  • finding rules: a title, a why of at least 60 characters, a fix, and at least one https reference for refactor, rewrite and blocker findings;
  • plan rules and failure-rule fixes only use known build-plan keys;
  • failure rules: stage, outcome and a match that does not match an empty log;
  • packages: a valid expression that does not match (almost) any package name.

docs.title: Setting up the internal rules repository
docs.text:
1. Create a private or internal Git repository for the approved rules. It needs one commit (a README is enough); the rules folder is created by the first approval.
  2. Under Admin → Source control, add a write token for that repository's URL. It must be able to push a branch and open a pull request in that one repository: GitHub fine-grained token with Contents and Pull requests: Read and write, GitLab project access token with the role Developer and the scopes api and write_repository, or Azure DevOps Code: Read & write.
  3. Under Admin → Rule review → Internal rules repository, enter the repository URL, the branch the pull requests target (default main) and the folder of the rules in it (default rules). The provider is worked out from the URL for github.com, gitlab.com and gitlab.* hosts, dev.azure.com and *.visualstudio.com; choose it for other servers, and give the API URL of a self-hosted GitHub Enterprise Server or GitLab if it is not at the usual address.
  4. Allow the Git server on Admin → Firewall.

Until all of this is in place, the Rule review page says what is missing, and candidates keep waiting. The settings are in the change history.

Like every source control token, the write token is sealed for the scan worker: the web UI cannot use it. So approving hands the rule to the scan worker, which opens the pull request within a minute, also while a scan is running. The candidate shows the pull request is being opened until then, and approved with the pull request's link after. If it fails (a token without the permission, a repository the token cannot see), the page shows why and the rule waits for a new decision.

The worker clones the internal repository, appends the rule to the right file on a branch containerizer/rule-review-<candidate>, pushes it and opens a pull request that names the reviewer and their note. It contains the rule, not the evidence logs. Safeguards:

  • The repository's visibility is read with the token first: only private or internal repositories (Azure DevOps: a private project) are accepted. A public repository, or one whose visibility the token cannot read, is refused and the rule stays pending.
  • Approved rules are never written into this tool's rules/ folder.
  • Approving the same candidate again after a failure reuses the branch and the open pull request.

Before every scan the worker fetches the repository again, so scans use an approved rule as soon as its pull request is merged. If the Git server cannot be reached, the scan uses the rules it fetched last.

Approved rules are loaded after the curated ones and carry reviewed: {candidate, by, at}. Editing or deleting them by hand in the internal repository later is fine.

docs.title: Sandbox HTTPS
docs.text: Publish the apps that the organization scans deploy to the sandbox cluster over HTTPS, under one wildcard domain that an administrator sets up. Each component that serves HTTP gets its own address, recorded on its generated Ingress (containerizer.io/url).

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A domain for the sandbox apps, for example sandbox.example.com. Give the sandbox a domain of its own: not the domain the admin pages are under. The appliance refuses a domain that contains its own host name, so an app can never share a name with the admin pages. A separate registrable domain (example-sandbox.net) isolates the apps from your other sites best.
  • A wildcard certificate for *.<domain> with its private key, both in PEM:
    • the server certificate first, then its intermediates (the root is optional);
    • RSA with at least 2048 bits, or ECDSA P-256 or P-384;
    • the key without a password (openssl pkey -in key.pem -out plain.pem);
    • valid now. The page warns when it expires within 30 days. Renew it before then and paste the new one.
  • A DNS record that points the wildcard name at the appliance (see DNS).

A certificate from a public CA works in every browser. A certificate from your internal CA works where that CA is trusted. Inside the cluster, the sandbox identity provider's sync job trusts the certificate you set here whoever issued it, also a self-signed one: the appliance publishes its chain (never the key) as ConfigMap containerizer-sandbox-ca in namespace containerizer-idp.

docs.title: Set it up
docs.text:
Admin → Sandbox HTTPS (administrators only): enter the domain as *.sandbox.example.com, paste the certificate chain and the private key, and save. The page checks that the certificate names *.<domain>, matches the key, is valid now, comes with its chain in order and is a server certificate, and says which check failed. The system agent (root) then checks it all again and:

  • writes the certificate and key to /var/lib/containerizer/system/sandbox-https.{crt,key}, the key readable only by root and Caddy;
  • adds a site for *.<domain> to Caddy. Caddy validates the site before it is restarted, so a broken site never takes the admin pages down; if anything fails, every file goes back to what it was;
  • installs the certificate in k3s as Traefik's default certificate (see How it works).

The key is never shown again, and the change history records the domain and the certificate's fingerprint and expiry, never the key or the certificate text. Turn off deletes the certificate and key from the appliance, Caddy and k3s; generated Ingresses stay in the output repository until the next scan. Every organization scan after setup generates the Ingresses.

docs.title: Names
docs.text:
Each component that serves HTTP gets exactly one DNS label under the domain:

Component App (namespace) URL web shop https://web-shop.sandbox.example.com/ shop shop https://shop.sandbox.example.com/ api expense-claims https://api-expense-claims.sandbox.example.com/

The rule is <component>-<app>.<domain>, or just <app>.<domain> when the component has the app's name. Both parts are the Kubernetes names (lower case, letters, digits and hyphens). A name longer than 63 characters is cut and gets 8 hex characters of a SHA-256 of <app>/<component>, so it stays unique and does not change between scans. The names containerizer-edge and containerizer-idp are the appliance's own (Caddy's check of Traefik, the sandbox identity provider): a component that would get one of them gets the hash suffix instead. The name has one label because a wildcard certificate covers exactly one label: *.sandbox.example.com covers web-shop.sandbox.example.com but not web.shop.sandbox.example.com.

Two different apps can end up with the same name, for example component a of app b-c and component a-b of app c. That is rare but possible. The health check then marks the one that does not answer as failing. Rename a component or an app to fix it.

docs.title: DNS
docs.text:
Point the wildcard at the appliance, in the zone of the domain:

*.sandbox.example.com.   300  IN  A      192.0.2.10                 ; the appliance's address
; or, when the appliance has a DNS name:
*.sandbox.example.com.   300  IN  CNAME  containerizer.example.com.
  • Use an AAAA record as well if the appliance has an IPv6 address that clients use.
  • An internal-only sandbox needs the record only in your internal DNS zone. The certificate can still be from a public CA if the domain is one you own publicly.
  • Check it with dig +short web-shop.sandbox.example.com (any name under the domain must return the appliance), then curl -I https://web-shop.sandbox.example.com/.
  • The record is for your users: the appliance itself never needs to resolve these names, and nothing needs to be allowed on the Firewall page.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
browser ──https://web-shop.<domain>──► :443 Caddy (appliance) ──TLS──► Traefik (k3s, 10.43.0.80) ──► Service web ──► pods
             wildcard certificate          *.<domain> site            same certificate, Host routing      namespace shop
  • Port 443 is not opened for this: it is already open. Caddy answers on 443 for the admin pages and picks the site by the name the browser asks for. *.<domain> is a second site next to the admin pages' own name. The firewall's inbound rules stay the same: TCP 22 and 443, nothing else. Port 80 stays closed, so the apps are never reachable over plain HTTP from outside.
  • Caddy terminates TLS with the wildcard certificate and adds Strict-Transport-Security. It removes its Server header and passes the request to Traefik over TLS. It checks Traefik's certificate against the same certificate chain, so the hop from the host into the cluster is encrypted and authenticated too.
  • Traefik, the ingress controller that k3s ships, runs again on the appliance. It is configured by /var/lib/rancher/k3s/server/manifests/containerizer-traefik.yaml, which lives in the OS image. Its Service has the fixed cluster address 10.43.0.80 and no load balancer or host ports, so nothing outside the appliance reaches it directly. Its HTTP entry point only redirects to HTTPS. Its default certificate is the wildcard: TLSStore default points to the TLS Secret containerizer-sandbox-tls in kube-system. It trusts X-Forwarded-For only from the node's bridge address (Caddy), so apps see the client's address.
  • The certificate in k3s goes through External Secrets when External Secrets Operator is installed on the sandbox:
    • The value goes into the sandbox's secret store (Secret containerizer-sandbox-tls in namespace containerizer-secrets, read by ClusterSecretStore app-secrets).
    • kube-system may read that one key only (ServiceAccount app-secrets-reader, a Role with resourceNames).
    • An ExternalSecret in kube-system creates the TLS Secret from it.

Before ESO is installed, the system agent writes the TLS Secret directly. Either way, k3s encrypts Secrets at rest (secrets-encryption: true). containerizer-sandbox runs python -m containerizer.sysagent sandbox-https sync every 2 minutes. That brings k3s in line with the setting, including right after a restart, before Traefik is up. - No key in the apps' namespaces or in Git. The generated Ingress names its host under spec.tls without a secretName, so the ingress controller's default certificate serves it. The private key is never copied into an app's namespace, where the app's own reconciler could read it. The output repository never contains a Secret for it.

docs.title: The generated Ingress
docs.text:
For each component with a Service (web and spa components), <component>/k8s.yaml gets:

apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
  annotations:
    containerizer.io/url: https://web-shop.sandbox.example.com/
    traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.entrypoints: websecure   # HTTPS only on Traefik
    traefik.ingress.kubernetes.io/router.tls: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"              # HTTP -> HTTPS on ingress-nginx
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/force-ssl-redirect: "true"
spec:
  tls:
    - hosts: [web-shop.sandbox.example.com]                        # default certificate: no secretName
  rules:
    - host: web-shop.sandbox.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - {path: /, pathType: Prefix, backend: {service: {name: web, port: {name: http}}}}
  • No ingressClassName is set, so the cluster's default class applies. On k3s that is Traefik.
  • The component's NetworkPolicy already admits its port from other namespaces, so the ingress controller can reach it. The default-deny policy stays.
  • The Flux tenant's admin role covers Ingress in the namespace.
  • On another cluster, give the ingress controller the wildcard certificate as its default. For ingress-nginx, use --default-ssl-certificate. For Traefik, use a default TLSStore. Redirect HTTP to HTTPS at the entry point: the Traefik annotations above put the route on websecure only.
  • The same k8s.yaml also has the component's HTTPRoute for the real environment's Gateway. The sandbox does not apply it: the appliance's Traefik has no Gateway API provider, so the sandbox's copy of each app's Flux Kustomization drops every HTTPRoute (a $patch: delete patch), and the Ingress above serves the sandbox.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: What you see Where to look "Not saved: …" on the page The sentence says which check failed: name, key, order, validity "The last change was not applied" Caddy or the agent refused it: journalctl -u containerizer-sysagent Browser: certificate error The chain is incomplete (paste the intermediates) or the CA is not trusted on that machine 404 at a URL No Ingress with that host: was the app scanned after the domain was set? kubectl get ingress -A 502 at a URL Traefik is not up or does not have the certificate yet: kubectl -n kube-system get pods,tlsstore, journalctl -u containerizer-sandbox

docs.title: Sandbox identity provider
docs.text:
Apps that sign users in usually point at a corporate identity provider: Entra ID, AD FS or an Okta tenant. They can't use it in a sandbox, because nobody will register a lab URL there. So containerizer org deploys its own identity provider into the sandbox cluster. Every component that signs users in with OpenID Connect, SAML 2.0 or WS-Federation is registered there and pointed at it, through configuration only. The app's code is never changed. Test users and groups are created too.

Everything is declarative and lives in the output repository under clusters/sandbox/idp/, next to the apps. Flux applies it with the apps; the secrets come from the secret store (External Secrets).

docs.title: What you get
docs.text:
IdP WSO2 Identity Server 7.3 at https://containerizer-idp.<sandbox domain>/ (console: /console) OpenID Connect issuer https://containerizer-idp.<domain>/oauth2/token, discovery …/oauth2/token/.well-known/openid-configuration SAML 2.0 entity ID https://containerizer-idp.<domain>, metadata …/identity/metadata/saml2 WS-Federation metadata …/wsfed-metadata/FederationMetadata/2007-06/FederationMetadata.xml, passive endpoint …/wsfed Test users alice (group sandbox-admins), bob and carol (sandbox-users), e-mail <user>@<domain> Where the details are shown application page of the results UI (Sign-in in the sandbox), clusters/sandbox/idp/README.md, each component's idp.json

On the appliance, containerizer idp users on the console prints the test users' passwords.

The IdP needs a sandbox domain (--ingress-domain, or the appliance's Sandbox HTTPS setting): issuer, metadata and redirect URLs have to be the same for the browser and for the apps. Without a domain, or with --no-sandbox-idp, nothing changes.

docs.title: Why WSO2 Identity Server
docs.text:
The IdP had to speak all three protocols that .NET line-of-business apps use, with the least to run. That means one process, an embedded database, no licence key, and an open-source licence that lets us ship it.

OIDC SAML 2.0 WS-Federation Licence Notes WSO2 Identity Server 7.3 yes yes yes (passive STS, built in) Apache 2.0 one JVM container, embedded H2, about 1 GiB RAM, REST APIs for everything Keycloak + keycloak-wsfed yes yes extension Apache 2.0 + AGPL-3.0 the WS-Fed extension's last release targets Keycloak 8 (WildFly); it does not load in current Keycloak authentik yes yes Enterprise edition only MIT / commercial the WS-Federation provider is not in the open-source edition Shibboleth IdP (plugin) yes no Apache 2.0 SAML-first; no WS-Federation A .NET IdP (Duende IdentityServer + WS-Fed plugin) yes plugin plugin commercial needs a licence and code we would have to write and maintain

WSO2 is the only option that covers all three protocols out of the box under a permissive licence. It also configures entirely over documented REST APIs (applications, SCIM 2.0 users and groups, claims), which is what makes a declarative, Git-driven setup possible.

docs.title: How a component is detected and configured
docs.text:
Detection rules (rules/38-sandbox-idp.yaml) set facts from packages and code:

Protocol Detected from Settings section looked for in appsettings.json (+ appsettings.Production.json) OpenID Connect Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect, .AddOpenIdConnect(; Entra ID (Microsoft.Identity.Web) is reported a section with ClientId and Authority or MetadataAddress WS-Federation Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.WsFederation, .AddWsFederation( a section with Wtrealm, or MetadataAddress and Realm SAML 2.0 Sustainsys.Saml2.AspNetCore2, ITfoxtec.Identity.Saml2, .AddSaml2( a section named like Saml* with an IdP metadata key

For each section found, the generator:

  1. registers the component at the IdP as <app>--<component>, with its sandbox URL (https://<component>-<app>.<domain>/) as redirect URI, realm or SP entity ID;
  2. overrides the keys of that section with environment variables in the component's k8s.yaml, for example OpenIdConnect__Authority, OpenIdConnect__ClientId, WsFederation__MetadataAddress, WsFederation__Wtrealm, Saml2__IdpMetadata, Saml2__IdpEntityId, Saml2__EntityId. It also sets ASPNETCORE_FORWARDEDHEADERS_ENABLED=true, so the app builds https:// redirect URLs behind Traefik;
  3. gives an OIDC client a secret when the section has a ClientSecret key. The value is made once and kept in the secret store, and the component reads it through its existing <component>-secrets ExternalSecret (remote key <namespace>--<component>, property e.g. OpenIdConnect__ClientSecret). Without a ClientSecret key the client is public with PKCE;
  4. lets the component's pods reach the IdP's public name: a CoreDNS override sends containerizer-idp.<domain> to Traefik in the cluster, and the component's egress policy allows Traefik.

The key names it matches are listed under idp.protocols in the rules file. A component whose sign-in settings are only in code (no section found) is not changed; its idp.json and the application page say so.

Claims, as the apps expect them from Entra ID or AD FS:

  • OIDC: sub, name, given_name, family_name, email, preferred_username, groups;
  • WS-Federation and SAML: the AD FS claim types (…/claims/name, …/emailaddress, …/givenname, …/surname, …/role from groups). The name identifier is the user name.

docs.title: What is in Git
docs.text:
sandbox/idp/
  kustomization.yaml     ConfigMaps from the files below, all resources
  namespace.yaml         containerizer-idp, Pod Security "restricted"
  secrets.yaml           ExternalSecret cz-idp (remote key containerizer-idp--cz-idp) and its store access
  server.yaml            WSO2 (PVC on the data partition, init container, Deployment, Service, Ingress, /wsfed redirect)
  sync.yaml              CronJob cz-idp-sync, every 5 minutes
  network.yaml           default deny; Traefik in, DNS + Traefik out
  dns.yaml               coredns-custom key containerizer-idp.override
  config/                deployment.toml, init.sh, FederationMetadata.xml.in
  sync/                  idp.json (claims, groups, users), apps__<app>--<component>.json, idp_sync.py
  README.md              the IdP's URLs and every registered client

cz-idp-sync applies sync/ through WSO2's REST APIs and can run as often as you like. It creates missing groups and users, creates or updates applications, and deletes the applications it created that are no longer in Git. Applications someone added by hand in the console stay. It uses only the Python standard library, talks to the IdP's public HTTPS URL and never prints a secret.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text:
Nothing secret is in Git. The remote key containerizer-idp--cz-idp in the secret store holds:

Property admin-password the IdP's admin user (console and the sync job) keystore-password the IdP's own key store; the key is generated on first start and never leaves the volume user-<name> test users' passwords client-<app>--<component> OIDC client secrets; the same value is put under the component's own remote key

On the appliance, cz-sandbox runs containerizer idp secrets every 2 minutes. Once Flux has deployed clusters/sandbox/idp, it creates the values that are missing and keeps the ones that exist, through server-side apply with field manager containerizer-idp. With another store (Vault, a cloud secret manager), create these properties there yourself.

docs.title: Limitations and quirks
docs.text:
• One IdP host name per repository. When the domain changes, the IdP starts afresh: new key, empty database, everything rebuilt by the sync job.
  • WS-Federation tokens are SAML 2.0. WSO2's SAML 1.1 tokens use an xsi:type that the .NET SAML 1.1 reader rejects. The metadata therefore advertises /wsfed, which Traefik redirects to WSO2's /passivests with a request for a SAML 2.0 token.
  • WS-Federation: one role value. WSO2 sends a user's groups as one comma-separated role value, so each test user is in one group.
  • .NET 8 and WS-Federation. ASP.NET Core 8's WS-Federation handler depends on Microsoft.IdentityModel 7.1.2, which rejects every token (IDX10204, dotnet/aspnetcore#52099), with AD FS as with this IdP. Rule wsfed-identitymodel-issuer-bug reports it; the fix is a package reference to 7.4.1 or later.
  • OIDC Identity.Name. Like Entra ID, the token has a name claim, not unique_name. An app that reads User.Identity.Name needs TokenValidationParameters.NameClaimType = "name", as it would with Entra ID.
  • Trust of the wildcard certificate. Apps call the IdP's metadata over HTTPS. A certificate from a private CA must be trusted by the app's image too (see the sandbox HTTPS settings).
  • The console is exposed at /console on the sandbox domain, protected by the admin password. The sandbox should only be reachable from your network.
  • Entra ID-only apps (Microsoft.Identity.Web) are reported, not changed: the library expects Entra ID's endpoints.

docs.title: How it was verified
docs.text: The generated clusters/sandbox/idp/ files were run in Docker: the WSO2 container with the same mounts, the init script under a read-only root file system, a TLS proxy in front, and the sync job. Then three unmodified ASP.NET Core 8 apps (examples/sandbox-idp/) signed in as alice in a real browser, configured only with the generated environment variables. OIDC, WS-Federation and SAML 2.0 (Sustainsys) all returned the expected claims. The Traefik redirect middleware and the CoreDNS override are standard k3s resources but have not yet been run in a k3s cluster: they wait for the sandbox cluster CI job.

docs.title: Organization scans
docs.text: An organization scan reads every Git repository of one Azure DevOps organization (or Azure DevOps Server collection), GitHub organization or GitLab group, assesses them, and deploys the ones that are ready to the sandbox cluster. Administrators and operators define scans under Admin → Organization scans: the organization, filters, where images and generated files go, and the days and time (UTC) to run, or Run full scan. The scan worker on the appliance runs them. Before the first scan, an administrator registers a read-only token for the organization and a write token for the output repository (source control tokens), and allows the hosts on Admin → Firewall.

docs.title: Discover first, then scan
docs.text:
A scan runs in two phases, so time is not spent on repositories nobody uses any more:

  1. Discover (on the scan's page) lists the projects, every Git repository in them and each repository's latest commit on its default branch, through the provider's API only. Nothing is cloned, assessed, built or pushed, and the output repository is not touched, so even a large organization is listed in minutes. Discovery also marks the automatic skips the API alone shows (archived, empty, fork, not updated recently, left out by the filter). Every run also reads who committed where in the last six months, for Developers and ownership.
  2. An administrator or operator reviews the result and disables what is deprecated:
  3. Admin → Repositories shows each repository's latest commit. Commit in 6 months lists the ones someone works on and Latest commit first puts them on top (unknown ones last); select them (the box in the header selects every repository listed) and Enable or Disable, with a note. The same two are on the projects page.
  4. Admin → Repositories → Projects lists the projects (Azure DevOps projects, GitLab subgroups) with their number of repositories and latest commit. Disabling a project disables all its repositories, including ones added to it later, and moves them on Admin → Repositories to Hidden: no other view, not even All, lists them (the project's page links to them too). GitHub organizations have no project level: disable the repositories, or pause the scan.

Or work the other way round: set the scan's New repositories to Disabled by default before the first discovery. Every repository it finds then starts disabled (note new repository: disabled by default), and you enable only the ones to process. The setting also applies to repositories added to the organization later; repositories already found keep theirs. 3. Run full scan (or the schedule) then processes only the enabled repositories. Disabled ones are never cloned, and one that was deployed before leaves the sandbox at that run.

Disabled repositories and projects are also hidden from the results pages: the overview, the trends and the application pages leave out the applications that come from them (they stay on the admin pages). Enabling them again brings their results back at once. Repositories the scan skips automatically are not hidden. Every change to a project or repository, with who made it and the note, is in Admin → Change history (Projects, Repositories) and on the project's or repository's own page.

The sandbox of one application can be turned off without disabling its repository: Admin → Applications → the application → Sandbox → Disable the sandbox (administrators, and the product owners of its product). It is on by default.

  • Off: nothing of the application runs in the sandbox cluster. That includes its original components and its Make it A copies. The scans still assess it, so its results stay current, but they build and deploy nothing of it. New Make it A patches for it are made and verified, but not deployed.
  • The files stay: its folders in the output repository and its images in the appliance's registry are kept. clusters/sandbox/ leaves them out, so Flux removes them from the cluster.
  • On again: clusters/sandbox/ lists them again, and Flux deploys the same manifests with the same images (the patched ones of a Make it A copy too), without a build. The next scan of its repository then builds the original as usual.

The LLM queue runner applies a change within a few minutes: it regenerates clusters/sandbox/ in every output repository and commits it. A scan also leaves the application out when it writes clusters/sandbox/. The change history records who switched it and when. A Make it A copy stays until a scan assesses newer code of its application, also while the sandbox is off.

docs.title: Debug mode: a container that crashes at start
docs.text:
A container that crashes when it starts is hard to look into: there is nothing running to kubectl exec into, the generated images have no shell (chiseled and distroless), and an ephemeral debug container (kubectl debug, kubemg's debug session) only sees the processes and files of a container that is running. First read what the application wrote before it stopped: kubectl -n <namespace> logs <pod> --previous, or the Sandbox cluster details on the application's results page.

When that is not enough, an administrator turns on debug mode for the application: Admin → Applications → the application → Sandbox → Turn debug mode on.

Within a few minutes the application's pods in the sandbox restart and stay running without starting the application:

  • The container runs sleep in place of the application, with one replica and without probes. Everything else is the application's own: its image, user, environment variables, mounted settings and secrets, read-only root filesystem and network policies. What you see is what the application starts in.
  • /cz-debug holds a static Bash and the BusyBox tools (ls, cat, vi, ps, env, wget, nc, nslookup, ...). They are copied in by an init container; nothing is installed into the image and nothing is built again.

Open a shell in a pod, as root on the appliance or from kubemg, and start the application by hand to see it fail:

kubectl -n <namespace> get pods
kubectl -n <namespace> exec -it <pod> -- /cz-debug/shell
/cz-debug/start        # the application's own start command, in the foreground ($CZ_DEBUG_START)

/cz-debug/shell is Bash with the tools on PATH; it prints the start command (the image's ENTRYPOINT and CMD with the arguments of the Deployment). Start it as often as you like, with other arguments or environment variables.

  • Only the sandbox: debug mode is a patch in clusters/sandbox/flux/apps of the output repository. The application's own folder, and with it the other clusters of the output repository, never see it.
  • Off again: Turn debug mode off; within a few minutes the pods start the application again.
  • While it is on, the sandbox check reads the application as healthy, because its pods run: the page's Debug mode mark is what says the application itself is not started. Scheduled jobs (CronJobs) are not put in debug mode.
  • The change history records who switched it and when. The tools image is <registry>/cz-debug-tools, made on the appliance from the static bash-static and busybox of its OS image and pushed to the appliance's registry; a machine without those two programs has no debug mode (the scan's log says so).

docs.title: An application's own output repository
docs.text:
What works in the sandbox can be the starting point of the application's real deployment. Admin → Applications → the application → Output repository (administrators) gives it a repository of its own, one with a write token under Admin → Source control, a branch, and a folder in it (deploy by default). Its files are then moved there once:

  1. Within a few minutes the LLM queue runner copies the application's folder from the scan's output repository to that folder, with its Flux files pointed at the new repository, branch and folder, and commits it there (moved here from ...). containerizer.json says where it came from, and MOVED.md says what follows. The folder must be empty or missing: one with other files in it is not overwritten (the page says so, and the runner tries again every 10 minutes). Until a scan has deployed the application, the move waits.
  2. In the scan's output repository, the application's folder becomes a stub: containerizer.json (with moved_to), the Flux tenant and sync files, pointed at the application's repository, each component's idp.json and k8s.yaml, and a README. clusters/sandbox/ still lists it, so the sandbox deploys it from its own repository: what its team changes there runs in the sandbox too.
  3. The page shows Moved, with the repository, the folder, the commit and when.

From then on the files are its team's. The scans still assess the application, so its results stay current, but they do not generate, build or deploy it, and they never change or remove its stub (the repository's state says Assessed: its files are in its own output repository). Its Make it A copies are still deployed beside it, in the scan's output repository, as before.

The sandbox reads the application's repository with a read token registered for the organization it is in, or else with its write token. On the appliance the LLM queue runner hands it to cz-sandbox (/var/lib/containerizer/refactor/sandbox-git/<namespace>, readable by the runner and root only), which puts it in the namespace's key of the secret store. Allow the repository's host on Admin → Firewall if it is another one.

Back to the scan's output repository (on the same page) undoes it: the runner removes the stub, so the application leaves the sandbox, and the next scan of its repository generates and deploys it in the scan's output repository again. The copy in its own repository stays. To move it somewhere else, go back first. Every change is in the application's change history.

Scan now, on a project's or repository's page or for the ones selected in the lists, runs a full scan of only those, outside the schedule, for example after a fix was pushed. The other repositories keep their results from the last full run. A selected one that is disabled (by an administrator, or as a new repository disabled by default) is enabled first, with the note enabled by Scan now; automatic skips (a Dockerfile, no application code) stay until you Enable it. A run of the scan that is already queued or running has to finish first.

Discovery can be run again at any time, for example before a scheduled run, to see the new projects and repositories first. Scheduled runs are always full scans; new repositories found by them are processed in that run unless their project is disabled.

docs.title: External application IDs (metadata.json)
docs.text:
A repository can name the application it belongs to in another system (a CMDB, a portfolio or service catalogue) in a metadata.json at its root:

{
  "applicationId": "3f2b8c1e-5d6a-4b7c-9e0f-1a2b3c4d5e6f"
}

Discovery reads it through the provider's API, disabled repositories too, without a clone; the full scan reads it again after the clone (a GUID's braces are dropped; letters, digits and . _ : -, at most 100 characters). It is kept with the repository; a repository that no longer has the file loses it at its next discovery or scan. Each application has an External ID (Admin → Applications → the application, administrators). Admin → Applications → External IDs lists the IDs repositories declare that no application has yet, with a proposal for each: Link it to the repository's application (one per application of a split repository), or Add application for a repository no scan assessed (an application for the whole repository, without results until a scan assesses it). Link proposals links every repository that has one application without an ID. The change history records every ID set.

docs.title: Forget an application
docs.text:
Admin → Applications → the application → Forget application (administrators; type the application's name to confirm) deletes everything recorded about it: its assessments and findings, components, sandbox checks, LLM jobs and Make it A orders, LLM usage, egress and link decisions, dev database and sandbox database edits. Its repository is disabled (the note says who forgot it), and a scan of that repository is queued: as for any disabled repository, it removes the application's files from the output repository and the sandbox prunes its namespace. When a scan of the organization is running, the next run does it.

To start over with it, enable the repository again on Admin → Repositories and scan it: it is assessed as a new application. The change history keeps the deletion. On the appliance its secret values go too: its OpenBao entries (apps/<namespace>/...), policy and the values copied to the secret store, once its namespace is gone from the sandbox (OpenBao).

docs.title: What happens to each repository
docs.text:
1. Listed through the provider's API, including private and internal repositories the token can read. Every run (discovery or full) lists the organization again: new projects and repositories are added (a full run processes the new repositories in that run), renamed ones are followed by the provider's id, and ones that are gone are marked removed. Repositories an administrator disabled, or whose project is disabled, stop here.
  2. Skipped automatically when there is nothing to do, with the reason shown on Admin → Repositories (automatic skips).
  3. Cloned shallow (default branch only, no tags, submodules, symlinks or LFS objects). Clones are kept on the appliance, and later runs only fetch the newest commit and reset the work tree to it.
  4. Assessed, built and run: every feasible component is built and run hardened, failures are matched and fixed where a rule knows how, and the application is assessed again (how it works). With Ask the LLM on, the LLM is consulted about what the rules are unsure of. Every assessment is stored, A or not, so the results pages and trends cover the whole organization.
  5. Selected: a component is deployed only when it is a server component (web, worker, console, SPA) rated A on its own (including the stateless requirement), a Linux image can be generated for it, and it built and ran in the verification (or ran and only lacked its database or broker).
  6. Security gate: lint, image build and a run with the pod's security context (security gate); the vulnerability scan only with scan.enabled (off by default), and its findings are reported, not a reason to drop the component (scan.block_deploy). A component that fails is dropped, and the rest are gated again so the namespace, network policies and GitOps files cover only what is deployed.
  7. Images pushed to the appliance's own registry as localhost:5000/sandbox/<app>/<component>:<tag> and :git-<commit>, which the sandbox cluster pulls from without credentials. The tag is 1.<yyyymmdd>.<hhmm> of the run (semver, so Flux image automation can follow it). Scans have no registry setting: an external registry is for the build pipelines generated for your real environment, not for the sandbox.
  8. Committed to the output repository (chosen in the scan's settings among the repositories with a write token under Source control; none: the results stay on the worker) after every repository, so a long run can be followed and survives interruptions.

A repository that is skipped or has no A component loses its folder in the output repository, so the sandbox stops deploying it. A repository that fails keeps its previous folder and is reported as failed.

A scan runs at most once at a time, and a paused scan does not run at all. If the worker was down at the scheduled time, the scan runs once when it is back. Cancel stops a running scan at once (the worker sees it within a few seconds): no further repository is started, its LLM calls stop (the connection to the LLM server is closed, so a self-hosted LLM stops generating), and the repositories in progress are ended with every tool they started (git, builds). Those are not recorded: they keep the result of their previous scan, and the next run scans them again. Stopping the worker (a restart, an update) still lets the repositories in progress finish the step they are on. A scan that has run cannot be deleted (its history is kept): pause it.

Repositories in parallel (the scan's settings, 1 to 8, default 1): how many repositories a full scan or Scan now processes at the same time. The assessment is CPU-bound, so each repository gets its own process and the scan uses that many CPU cores. Results are committed to the output repository one at a time, in the order the repositories finish. Each one also needs its own memory (about 1 GB, more with Build and run) and disk space, and with Ask the LLM each asks the LLM on its own, so a self-hosted LLM gets up to that many requests at once (give llama.cpp that many slots, --parallel). Start with the number of CPU cores minus one, and lower it if the machine runs short of memory.

docs.title: Progress of a run
docs.text:
Each full run has a Progress page (the link under its status in the scan's Runs table, or next to the progress count in the scan list). It reloads itself every 10 seconds while the run is in progress, and shows:

  • In progress: each repository being scanned, the step it is on (Cloning or Pulling, Looking for application code, Assessing (rules), LLM review, Verifying: build and run, Assessing again, Generating files, Development database, Security gate: build, scan, run, Building images, Pushing images, Writing the output files), how long it has been on that step and on the repository, and what it waits for inside the step (the LLM call, the components in the security gate). A step that has taken more than 15 minutes is marked slow.
  • The pace (the average time a repository has taken so far) and an estimated end at that pace, and what the run as a whole does between repositories (listing the repositories, committing to the output repository, checking the sandbox).
  • Where the time goes: each step's total time over the repositories of the run, its share, and its average per repository, so you can see whether a slow scan waits for the LLM, for builds and verification, for the security gate or for git. With Repositories in parallel above 1, the times are summed over the processes.
  • Finished most recently and Slowest: the repositories of the run with their result and how long each took.

Typical fixes when one step dominates: LLM review — queue the LLM reviews (LLM reviews: Queued) so the scan uses the rules only, or give a self-hosted LLM more slots; Verifying and Security gate — scan more repositories in parallel if the machine has the cores and memory; Cloning — the first run clones everything, later runs only pull. The Grafana dashboard has the same run over time.

docs.title: Files from the secret store
docs.text: An application may read files that are not in its repository and must not be in its image, such as a certificate with its private key. On the repository's page (Admin → Repositories → the repository → Settings), Files from the secret store with a folder (/secrets by default; not /app, /tmp or a system folder) makes every component of the repository mount its Secret <component>-files there, read-only and optional: every key is a file, its value the file in base64. On the appliance the files are an OpenBao entry, apps/<namespace>/<component>-files (OpenBao); in another cluster, the remote key <namespace>--<component>-files of its secret store, which has to exist (empty or not) before Flux's first sync. The scan points every setting whose value names a key or certificate file (.pfx, .p12, .pem, .key, .crt, .cer, .jks, .keytab; relative or a Windows path, not a URL or a release-pipeline placeholder) at that file name in the folder ("CertificatePath": "certs\\app.pfx" becomes /secrets/app.pfx): add the file under that name. Nothing to edit by hand, so a scan again keeps it. The next scan of the repository uses the setting. Without it, a .pfx or .p12 next to the code is still mounted where the app reads it.

docs.title: Repositories with several applications
docs.text:
A scan assesses each repository as one application. A mono-repo that holds several applications, for example one folder per application under apps/ or scenarios/, would then get one rating for all of them. On the repository's page (Admin → Repositories → the repository), Applications in this repository → One application per folder matching a folder pattern relative to the repository (scenarios/*, services/*, teams/*/apps/*) makes each matching folder its own application:

  • its own assessment, rating and results page (the application's source path is the folder), owner and product mapping;
  • its own sandbox namespace <repository app>-<folder> and its own folder in the output repository, <Organization>/<Project>/<Repository>@<folder>;
  • the repository's row sums them up: deployed when one of them is, the best rating, and a table of the folders with their results on the repository's page.

The repository is still cloned once, and enabling or disabling it applies to all its applications. Folders that stop matching leave the sandbox at the next scan, and switching back to The whole repository is one application removes the per-folder ones. The applications assessed before the change stay in the history: hide the old whole-repository one on its application page. Who changed the setting, and when, is in the change history.

A repository assessed as one application that looks like several (at least three folders at the same level that each have their own solution, package.json, pom.xml, build.gradle, go.mod or pyproject.toml, and hold nearly all of the repository's) gets a note on its page with the pattern filled in. Nothing is split automatically: it changes the applications' identities in the results, so an administrator decides.

The command line does the same with containerizer org ... --split '<project>/<repository>=<pattern>' (GitHub has no projects: _/<repository>).

docs.title: Automatic skips
docs.text:
Automatic skip Reason shown, for example Has a Dockerfile found src/Api/Dockerfile: the team already containerizes it. Enabled, it is moved from Docker Swarm, Compose, Nomad, Azure Container Apps or ECS to Kubernetes (platform migrations) No application code 14 files (.md 9, .yml 3, .json 2), no source code: documentation, configuration, pipelines, SQL or scripts Language not supported Ruby (32 files), but no project the tool can build (...) Nothing to deploy only library, test: 3 projects, nothing that runs on its own Not updated recently no update since 2026-01-07: no commit on the default branch for the scan's skip repositories not updated for days (default 183) Archived, Empty, Fork as the provider reports (forks only with skip forks) Left out by the filter the scan's include/exclude regular expressions on project/repository

Automatic skips are checked again at every run, so a repository that gets new commits or loses its Dockerfile is processed again by itself. Archived, empty, filtered and stale repositories are decided from the provider's API without fetching anything. An administrator can Enable a repository (process it even though a skip applies), Disable it (never fetch it; it also leaves the sandbox at the next run and its results are hidden from the results pages) or set it back to Automatic, with a note in the change history. A disabled project overrides the settings of its repositories.

docs.title: Output repository layout
docs.text:
cluster/                     the cluster-level kit for every app, once: secret store, signed images (Kyverno), audit policy
<Organization>/
  README.md                  every repository: status, rating, deployed and excluded components with reasons
  org-run.json               the same as data (merged across runs)
  <Project>/<Repository>/    one application (namespace <app>)
    kustomization.yaml       namespace, security policies, components, image tags
    namespace.yaml security.yaml HARDENING.md SECURITY.md MIGRATION.md
    containerizer.json       source URL, commit, images, digests, verification
    gitops/flux/             tenant.yaml, git/sync.yaml, oci/, image automation
    <component>/             Dockerfile, Dockerfile.dockerignore, plan.json, and its objects: a file per kind
                             (deployment.yaml, service.yaml, settings.yaml, ...) and the kustomization.yaml listing them
    gitops/sandbox/          the sandbox's copy of gitops/flux, with its patch (clusters.md)
    pipeline/<provider>/     the image build pipeline for the application's own repository (build-pipelines.md)
    make-it-a.patch          while a Make it A copy runs here in place of the scan's output (refactoring.md)
sandbox/
  README.md namespaces.txt
  flux/bootstrap.yaml        GitRepository + root Kustomization
  idp/                       sandbox identity provider, when a component signs users in
clusters/<cluster>/          development, acceptance, production: the same apps with each cluster's own app list,
                             registry, image promotion and settings (clusters.md)

The project folder is the Azure DevOps project, _ for GitHub (no projects), or the GitLab subgroup path with -- for /. The app name (Kubernetes namespace and image path) is <project>-<repository> in DNS form, prefixed with app- when it would be a reserved namespace, shortened with a hash past 63 characters, and given a hash suffix when two repositories would map to the same name. Reserved are the cluster's, the platform's and Containerizer's own namespaces: default, kube-*, openshift*, flux-system, external-secrets, containerizer-*, cert-manager and other common add-ons (generate.RESERVED_NAMESPACES). So a repository called kube-system or external-secrets (a fork of External Secrets Operator, say) is deployed as app-kube-system / app-external-secrets, never into the real one; the same goes for a folder of a split repository (flux + system) and for containerizer generate. The sandbox never deploys an app folder that names a reserved namespace, whatever made it.

docs.title: The sandbox cluster
docs.text:
The appliance's k3s cluster deploys what the scans commit. Fill in /etc/containerizer/sandbox.env (output repository URL, branch and a read-only token for it, separate from the scan's write token) and allow the Git server on Admin → Firewall. Every 2 minutes the appliance then:

  • puts the read-only token in the secret store for Flux's root sync and for every app namespace listed in clusters/sandbox/namespaces.txt;
  • creates the root GitRepository and Kustomization of clusters/sandbox/flux/. The root creates each tenant (namespace with Pod Security "restricted", ServiceAccounts, a namespace-only RoleBinding, read access to its own secret store keys), and each app then reconciles as its own ServiceAccount;
  • keeps the Flux webhook up to date (below).

Polling and the webhook. Flux polls the output repository: the root sync and each app's own GitRepository every 5 minutes. So that a deploy does not wait for the next poll, cz-sandbox keeps a Flux Receiver (notification-controller, type generic) named containerizer-sandbox in flux-system that names the root sync's GitRepository and every GitRepository containerizer generated in the app namespaces. After each push to the output repository (a scan, a Make it A variant, a connectivity or link decision, an application moved to its own output repository, the sandbox switches, the configuration backup) the scan worker and the LLM queue runner call it, and Flux fetches the new commit at once. Its token is made once and kept in the secret store (flux-system--cz-webhook, read by the ExternalSecret containerizer-sandbox-webhook); the URL, the webhook-receiver Service's cluster address and the path Flux derives from the token, is in /run/containerizer/flux-webhook (root:containerizer, 0640). The receiver is reached from the appliance itself only: nothing publishes it.
