A call that fails (Flux restarting, the receiver not ready yet after the first boot) is logged once and never fails the push; polling picks the commit up as before.

On another cluster (the generated gitops/ or clusters/sandbox/README.md), Flux polls unless you add a receiver yourself. To deploy on each push, create a Receiver of your Git server's type for the app's GitRepository and point the repository's push webhook at it (Flux webhook receivers):

apiVersion: notification.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1
kind: Receiver
metadata: {name: <namespace>, namespace: <namespace>}
spec:
  type: github                 # gitlab, bitbucket, ... ; Azure DevOps: generic (a service hook to the URL)
  events: [push]
  secretRef: {name: <namespace>-webhook}   # key `token`: an ExternalSecret from the store, never in Git
  resources:
    - {apiVersion: source.toolkit.fluxcd.io/v1, kind: GitRepository, name: <namespace>}

The webhook URL is https://<receiver address> + the Receiver's .status.webhookPath; expose the notification-controller's webhook-receiver Service through your Ingress for the Git server only, and set the webhook's secret to the same token.

Nothing in the output repository is a Secret: credentials are ExternalSecrets (secrets). Apps that need a database, cache or object storage get one from the lab services, or a restored copy of their development database. Apps that sign users in with OpenID Connect, SAML 2.0 or WS-Federation are pointed at the sandbox identity provider. kubectl as root on the appliance shows the result. To deploy the same output repository to another cluster, follow clusters/sandbox/README.md in it (Flux).

Health in the sandbox. Each app's Flux Kustomization waits for its Deployments and StatefulSets and for the ExternalSecrets of the Secrets a pod cannot start without (Data Protection keys, the image pull credential), not for every object: the ExternalSecrets of a component's secret settings, secret files and keytabs read remote keys that nobody fills in the sandbox, and the workloads' references to them are optional. clusters/sandbox/flux/apps sets this (wait: false with healthChecks) on the sandbox's copy only; the app folder's own gitops/flux keeps wait: true, so a real cluster waits for every secret (secrets).

The sandbox check. At the end of each scan, while the sandbox is connected to the output repository, the worker waits (up to 15 minutes) for Flux to apply the scan's commit and reads back every component's rollout, readiness, restarts and Warning events, as the read-only verifier account cz-sandbox keeps up to date. The result is the Sandbox cluster column and details on each application's results page, and clusters/sandbox/HEALTH.md in the output repository. Stop on a running scan ends the wait; the check is then not recorded. An application whose latest check found a component failing or not ready is read again every 10 minutes (for 14 days): once it is healthy, say after someone filled its secret values in OpenBao, a new check says so, without another scan. One still failing keeps the scan's diagnosis. HEALTH.md changes with the next scan.

docs.title: The LLM queue
docs.text:
With Ask the LLM on, LLM reviews chooses when the LLM is asked:

  • Inline (the default): during the scan, as before.
  • Queued: the scan asks the LLM nothing and the rules decide; the component reviews wait in the LLM queue and their answers are used by the next scan of each repository (queued LLM reviews: what is queued, in what order, and how an answer takes effect). Use it with a slow self-hosted LLM. LLM-heavy mode needs inline reviews.

Admin → LLM queue (administrators and operators) shows:

  • the jobs waiting, in the order the runner takes them: the repository and component, why it is queued (uncertain, or a second opinion on the rules' blocker or rewrite verdict) and the estimated tokens and time; for a running job, what it does now: Asking an LLM (named) only while one of its calls is answered, Waiting for an LLM while a call waits for a free request, else Running with its progress (generating, verifying, deploying). Top, Up, Down and Bottom move a job; new jobs still go in by their priority. Skip takes one out of the queue. Cancel stops a running job: the runner sees it within a few seconds, its LLM calls stop at once (the connection is closed, so a self-hosted LLM stops generating), a refactoring order does not go on to its build, the sandbox or the next order of an LLM-heavy chain, and the job is recorded as skipped (cancelled by …); Requeue starts it again;
  • at the top, the totals: jobs waiting and running, by kind (uncertain, second opinion); their estimated tokens in and out; the LLM time they need at the measured speed with the parallel requests set, for example ~7 h 20 min of LLM time (3 in parallel), and when they would all be done if the queue ran without a pause; what the estimate is learned from; and, outside the hours, when they next start;
  • the finished jobs: each answer (verdict and confidence, the reasoning and the question on the job's page), with the tokens and time it really took, failures (a job is tried three times, five minutes apart and more, before it fails) and skipped jobs. Requeue puts a failed or skipped one back;
  • repositories whose reviews are all answered since their last scan, with Re-scan now: a full scan of only that repository, so the answers apply without waiting for the schedule;
  • the settings: Paused; the days and hours (UTC) the runner may start jobs (no day selected: every day; From and To empty: all day; 22:00 to 06:00 runs past midnight, and the night belongs to the day it started); Only when idle: no organization scan running and the machine's 1-minute load average per CPU below the limit (0: the load is not looked at); Parallel requests, as many as the worker's own LLM answers at once (a registered LLM has its own, see several LLMs at once); Jobs at once, how many jobs the runner works on at the same time, asking an LLM or building and verifying (0, the default: every LLM request at once plus one); and the built-in LLM's order and calls up to beside the registered LLMs (the appliance only). The page lists the LLMs in their order with the requests in progress on each (Asking now): each LLM call of a job goes to the first that takes its size and has a free request, and gives it back once answered, so a job that builds or deploys holds no LLM (how jobs and LLM requests are scheduled). The runner looks at the settings before each job; a job it has started finishes.
  • Approval: which kinds of job wait for an administrator's approval (component reviews, refactoring orders, egress reviews and link reviews; all of them by default), and the rules that approve some by themselves: Approve automatically under a number of estimated input tokens (0: none, every job of the ticked kinds waits), while fewer jobs are queued or running than a number (0: any length of the queue). A small job that arrives when the queue is full waits, and is approved by itself, highest priority first, as the queue gets shorter; a big one always waits for an administrator. Each automatic approval says so on the job (automatic: estimated under 2,000 tokens and the queue had room). Approve all approves every waiting job.
  • Reject automatically after a number of hours (0: never): a job waiting for approval or queued that long (counted from its approval when it had one) is skipped, with the reason. Requeue starts its wait again.

After a button on a job (move, skip, approve, reject, requeue) the page opens at that job, or at the one that takes its place, not at the top.

Every change to a job (queued, moved, skipped, requeued, answered, failed) and to the settings is in Admin → Change history.

Estimates. Each queued job's input tokens are estimated from the length of its question (3.5 characters a token to begin with) and its output from the answers before it (1,500 tokens to begin with). From every answer the runner learns, separately for each LLM (server and model): the characters per token of its tokenizer, the answer length of each kind of job, and its speed (prompt and generation tokens per second when the server reports its timings, as llama.cpp does, otherwise tokens per second from the time each answer took). Each figure is a moving average that gives the newest answer a weight of 0.2. The queue's time is the sum of the jobs' times divided by the parallel requests; the speeds are as measured with the parallel requests of the time, so this is a rough estimate. It does not include waiting for the hours or for the machine to be idle. Until an LLM has answered once, the page says time: learning.

The runner is containerizer llm-queue, a process of its own next to the scan worker (containerizer-llm-queue on the appliance). It uses the worker's database login, opens the LLM registered under Source control & LLM with the worker's key (or uses the worker's environment settings), writes into the worker's answer cache, and serves its metrics on port 9465: the jobs by status, kind and reason, the oldest waiting job, the estimated tokens and LLM time waiting, jobs finished, and the LLM usage of its answers (feature assessment-queued). On another machine, give it the worker's settings and the same CONTAINERIZER_AI_CACHE (shared), or rely on the next scan finding the answer in the queue; monitoring/systemd/containerizer-llm-queue.service is a unit for it. A job it is asking when it stops goes back to the queue.

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
• Each token is only sent where it belongs: the read-only token to its own server's API and its own organization's clone URLs, the write token only to push the output repository, which is never scanned (how the tokens are protected). Git gets each token scoped to one repository URL, not in .git/config, the process list or clone URLs.
  • Clones are made with symlinks off, no submodules, and the file/ext transports disabled. The scanner never executes scanned code, but building and running the images does execute the repositories' build steps. That is why the appliance is a dedicated machine with an outbound allow-list for every build.
  • Registry credentials are written only to a temporary Docker config (mode 700) for the run.
  • Nothing secret is written to the output repository, and build logs are not copied there.

docs.title: Metrics and Grafana
docs.text:
The worker exports Prometheus metrics about the scans, the worker process and the machine, and the appliance's Grafana (https://<appliance>/grafana/, linked as Grafana ↗ on the admin pages) has a dashboard of them: scans running and waiting, time since the last successful run, progress of the current run, repositories by state (disabled_admin counts repositories disabled directly or through their project) and latest result, time per repository, clones and pulls, pushed images, LLM usage (calls, tokens and estimated cost by repository and feature, platform migrations), the LLM queue (jobs waiting, the oldest one, the runner open or waiting, jobs answered and failed), and the machine's CPU, memory, disk and network.

Alert rules are included (monitoring/prometheus/containerizer-alerts.yml): worker down, run failed, no successful run for 8 days, runs not starting, repositories failing, disk over 90 %, memory low. The metric names are listed in containerizer/metrics.py.

docs.title: Sign-in and roles
docs.text:
The web UI signs people in with your identity provider over OpenID Connect (Microsoft Entra ID, Okta, Keycloak, Google Workspace, ...). The admin pages, the System and Firewall pages and the API appear only once sign-in is set up. Sign-in and roles are the only web UI settings that are not on the admin pages: they are in /etc/containerizer/web.env on the appliance (mode 600), because they decide who may use the admin pages in the first place. Restart the web UI after a change (systemctl restart containerizer-web).

For development without an identity provider (never on the appliance, where it is refused), see admin pages without sign-in.

docs.title: Register the app at your identity provider
docs.text:
The redirect URI is https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>/auth/callback, where CZ_HOSTNAME is the name set in appliance.env (first boot). Then fill in:

Variable Meaning CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_ISSUER Issuer URL, e.g. https://login.microsoftonline.com/<tenant id>/v2.0 (Entra ID), https://<org>.okta.com, https://<keycloak>/realms/<realm> CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_CLIENT_ID / CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET The app registration. The secret is optional (PKCE is always used); prefer a confidential client. CONTAINERIZER_ADMINS Who is an administrator (see the rules below). CONTAINERIZER_OIDC_SCOPES Optional. Default openid profile email. CONTAINERIZER_PUBLIC_URL Optional. Default https://<CZ_HOSTNAME>.

Allow the identity provider's host on Admin → Firewall (or in egress.json before the first sign-in, e.g. login.microsoftonline.com): the web UI fetches its signing keys.

Microsoft Entra ID: register a web application (App registrations) with the redirect URI above and add a client secret. Roles can come from groups, app roles or both:

  • Groups: under Token configuration, add a groups claim (security groups, or only the groups assigned to the application) for the ID token. The claim holds the groups' object IDs, so the rules are group:<object id>. For a user in more than 200 groups Entra ID leaves the claim out of the token (it points to Microsoft Graph instead, which the web UI does not query), so such a user matches no group: rule; "Groups assigned to the application" avoids that.
  • App roles: create app roles (for example Containerizer.Admin, Containerizer.Operator, Containerizer.Read, Finance.Owner) and assign users or groups to them under Enterprise applications. The rules are role:<value>: readable names instead of IDs, and no group limit.

Assigning groups to an application (for app roles, or "Groups assigned to the application") needs Entra ID P1 or P2. Entra ID does not send email_verified, so email: and domain: rules never match there.

docs.title: Roles
docs.text:
The operator, product owner and viewer roles come from one of two places, chosen with CONTAINERIZER_ROLE_SOURCE:

  • env (the default): allow-lists in web.env, described in this section.
  • ui: an administrator gives them to people on Admin → Users and roles (below).

The two are never mixed. Administrators always come from CONTAINERIZER_ADMINS, in both.

Each role is an allow-list of rules, comma separated:

Rule Matches group:<id> a group claim (Entra ID: the group's object id) role:<name> an app role email:<address>, domain:<e-mail domain> the e-mail address, only when the provider marks it verified (email_verified) sub:<subject id> one user Role Variable Can Admin CONTAINERIZER_ADMINS Everything, including business units, application tags, the sandbox databases, Source control & LLM, Rule review, Lab services, Firewall, System and the access log. Operator CONTAINERIZER_OPERATORS Read everything, including the change history. Run and schedule organization scans (discovery and full scans), enable and disable projects and repositories, order and pause the LLM queue and set when it runs, order refactoring patches of B-rated applications and download them (Admin → Refactoring), upload dev database backups, browse and fix the sandbox databases, tag applications. Cannot change the mapping. Product owner CONTAINERIZER_PRODUCT_OWNERS Read everything, including the change history. Map applications and change their display name, owner, description, hidden flag and sandbox switch, and change their products, but only within their scope (below). Viewer CONTAINERIZER_VIEWERS Read the results pages. Only matters when sign-in for the results pages is on.

Applications not yet mapped to a product appear on the front page for administrators only.

Refactoring patches contain source code: product owners and viewers see an order's status on the application's results page, but not the patch, and only administrators and operators see the Make it A button (who can order one).

Nobody outside these lists gets into /admin. One person can have several roles; admin includes all of them. The roles are enforced by the web UI and the API, and every change in the change history records the role it was made in.

Product owner scopes. Each entry is <rules>=<scopes>; entries are separated by ;, rules and scopes within an entry by ,:

CONTAINERIZER_PRODUCT_OWNERS="role:Finance.Owner=bu:Finance; group:6f1c...=product:Billing,product:#12"
  • bu:<name>: a business unit and every product in it, now and later. With a business unit in scope, the owner can also add products to it and delete empty ones.
  • product:<name>: one product and its applications.
  • bu:#<id> / product:#<id>: the same by id (the number in the admin page address). An id keeps working after a rename; a name scope does not. Names are matched without regard to case.

A product owner can take over unmapped applications by mapping them to one of their products, and move their applications between their products. Everything outside their scope shows as view only. Scopes are checked on every request, so a product moved to another business unit leaves (or joins) that owner's scope at once.

docs.title: Roles on the admin pages
docs.text:
With CONTAINERIZER_ROLE_SOURCE=ui administrators give the viewer, operator and product owner roles on Admin → Users and roles instead of in web.env:

CONTAINERIZER_ROLE_SOURCE=ui
CONTAINERIZER_ADMINS=group:6f1c...            # still required: the only way to be an administrator
CONTAINERIZER_VIEWERS_REQUIRED=true           # optional: the results pages need sign-in and a role

CONTAINERIZER_OPERATORS, CONTAINERIZER_PRODUCT_OWNERS and CONTAINERIZER_VIEWERS must then be empty or unset: the web UI does not start, and names them, if one is set. Nobody can be made an administrator on the page (the database refuses it too).

  • Who is listed. Everyone who has signed in, with the e-mail address or user name and the time of their last sign-in. Administrators show as admin (from configuration): that is whether CONTAINERIZER_ADMINS matched at their last sign-in, and it cannot be changed here.
  • Giving a role. Choose the person, the role and, for a product owner, one or more business units and products (a business unit covers all its products, as bu: does above), and optionally a note. For someone who has not signed in yet, type their e-mail address instead.
  • Matching. Roles follow the person's account at the identity provider, its stable subject (sub), not their e-mail address. A role given to an address waits until someone signs in with that address verified by the provider (email_verified; Entra ID, which does not send it, the address or user name the change history shows). It then belongs to that person's account; whoever gets the address later does not get the role.
  • Effect. Roles are read from the database on every request, so a removed role is gone at the person's next click, without signing out.
  • History. Every role given or removed is in the change history (Users and roles), with the administrator who did it and the note.
  • API. A person's access token gets the operator and product owner roles of the account with the token's sub. With Entra ID, where sub differs from one application to another, that needs the API's audience to be the sign-in app registration; otherwise use API keys. API clients (CONTAINERIZER_API_CLIENTS) and API keys are unchanged.

With CONTAINERIZER_ROLE_SOURCE=env the page is read-only: it lists the rules of each role from web.env.

docs.title: Application tags
docs.text:
Administrators and operators tag applications on their results page: Tags, under the owner and the source, takes a comma-separated list such as customer-facing, pci, wave 1 and Save tags replaces the application's tags (an empty list removes them). Product owners and viewers see the tags but cannot change them. A tag is up to 40 letters, digits, spaces and - _ . + / & #; an application has up to 20. Tags are compared without regard to case, so PCI and pci are one tag, and the change history records every change.

Containerizer adds automatic tags from the assessment: stateful on an application with a server component that keeps its own data (it runs with a persistent volume, one replica: see Application data on persistent volumes). It shows in italics with the others and the filter finds it, but the editor neither shows nor stores it: nobody can add or remove it, and it goes away when a scan no longer finds such data. The API returns people's tags only.

Everyone who can read the results filters the front page by them: the Tags row under the business units lists the tags of the applications shown, with how many have each. A tag, on that row or next to an application's name, shows only the applications with it, and the tiles, bars and groups count only those; Any (or the selected tag again) clears it. A tag filter and a business unit filter combine, and the address (/?bu=3&tag=pci) can be shared or bookmarked. The API returns the tags ("tags": ["pci", "wave 1"]) and filters by one (/api/v1/applications?tag=pci).

docs.title: Sign-in for the results pages (optional)
docs.text:
By default anyone who reaches the web UI over HTTPS can read the results. Set CONTAINERIZER_VIEWERS to limit that to named people (with CONTAINERIZER_ROLE_SOURCE=ui: CONTAINERIZER_VIEWERS_REQUIRED=true, and give the viewer role on Admin → Users and roles); admins, operators and product owners can always read. Opening a results page without a session then goes straight to the identity provider and back. People who match no list get a "not allowed" page, and the database is not read for them.

CONTAINERIZER_VIEW_AUDIT=true (needs CONTAINERIZER_VIEWERS, or CONTAINERIZER_VIEWERS_REQUIRED=true) records every sign-in, refused sign-in, results page opened and sign-out in the access log, which admins see on the admin pages. If a row cannot be written, the page is not shown, so a view is never left unrecorded. The access log is personal data: tell users their access is recorded, and keep it only as long as your policy says (deleting old rows needs the database owner).

docs.title: Session security
docs.text:
• Authorization code flow with PKCE (S256), state and nonce. The ID token's signature is verified with the provider's published keys, as are issuer, audience and expiry; unsigned and HMAC tokens are refused.
  • The session is a random id in an HttpOnly, SameSite=Lax, Secure, __Host- cookie, new at every sign-in, ending after 8 hours, 1 hour idle, or at sign-out. Sessions are kept in memory, so a restart signs everyone out.
  • Every form carries a per-session CSRF token and cross-site posts are refused by Origin. Responses carry a strict Content-Security-Policy (no inline script), X-Frame-Options: DENY, HSTS and no-store; errors are logged on the server and never shown.
  • The change history (business units, products, application mapping, scans, repositories, tokens, lab services, roles given on the admin pages, rule decisions) is written by database triggers, so even direct SQL changes are recorded. No database role of the web UI can update or delete audit or access log rows; forward them to your SIEM if they must be tamper-proof.

Grafana has its own sign-in: user admin with the password in /etc/containerizer/secrets/grafana-admin, or your identity provider through GF_AUTH_GENERIC_OAUTH_* (or GF_AUTH_AZUREAD_*, ...) settings in /etc/containerizer/grafana.env. Once a provider is enabled there (GF_AUTH_<provider>_ENABLED=true), the appliance hides Grafana's user name and password form and sends people straight to the provider (GF_AUTH_DISABLE_LOGIN_FORM=true, GF_AUTH_<provider>_AUTO_LOGIN=true; set either in grafana.env to choose yourself, e.g. GF_AUTH_DISABLE_LOGIN_FORM=false to sign in as admin again). The admin password still works for Grafana's API. Reboot after a change (the settings are worked out at start-up). Grafana's home page is the Containerizer: organization scans dashboard.

docs.title: Source control tokens and the LLM
docs.text:
Organization scans (scheduled-scans.md) read Azure DevOps, GitHub and GitLab organizations and push the generated files to an output Git repository. The tokens for both are registered by administrators under Admin → Source control & LLM, together with the LLM the scans ask (see The LLM below):

  • Organizations (read-only): one token for each Azure DevOps organization (or Azure DevOps Server collection), GitHub organization or GitLab group the scans may read, on the cloud service or a self-hosted server. This is the allow-list: a scan of an organization without a registered, enabled token does not run, and nothing is ever read anonymously.
  • Output repositories (write): one token for each repository the generated Dockerfiles, manifests and GitOps files are pushed to, matched by the repository's URL. The internal rules repository of the rule review gets its write token here too.
  • Package feeds: a token for each NuGet, npm or Maven/Gradle feed that needs a sign-in, which the builds of scanned code restore packages from (below). The builds never see it.

docs.title: How the tokens are protected
docs.text:
• Sealed for the worker. The moment a token is saved, the web UI seals it for the scan worker's public key (X25519 key agreement, HKDF-SHA256, AES-256-GCM). The web UI has only the public key, so it cannot open what it stored; only the worker, with the private key, opens a token, just before a run. The sealed token is bound to its purpose, provider, server and organization or repository: it does not open if it is moved to another row or another purpose in the database.
  • Never shown again. The page has a password field to enter a token and a button to replace it, nothing that shows it. The admin database role may write the sealed token but is not granted SELECT on it.
  • Audited, without the token. Adding, replacing (Token saved changes), enabling, disabling and removing a token are in the change history with who did it. The token itself is never copied there.
  • Only sent where it belongs.
  • The read-only token goes to its own server's API, and with the clone URLs of its own organization only (https://github.com/<org>/…, https://gitlab.com/<group>/…, https://dev.azure.com/<org>/… or https://<org>.visualstudio.com/…, or the self-hosted server's equivalent). A repository whose clone URL is elsewhere is refused. An API redirect or pagination link to another host does not get the token, and https is never followed down to http.
  • The write token is chosen by the output repository's URL, never by host or organization, and is only used to clone and push that repository. The output repository can therefore be in a scanned organization: it is never scanned itself, and the read-only token is never used to push.
  • Git gets each token as an http.<repository URL>.extraHeader in its environment, so it is valid for that one repository URL only, is not written to disk or the process list, and no credential helper sees it. Errors and logs are redacted.
  • Least privilege is checked where the provider allows it. The worker records on the page when a token last worked, and warns when a GitHub classic token has scopes that can write or a GitLab token has more than read_api / read_repository. Registering the same token as both an organization's read-only token and its output repository's write token is refused.
  • Admins only. The Source control page is for administrators; operators can schedule scans, but only of organizations an administrator registered.

docs.title: The sealing key
docs.text: The appliance makes the key pair at first boot: /etc/containerizer/secrets/credential-key for the worker and credential-key.pub for the web UI. Back up credential-key with the database: the registered tokens open only with it. A new key pair means entering every token again (the page marks tokens sealed for another key). Also allow each Git server's host on Admin → Firewall.

docs.title: Making the tokens
docs.text: Give every token an expiration date and enter the same date on the page: it warns 14 days before, and an expired token stops its scans with a clear message. Revoke a token where it was made when you replace or remove it here.

docs.title: Read-only token for an organization
docs.text:
Provider Token Permissions Server (self-hosted) GitHub Fine-grained personal access token: resource owner the organization, repository access All repositories Contents: Read-only and Metadata: Read-only, nothing else https://ghe.example.com/api/v3 GitLab Group access token on the group, role Reporter (on GitLab.com group tokens need Premium or Ultimate; otherwise a personal access token of a Reporter in the group) scopes read_api and read_repository https://gitlab.example.com Azure DevOps Personal access token for this organization only Custom defined: Code: Read and Project and Team: Read (scopes) https://tfs.example.com/tfs, the collection as the organization

Notes:

  • GitHub: no owner permissions needed. The scan lists and reads every repository the token's user can read, nothing more. What can need an owner is the organization's token policy: it can require approval of fine-grained tokens (until then they reach public repositories only) or forbid them. Without an owner's approval:
Token Reaches Fine-grained, resource owner the organization (above) every repository you can read when the policy lets members use them Classic, scope repo (with SAML SSO: Configure SSO → Authorize for the organization) every repository you can read, private and internal too can also write: the page warns; Containerizer only reads Classic, no scope at all public repositories only read-only

Leave Server empty for github.com (https://github.com works too: it means https://api.github.com). For GitHub Enterprise Server, give its API: https://ghe.example.com/api/v3. - GitLab: the organization is the group path; subgroups are included (acme covers acme/platform/*), or register a subgroup alone (acme/platform). - Azure DevOps is retiring PATs for All accessible organizations: make one per organization. Use a dedicated account that can read the repositories but not change them.

docs.title: Write token for an output repository
docs.text:
Provider Token Permissions GitHub A separate fine-grained personal access token with repository access Only select repositories: the output repository alone Contents: Read and write GitLab Project access token on the output project, role Developer (Maintainer if Developers may not push to the branch) scopes read_repository and write_repository Azure DevOps Personal access token of a dedicated account whose only Contribute permission is on the output repository (repository permissions) Code: Read & write

Enter the repository's https URL exactly as on the scan's Output repository (with or without .git).

docs.title: Package feeds
docs.text:
Applications that restore packages from a private feed (an internal NuGet feed on Azure Artifacts, npm packages on GitHub Packages, a Maven repository on Nexus) do not build without its credentials, and verification then reports Build failed. Register the feed under Admin → Source control & LLM → Package feeds: its kind (NuGet, npm, Maven or Gradle), its URL, a user name if the feed wants one, and a read-only token.

The token never enters a build, an image or the generated files. The scan worker (and the LLM queue runner, for refactoring orders) runs a small HTTPS proxy, the feed proxy, and hands its builds its address as HTTPS_PROXY, which dotnet, npm, Maven and Gradle use (the generated Dockerfiles pass a proxy on to Maven and Gradle themselves):

  • A connection to the host of a registered feed is opened by the proxy: it answers with a certificate of its own CA, checks the feed's real certificate itself, and adds Authorization to the requests whose URL is under the feed's URL: Basic with the user name and the token, or Bearer with the token alone when the user name is empty. Requests to other paths of that host get nothing. The builds trust the proxy's CA through the optional build secret ca the generated Dockerfiles already read for TLS-inspecting corporate proxies (the bundle holds the system's CAs, the corporate bundle if one is set, and the proxy's CA).
  • Connections to every other host pass through untouched (a plain tunnel).
  • The proxy refuses this machine's own addresses, loopback and link-local addresses, and the networks of Docker and the sandbox cluster, so it opens nothing to a build that the build could not reach itself. On the appliance the firewall lets Docker's bridges reach the proxies' ports (3128 for the scan worker, 3129 for the LLM queue runner, on the DNS filter's address) and nothing else on the host, and the feed's host must be on the Firewall page as before. Elsewhere it listens on docker0's address (CONTAINERIZER_FEED_PROXY_LISTEN=host:port to choose); a corporate HTTPS_PROXY of the worker is used upstream.

Which URL to register: the token goes with every request under it, so register the narrowest URL that still covers the downloads. Azure Artifacts downloads packages by the feed's id rather than its name, so register the organization's packaging URL, e.g. https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/contoso/ (or https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/contoso/project/ for a project-scoped feed). The repository's own nuget.config, .npmrc, pom.xml or build.gradle still names the feed as before; a credentials entry it has (for example %NUGET_PAT%) is replaced by the proxy's.

Feed Token User name Azure Artifacts Personal access token with Packaging: Read, for this organization any text, e.g. containerizer GitHub Packages Personal access token (classic) with read:packages the token's account (npm: empty) GitLab package registry Deploy token or group access token with read_package_registry the deploy token's user name Nexus, Artifactory, ProGet A read-only user's password or token the user

The page shows when a feed was last used and whether the feed accepted the token (Working, or Last use failed with the HTTP status). Yarn 2 and later (.yarnrc.yml) and the Maven wrapper's own download of Maven do not use HTTPS_PROXY: their feeds are not covered.

docs.title: NuGet source names
docs.text:
A NuGet.Config with package source mapping maps packages to a source by its name (<packageSource key="Contoso">). Often the repository does not define that source: the developers and build agents have it in their own user or machine NuGet.Config, under whatever name the project chose, so one feed may be internal in one repository and Contoso in another. A container build has none of those files, and restore cannot find the mapped packages (NU1100 ... PackageSourceMapping is enabled).

Give a NuGet feed the names projects use for it in NuGet source names, one source per line:

internal, Contoso, AzureArtifacts = https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/contoso/_packaging/main/nuget/v3/index.json
ContosoLegacy = https://pkgs.dev.azure.com/contoso/_packaging/legacy/nuget/v3/index.json

The URL is the source's own (index.json for v3), and must be under the feed's URL so the proxy signs its requests; a line of names alone means the feed's URL itself. A name belongs to one feed only (names compare case-insensitively, as NuGet's do).

Many repositories do not name the internal feed at all: no NuGet.Config, or one without package source mapping, and restore takes the feed from the machine's own NuGet.Config. In the container that ends with NU1101: No packages exist with this id in source(s): nuget.org. So the registered sources count as the machine's too.

For each .NET component the scan reads the NuGet.Config files of the project's folder and the folders above it, up to the repository's root, and the generated Dockerfile adds before restore (dotnet nuget add source; the URL only, never a token):

  • when the repository does not clear the sources (no <clear/> in <packageSources>): into the build's user-level NuGet.Config (/root/.nuget/NuGet/NuGet.Config), where a developer's machine has them,
    • the mapped names it does not define, with the URL registered under that name, or
    • without package source mapping: every registered NuGet source whose URL the repository does not have yet (each URL once, under the first name of its line);
  • when it clears them: only the mapped names it does not define, into its config nearest to the project (the user-level one does not count then). nuget.org needs no registration: it is added with its own URL when the <clear/> removed it.

MIGRATION.md lists what was added under NuGet package sources, so the real build pipeline gets it too, or you add the sources to the repository's NuGet.Config and the step goes. It also lists:

  • a mapped name no registered feed has: restore cannot find its packages until a feed gets the name or the repository defines the source;
  • a name whose URL is already a source of the repository under another name: NuGet uses a URL once (the first name wins), so it is not added, and its packages must be mapped to the other name.

docs.title: The LLM
docs.text:
Scans with Ask the LLM on consult an LLM about the components the rules are unsure of and the build or run failures no failure rule explains. Scans with LLM-heavy mode also let it translate, review and fix platform migrations; every call is counted on the Grafana dashboard. Set it once on the same page:

Kind Server Model API key Claude API empty, or the https URL of a gateway in front of it e.g. claude-sonnet-5-5 required: a key from the Claude Console, in a workspace only for Containerizer, with a spend limit OpenAI-compatible server (Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio, llama.cpp llama-server, LocalAI, TGI, ...) the URL up to and including /v1 the name the server knows optional; only sent over https, or plain http to the appliance itself

The key is sealed for the worker like the tokens and never shown again; the model can be changed without re-entering it, while a different server means removing it and adding it again. The worker hands the setting to the AI code for the run only, never through its environment, so the git and docker processes a scan starts never see the key. Allow the server's host on Admin → Firewall.

Several LLMs at once. More than one LLM can be registered: a GPU server, a CPU server, the Claude API. Each one has an Order, Jobs up to (the biggest LLM call it takes, in estimated input tokens; 0: any size) and Requests at once. The LLM queue gives each LLM call of a job to the first LLM in the order that takes the call's size and has a free request, and they all answer at the same time: put the small, cheap servers first with a size limit and a big one last with any size. A review, an egress or a link review is one call, so the limit is the job's size; a refactoring order makes one call per file (and per repair round), each of its own size, which may go to different LLMs. A job whose estimated size no LLM takes waits (the LLM queue page warns about it). On the appliance the built-in LLM can join the list too (LLM queue → Settings: its order and the biggest call it takes), with one request per server it runs. Scans that ask the LLM directly, outside the queue, use the first LLM in the order. Two LLMs on the same server need different hosts (one registration per server). See how jobs and LLM requests are scheduled.

Example Order Jobs up to At once Built-in LLM (CPU, two NUMA nodes) 10 4,000 tokens 2 (its servers) A CPU server with a bigger model 20 15,000 tokens 1 A GPU server 30 any size 4

The appliance's built-in LLM. Without an LLM server of your own, the appliance can run one on its CPU: Qwen3-Coder 30B-A3B with llama.cpp, turned on under Admin → Source control & LLM (off by default; it needs a machine with at least 40 GB of memory, see Running the appliance). Scans with Ask the LLM use it when no LLM is set on that page; an LLM set there is used instead, unless the built-in LLM has a place in the LLM queue's order (see Several LLMs at once above). Expect about 7 to 12 tokens per second and a few minutes per answer: fine for the components the rules are unsure of, too slow for LLM-heavy mode. Use the queued LLM mode for organization scans where it is offered, so the scans do not wait for each answer.

Choosing a model. The quality of the fallback follows the quality of the model. With a self-hosted server, use the largest instruction-tuned model your hardware serves comfortably, ideally one that knows .NET well (a 30B+ Qwen, Llama, Mistral or DeepSeek model). Smaller models propose more wrong regexes; the scan keeps only ones that compile, do not match trivial code and fire on the code they were learned from, and an administrator still reviews every learned rule (rule review).

How answers are kept reliable.

  • The rules stay first: the LLM never decides alone what the rules are sure of.
  • Every request carries the JSON schema of the answer, as response_format (which Ollama, vLLM, LM Studio and llama.cpp enforce with constrained decoding) and in the prompt. A server that refuses json_schema gets json_object, then plain text.
  • Every answer is checked against the schema. An invalid answer is retried once with the errors listed; a second one is an error, and the component keeps the rules' verdict. <think> blocks of reasoning models are ignored.
  • A self-hosted server that is restarting or still loading its model (connection refused or reset, HTTP 429, 502, 503 or 504) is retried with growing waits, for up to 10 minutes in all (CONTAINERIZER_LLM_RETRY_SECONDS), so a restart does not cost the scan its answers. Timeouts and other errors are not retried: the component keeps the rules' verdict.
  • Requests use temperature: 0 and answers are cached by prompt, model and server, so runs repeat.
  • The LLM never runs commands or edits the application: it returns JSON, and build-plan patches are limited to an allow-list of plan keys. What it proposes is recorded with source: ai and the model.

What it sees. Evidence packs contain source code excerpts, project files and the README of the assessed application. A self-hosted server keeps them inside your network.

docs.title: Queued LLM reviews
docs.text:
A self-hosted LLM on CPUs can take five minutes or more per answer, which would hold up every scan. Set LLM reviews on the scan (Admin → Organization scans) to Queued and the scan asks the LLM nothing while it runs: the rules decide, and the questions go to the LLM queue instead (Admin → LLM queue, organization scans). The queue runner answers them when the queue's settings let it, for example at night or only while no scan runs.

In queued mode the scan does not ask the LLM about build or run failures, dev databases, platform migrations or the sandbox tester either, so LLM-heavy mode needs inline reviews.

docs.title: LLM-heavy for a while
docs.text:
When one application, or one of its components, needs the LLM's full attention for a while (a migration being worked on, a component the rules keep getting wrong), an administrator turns LLM-heavy mode on for it on its page (Admin → Applications → the application → LLM-heavy mode): the whole application or one component, for 1 hour to 7 days.

Until it ends:

  • its LLM jobs of every kind need no approval: those waiting are approved at once, new ones are queued approved (automatic: LLM-heavy until …);
  • they go before every other job in the queue, whatever their priority or position;
  • scans with queued LLM reviews queue a review of every component it covers, not only the uncertain ones and the second opinions (reason LLM-heavy; the answer changes a verdict when the LLM is at least 0.85 sure, as for a second opinion);

  • scans run LLM-heavy mode for it (platform migrations and the sandbox tester ask the LLM as often as they need, even in a scan with queued reviews) when the appliance allows LLM-heavy mode (CZ_LLM_HEAVY=true) and the scan has Ask the LLM on. These calls are made during the scan, as for a scan in LLM-heavy mode.

  • a Make it A order of the whole application keeps going, one order after another, until its patched copy runs in the sandbox or the window ends;

  • a refactoring order of chosen findings (of the whole application, or of the component the window is on) makes up to 40 LLM calls instead of 8 and keeps going, with repairs and the findings left, until every finding is fixed and the patched copy builds and runs, or the window ends.

Scan its repository now (ticked by default) starts a scan of its repository at once, so the reviews are queued without waiting for the schedule. The windows open now are listed on the application's page and on the LLM queue page (LLM-heavy now), each with End now; their jobs then take their usual place again. Turning a window on or ending it is in the audit log.

Each job's page shows the question sent, the answer with its reasoning per finding, and the actual tokens and time against the estimate:

What is queued. The components an inline scan would ask about (server and platform components the rules are less than 85 % sure of) are queued as uncertain. Server and platform components the rules rate blocker or rewrite with confidence are queued too, as a second opinion. Each gets a priority; the runner takes the highest first, and administrators can move any job:

Priority Uncertain 1000 + 400 × (1 − the rules' confidence) Second opinion 0 + 400 × (1 − the rules' confidence) Both: the component keeps no state and only its verdict keeps it from rating A + 300 Both: a server component (not a Windows platform product) + 100

So every uncertain review comes before every second opinion, the less sure the rules the sooner, and a review whose answer can get a component deployed comes first.

How an answer takes effect. The queue keeps the exact question the scan would have asked. The runner asks it with the same model, so the answer is stored in the answer cache under the same key as an inline answer. The answer shows on the queue page at once, and on the component in the results pages. The next scan of the repository asks the same question, finds the answer (in the cache, or in the queue) without calling the LLM, and applies it as an inline scan would: the component's verdict changes when the LLM is at least 0.6 sure and disagrees with the rules (0.85 for a second opinion, as it goes against rules that were sure). Assessments already stored never change. Re-scan now on the queue page scans a repository whose reviews are all answered, without waiting for the schedule. When the code or the rules change before the answer, the next scan asks a new question and the old one is skipped as superseded. Changing the LLM (another server or model) means new questions too.

The command line does the same with --ai-queue (with --ai, on assess, analyze and org): with --sql or CONTAINERIZER_SQL the jobs go to the same queue; without SQL Server they are written to llm-queue.json in the output folder (--work-dir for org), and containerizer llm-queue --file <that file> answers them once each, in queue order. Run the command again afterwards to apply the answers.

Kinds of jobs. The queue holds every kind of LLM job; the page filters by kind:

Kind Queued by Priority Result Component review (review) a scan with queued LLM reviews as above the LLM's verdict, applied by the next scan Refactoring (refactor) a person, on a B-rated application's results page, or containerizer refactor --queue 1800: before the automatic reviews (move it like any job) a refactoring patch, verified by building and running it Make it A (refactor, goal rating-a) a person, on a B-rated application's results page, or an administrator for every B app (Make it A: every B application, smallest first) 1800, as a refactoring one patch for every finding, repaired and assessed again in a loop; a sandbox variant when the patched copy rates A

A refactoring asks the LLM once per file it changes (at most 8), so it is a long job; its estimate is made from the size of what it will send, and the output tokens are learned per kind like the reviews'. While it runs, the queue page says how far it is (generating, verifying, deploying; for Make it A also the pass and the repair round), and the job links to its patch page (Admin → Refactoring). A Make it A order makes up to 16 LLM calls.

docs.title: How jobs and LLM requests are scheduled
docs.text:
The queue holds LLM work and other work side by side: a refactoring order spends most of its time building, running and assessing its patched copy and deploying its sandbox variant, and a rebuild or an order whose answers are reused from other orders makes no LLM call at all. The runner keeps two limits apart:

  • Jobs at once (LLM queue → Settings; 0, the default: automatic, every LLM request at once of the LLMs in the order plus one): how many jobs it works on at the same time, whatever they do. A build takes CPU and memory, as does the appliance's built-in LLM on a CPU, so the automatic number stays modest; raise it on a big machine with a GPU LLM elsewhere, lower it when builds and the built-in LLM slow each other down.
  • Requests at once of each LLM (Admin → Source control & LLM, and Parallel requests for the built-in LLM or the worker's own LLM settings): an LLM call takes one only while it is answered, and gives it back at once. A job that builds, verifies or deploys holds none.

The runner starts the jobs in the queue's order (LLM-heavy first, then priority and the administrators' moves) while a job slot is free and the hours, idle check and pause allow it. A job whose estimate needs the LLM starts only when an LLM that takes its size has a request no call is waiting for and no job just started is about to use; until then the jobs after it that need no LLM start in its place, so work without LLM calls does not wait for an LLM, and LLM work does not wait for builds while an LLM is free. Each call of a running job goes to the first LLM in the order that takes the call's size and has a free request; when none is free, the call waits, and waiting calls are answered in the order their jobs started. An answer already in the cache needs no request.

On the queue page a running job says what it does now: Asking and the LLM while one of its calls is answered, Waiting for an LLM while a call waits for a request, else Running with its progress (generating, verifying, deploying). The LLMs table shows the requests in progress on each (Asking now). The speed statistics are learned per call: each LLM's figures come from the calls it answered (their size, tokens and time, and the requests at once on it), not from the job's time with its builds.
